items.title: Fridges in French supermarkets hit by cyber attack
items.summary: Hundreds of stores were targeted by the overnight hack, which spoiled fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.
items.body:
Fridges in French supermarkets hit by cyber attack
- Published
Hundreds of French supermarkets have been hit by a cyber attack that caused their fridges and freezers to heat up, spoiling fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.
Hackers reportedly gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units, forcing some to warm to 50C (120F) overnight.
The chief executive of CoopÃ©rative U said several of its supermarkets had been hit by the "extremely serious and unprecedented" attack.
More than 100 of the chain's supermarkets were targeted, while at least 300 stores from IntermarchÃ© and its Netto brand were affected, according to the AFP news agency.
IntermarchÃ© said its fridges had heated up to 50C for six hours overnight into Monday, and the retailer had thrown away all the affected food to avoid health risks, the Reuters news agency reported.
Some supermarket staff reportedly said they were hit by waves of hot air when they opened freezer units on Monday morning.
French broadcaster BFMTV published an image showing a freezer in an ice cream aisle displaying a temperature of 26.5C.
Two supermarkets in the Alsace region reported losses of â¬270,000 (Â£228,000) between them, the broadcaster added, meaning the nationwide total could run into the millions.
The Paris prosecutor's office told AFP it had opened an investigation into the incident, which it called a "large-scale cyber-attack affecting the refrigerators of several major food retail chains across France".
Eoropean Food Commissioner Christophe Hansen condemned the hack in a post on X and added: "Food security requires more attention at all levels. Because the weaponisation of food has become a reality."
The full scale of the attack is so far unclear.
Reports in specialist retail and local media said stores from other food giants, including Carrefour, E.Leclerc and Monoprix, were also attacked. BBC News has approached the supermarket chains for comment.
In a post on X, CoopÃ©rative chief executive Dominique Schelcher said staff were "fully mobilised, in co-ordination with refrigeration specialists, to restore the situation as quickly as possible".
He called for an investigation into the hack and said targeting equipment essential to the French food supply was "unacceptable".

items.title: Asos hackers claim responsibility for Air France-KLM data breach
items.summary: The group behind the hack of fast-fashion retailer Asos have claimed responsibility for a data breach of airline group Air France-KLM, City AM can reveal. The individuals who claimed responsibility for the Asos data breach, who call themselves Xuanye Group, last week circulated data which they claimed was obtained from the airline group.  Air France-KLM [...]
items.body:
Asos hackers claim responsibility for Air France-KLM data breach
The group behind the hack of fast-fashion retailer Asos have claimed responsibility for a data breach of airline group Air France-KLM, City AM can reveal.
The individuals who claimed responsibility for the Asos data breach, who call themselves Xuanye Group, last week circulated data which they claimed was obtained from the airline group.
Air France-KLM confirmed to City AM that it recently detected a data breach. A spokesperson for the airline said: “The Air France-KLM Group continuously monitors all applications and data it uses for both its customers and employees.
“Although protected by mandatory multi-factor authentication (MFA) , the group’s IT teams recently detected unauthorised access to internal folders that did at this stage, not contain any sensitive data.
“This incident does not affect customers, service continuity, or the interfaces between Air France-KLM’s information systems and those of its partners and suppliers.
“The IT departments immediately secured the affected folders and files and notified the relevant authorities of these attempted accesses.”
On messaging app Telegram, Xuanye Group posted a screenshot of a number of files relating to Air France-KLM, which appeared to be owned by a number of former and current employees of the airline group.
Xuanye Group told City AM that the files relate to Air France-KLM.
Air France-KLM is listed on the Euronext stock exchange in Paris and Amsterdam. The group was formed in a merger of the two flag carriers in 2004.
Air France-KLM was the subject of a cyberattack in August last year, when another hacker group named ShinyHunters gained access to a third-party customer service platform used by the airline’s contact centers.
Hackers tricked Asos employee
Xuanye Group claimed responsibility for the Asos data breach last week, in which a notification was published from the e-commerce firm’s mobile app, threatening a leak of customer data.
The notification read: “Dear ASOS DPO and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance. Engage with us, or we will leak it,” and included a link to the Telegram channel where the Air France-KLM data was later shared.
On the social messaging app, the group said it had obtained customer information which is “safe” on their server and “will not be touched for a designated period”.
Asos said last week that the hackers gained access to the company’s platforms by posing as a “trusted contact” and tricking an employee into giving them their login details.
The company said it immediately locked down its platforms to prevent further activity and has referred the incident to “the relevant law enforcement and regulatory authorities”.
Claims are circulating online that ShinyHunters last week hacked into fast fashion retailer H&M, the Times has reported, though the Swedish company said it has not detected a breach.
A spokesperson for H&M said: “We are aware of information circulating online regarding a potential cyber security incident and are currently investigating the claims. To date, we have not found any indications that our IT environment has been compromised.”

items.title: HMV to close 'unsustainable' Oxford Street store just three years after reopening its flagship site
items.summary: HMV plans to close its flagship Oxford Street store just three years after reopening the site, blaming landlords for doubling its rent.
items.body:
HMV to close 'unsustainable' Oxford Street store just three years after reopening its flagship site
HMV plans to close its Oxford Street store just three years after reopening the flagship site, blaming landlords for doubling its rent.
The entertainment and music chain said it plans to leave 363 Oxford Street in March next year but vowed to keep a 'significant presence' in London as it searches for a new store in the West End.
It said landlords had proposed doubling the rent and is facing a 'substantial' bill for renovation works, which made it 'commercially unsustainable' to keep its doors open.
HMV first opened the site in 1921 and over the years has hosted performances and signings from the likes of Sir Paul McCartney and David Bowie.
It closed in 2019 after the chain fell into administration before reopening in November 2023 as Canadian Doug Putman, who also owns the Toys R Us chain, rescued it from insolvency.
Managing director Phil Halliday said: 'This is a special store, it's where we began 100 years ago and bringing it back to life in 2023 was a big moment in our recent history.
'It's frustrating that it has been made commercially unviable. However, we are looking ahead, and our focus is now on what we do to make exciting steps for HMV in 2027.'
Unsustainable: HMV will close its flagship Oxford Street next spring
HMV said it would look to transfer its 50 employees to its two other London stores and head office as it looks for a new shop.
It came as the chain, which has 123 stores across the UK, reported a 15 per cent uptick in sales in the first nine months of the year.
Revenues for shops and online trading are set to reach £240million, up from £212million in 2025.
Once seen as a casualty of online music streaming, HMV has enjoyed a renaissance, thanks to a revival in demand for physical CDs and vinyl in recent years.
Halliday said: 'We hope to redeploy affected team members through other London stores and head office roles and are exploring ways to minimise the impact on jobs while we seek a new flagship site.'
'We're actively looking for a new location in the West End and are determined to give London a store that music fans can be proud of,' he added.
The HMV boss has been vocal in his criticism of the Government's tax raids. Halliday told the Daily Mail last year that high street operators had paid more than online rivals such as Amazon and Apple.
'That burden should be more evenly spread. In the High Street we have had our share of the tax rises, and we would hope that they look somewhere else.'

items.title: M&S boss tells Healey: Take the handcuffs off business and get Britain growing - as he savages Labour's 'crushing' tax policies just weeks ahead of first Burnham Budget
items.summary: In a landmark intervention, Stuart Machin branded Labour's previous efforts 'disasters' and 'a crushing disappointment for customers, colleagues and businesses'.
items.body:
M&S boss tells Healey: Take the handcuffs off business and get Britain growing - as he savages Labour's 'crushing' tax policies just weeks ahead of first Burnham Budget
The boss of Marks & Spencer has urged John Healey to reverse 'the mistakes of the last two Budgets' to get Britain growing again.
In a landmark intervention, Stuart Machin branded Labour's previous efforts 'disasters' and 'a crushing disappointment for customers, colleagues and businesses'.
Writing in the Daily Mail, he says the new Chancellor must 'restore hope' within industry and 'get Britain growing by taking the handcuffs off business and putting money back in people's pockets'.
The damning assessment from one of the country's top chief executives will set alarm bells ringing in Downing Street less than three weeks before the first Budget of Andy Burnham's premiership.
Mr Machin was backed by other prominent figures as he warned rising taxes and other costs had pushed up the cost of doing business – which in turn has led to higher prices.
The man who dresses and feeds middle England and beyond highlighted the 'disastrous' National Insurance tax raid on employers as well as the threat to Saturday jobs posed by Angela Rayner's new rights for workers.
Mr Machin also attacked 'patently ridiculous' new recycling rules, a £2billion packaging tax, and the broken business rates system.
Other business leaders told the Mail that Britain needed 'a job–creation Budget' following Rachel Reeves' 'smash–and–grab raid' on enterprise.
M&S boss Stuart Machin with then-Chancellor Rachel Reeves and a long serving M&S staff member. In a landmark intervention, Mr Machin branded Labour's previous budgets 'disasters' and 'a crushing disappointment for customers, colleagues and businesses'
Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey's budget is due on October 28. Writing in the Daily Mail, Mr Machin says the new Chancellor must 'restore hope' within industry
The former chancellor, who was sacked by Mr Burnham, announced £75billion of tax rises in just two years at the Treasury – hammering households and businesses and leaving the economy on its knees.
City grandee Sir Martin Sorrell said 'we need real growth policies as opposed to statements about the importance of growth'.
He took a swipe at the Prime Minister's use of social media to drum up support, saying: 'Andy Burnham has said he is going to take the tough decisions and there are plenty of TikTok videos saying he is going to take them. We will see on October 28 if he does.'
The comments echo those of former Bank of England chief economist Andy Haldane, a one–time adviser to Mr Burnham, who last month said the PM was running what looks like 'a traditional tax–and–spend socialist government with better TikTok videos'.
Sir Martin also warned a 'political and social dislike of wealth creation' was driving top taxpayers out of Britain after analysis showed billionaires with £120billion to their names had fled since Labour came to power.
'High taxation discourages people from building businesses in the UK,' he said. And John Lewis boss Jason Tarry warned a tax raid on large shops such as department stores and supermarkets would 'only harm our high streets' by triggering closures.
He called for a 'clear commitment in the Budget' that 'no high street shop should face higher taxes'.
The flurry of interventions came just days after Jeremy Clarkson, the former Top Gear presenter turned farmer and publican, blasted Labour's treatment of farming and enterprise and asked: 'Why would anybody set up a business in this country right now?'
At the Conservative Party conference this week, leader Kemi Badenoch compared the Tories to the high street staple, telling the faithful: 'M&S is back in fashion. Great looks at affordable prices.
Rachel Reeve during her first budget on October 30 2024. In this budget, Ms Reeves raised the levy from 13.8 per cent to 15 per cent and cut the threshold at which it kicks in from £9,100 to £5,000 – costing business £25billion
The budget in two weeks time will be the first of Andy Burnham's premiership
'They have adapted their style for today's market and people are flooding back, including me as you've probably noticed this week.
'Just like M&S, we must learn from our mistakes, win back trust, and make people feel good about our party again.'
Mr Healey is facing a tough balancing act in his first Budget as Britain is battered on the global bond markets.
The cost of borrowing for the UK Government hit a 28–year high this week and is higher than any other country in the G7 – underlining concern among international investors over Labour's tax and spending plans.
Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey this week fired off a pre–Budget warning that the Chancellor must balance the books before the bond markets 'begin to doubt the fiscal trajectory'.
Mr Machin said: 'I've never hidden what I thought of the last two Budgets. They were a disaster. Britain needed a plan for growth and got a pile of new taxes and regulations instead.
'I know money is tight. I'm not asking the Chancellor to rip up his fiscal rules. But at the very least, he should start unravelling the mistakes of the last two Budgets.'
Mr Machin highlighted the 'disastrous' rise in National Insurance contributions paid by business that has driven up the cost of employing staff – leading to job losses and recruitment freezes.
In her first Budget, Ms Reeves raised the levy from 13.8 per cent to 15 per cent and cut the threshold at which it kicks in from £9,100 to £5,000 – costing business £25billion. 'It hit shops hard, because so many of our jobs are entry–level and part–time, often just a shift or two a week,' Mr Machin said.
Mr Machin has also highlighted the threat to Saturday jobs posed by Angela Rayner's new rights for workers
'It also hit our suppliers, particularly in farming and food manufacturing, and strict regulations meant most of those costs ended up with retailers.
'These pressures were always going to be felt at the till.' Pointing to his own start – a Saturday job 'pushing trolleys' aged 16 – Mr Machin also warned of the huge damage Labour's workers' rights Act could do to employment prospects for the young.
He said the Government must 'make sure the Employment Rights Act doesn't ban the Saturday job by treating normal weekend shifts as 'low hours' contracts'. Steve Perez, founder of Hooch and VK drinks maker Global Brands, said: 'Rachel Reeves mounted a smash–and–grab raid on business and we need to see that approach reversed.'
Mr Perez added: 'If the Government genuinely wants growth, it needs to stop adding costs and start making it easier for businesses to invest, employ and expand.' Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith said 'businesses and families are continuing the pay the price' of Labour's tax hikes.
He added: 'John Healey must give businesses a break and end the uncertainty by ruling out yet more tax rises in his Budget this month.'
Here are my six ways Healey can get Britain growing again
By Stuart Machin
I've never hidden what I thought of the last two Budgets – they were a disaster.
Britain needed a plan for growth and got a pile of new taxes and regulations instead.
At M&S, we were left facing £150million of new costs each year, on top of a tax bill of around half a billion pounds.
Attention is now turning to the next Budget, the first by Chancellor John Healey. I have written to him directly to set out what needs to change, and why it can't wait.
Last month the Prime Minister promised Britain 'hope again'. It struck a chord, and you can see why. People want to believe things can get better. But the speech left big questions unanswered, above all what it means for business and the economy in the coming year.
I was glad to hear the Chancellor reference growth 16 times in his conference speech. He said it's 'the only long–term answer'. He's right. Now the Budget must match his words.
Retail has a big part to play. It's the engine of the everyday economy, employing more than three million people and keeping customers supplied with what they need. But margins are wafer thin. When the Government piles on costs, there is very little room to soak them up.
At M&S, we're investing over £2billion in the next three years across our stores, supply chain and technology. But every pound that goes on new taxes is a pound we can't invest. I know money is tight. I'm not asking the Chancellor to rip up his fiscal rules. But at the very least, he should start unravelling the mistakes of the past two Budgets.
So here are six ways John Healey could get Britain growing by taking the handcuffs off business and putting money back in people's pockets. The first three wouldn't even cost the Treasury a penny.
Writing for the Daily Mail, Mr Machin has laid out six ways John Healey could get Britain growing by taking the handcuffs off business and putting money back in people's pockets. The first three wouldn't even cost the Treasury a penny
First, scrap the upcoming Deposit Return Scheme – it's patently ridiculous. Next October, you'll pay 20p more for every bottle or can of drink. To get it back, you'll have to lug bags of empties back to the shops – despite already paying your council for collections.
And stores need to rip out shelves to make space for monstrous recycling machines. Retailers are spending tens of millions just to set it up, and will pay millions more every year to run the scheme.
Second, make sure the Employment Rights Act doesn't ban the Saturday job by treating normal weekend shifts as 'low hours' contracts. The Chancellor spoke recently about his first job, washing pots in a pub.
Mine was pushing trolleys at 16. With nearly a million young people out of work or training, don't let the small print pull up the ladder.
Third, get a food and drink deal with the EU over the line. It's common sense. Cut the red tape with our nearest neighbours, so the European food we love costs less to bring in, and our brilliant British farmers can sell more abroad. Every month it's delayed, farmers and shoppers pay the price.
Fourth, undo the most damaging part of the disastrous rise in National Insurance: The cut to the threshold where employers start paying. It hit shops hard, because so many of our jobs are entry–level and part–time, often just a shift or two a week.
It also hit our suppliers, particularly in farming and food manufacturing, and strict regulations meant most of those costs ended up with retailers. These pressures were always going to be felt at the till.
Fifth, fix business rates. Retail makes up around 5 per cent of the economy but pays more than a fifth of all business rates.
That's not sustainable. M&S alone pays around £170million a year. It's right to support the pubs, bars and music venues on high streets that bring our towns to life. But if you do that by taxing supermarkets, you're paying for a cheaper pint by loading costs on to the weekly shop.
Sixth, get rid of the packaging tax. Extended Producer Responsibility was sold as an investment in recycling, but it's nothing of the sort.
It's a tax of almost £2billion on food and drink, and even the official forecasters at the OBR now treat it as one. In April, M&S had to pay an extra £40million in one go. Scrap it, and shoppers will feel the difference.
The past two Budgets were a crushing disappointment for customers, colleagues and businesses. Now there's a new Chancellor and a new chance.
The Prime Minister has promised 'hope again' and given us ideas for the next Parliament. But the Chancellor needs to restore hope among British businesses, and tell us what he'll do now.

items.title: The £10 Scratchcard returns: what Allwyn’s new pilot means for retailers

Seven years after £10 National Lottery scratchcards were withdrawn over gambling-harm concerns, the price point has returned to selected UK shops. Allwyn’s new When It’s Gold Outside game offers four £4 million top prizes and pays retailers 60p for each card sold, with a Christmas marketing campaign planned to support sales. The higher-priced product gives […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Seven years after £10 National Lottery scratchcards were withdrawn over gambling-harm concerns, the price point has returned to selected UK shops. Allwyn’s new When It’s Gold Outside game offers four £4 million top prizes and pays retailers 60p for each card sold, with a Christmas marketing campaign planned to support sales.
The higher-priced product gives retailers an opportunity to earn more commission per transaction, but its return is taking place through a monitored pilot rather than an unrestricted national rollout.
For shop owners, the important questions are whether the game generates additional business, how it affects existing scratchcard sales and whether the necessary player-protection measures can be maintained.
A premium scratchcard returns to the counter
Allwyn began introducing When It’s Gold Outside to selected National Lottery retailers in September 2026, marking the return of the £10 scratchcard after its withdrawal in 2019.
The new game offers four £4 million jackpots, doubling the previous highest scratchcard top prize of £2 million. Each card includes 37 opportunities to win, with prizes starting at £10 and additional tiers of £15 and £20.
Those 37 opportunities are part of the game’s design, rather than 37 independent chances of winning the jackpot.
The scratchcard comes in a larger format with metallic gold detailing, intended to distinguish it from lower-priced products at the counter. Cards are supplied in packs of 30, giving participating stores £300 worth of stock per pack at retail selling prices.
Allwyn is positioning the product as a premium purchase ahead of Christmas, when scratchcards are also promoted as gifts.
However, a larger jackpot and higher price do not automatically translate into stronger retailer performance. Much depends on how customers respond to the product and whether it attracts spending that would not otherwise have occurred.
What 60p commission means for retailers
The most immediate commercial benefit is the commission attached to each sale.
Retailers receive 60p for every £10 scratchcard sold, equivalent to 6% of the selling price. Selling an entire 30-card pack would therefore generate £18 in gross commission from £300 in scratchcard sales.
That provides a straightforward measure of potential income, although commission should not be confused with net profit after the costs of running a shop.
Allwyn has also confirmed that prizes ranging from £50 to £500 can be paid out in participating stores, creating opportunities to earn additional commission for handling eligible prize payments.
The more difficult question is whether the new game increases total sales.
A customer purchasing one £10 scratchcard may previously have bought two £5 cards or several lower-priced games. In that situation, the higher transaction value does not necessarily mean the retailer has gained additional spending.
Alternatively, the premium product could attract customers who would not otherwise have purchased a scratchcard, particularly during the Christmas gifting period.
Those two outcomes would have very different implications for store profitability.
Retailers will also need to consider stock turnover and whether the larger card earns enough to justify the display space allocated to it.
The pilot has not yet produced publicly available store-level figures demonstrating incremental sales, additional retailer earnings or displacement of existing scratchcard products.
Until those results are available, the 60p commission establishes the earning potential of each sale, not the overall commercial success of the new game.
Christmas marketing could increase its visibility
Allwyn is supporting the launch through a combination of in-store activity and local advertising.
Its plans include digital advertising displays near participating retailers, promotional materials within shops and a festive campaign presenting When It’s Gold Outside as a potential Christmas gift.
For convenience stores and newsagents, this could increase awareness of the scratchcard among shoppers who visit primarily to purchase other products.
A prominent display can introduce the game to customers already using the store, while advertising nearby may encourage some additional visits.
The seasonal timing is significant. Scratchcards have an established role in Christmas gifting, and the £10 format gives Allwyn a higher-priced product to promote alongside its existing range.
However, the potential benefit depends on actual customer behaviour.
There is no published evidence yet that the marketing activity has increased store footfall, average basket values or overall National Lottery sales.
Availability is also limited to participating retailers during the pilot. That could affect how consistently customers encounter the product and how much individual stores benefit from national awareness.
The commercial test will be whether the Christmas campaign delivers additional sales rather than simply shifting demand between existing scratchcard products.
Why £10 scratchcards were withdrawn in 2019
The return of the £10 price point is particularly notable because the previous National Lottery operator, Camelot, removed scratchcards in that category from retail sale in September 2019.
The decision followed concerns about their association with problem gambling.
In March 2020, the government confirmed in a parliamentary response that Camelot had withdrawn the products after evidence suggested a relationship between higher-priced scratchcards and gambling-related harm.
That evidence did not establish that purchasing a £10 scratchcard directly caused gambling problems. Nevertheless, it raised sufficient concerns for the operator to take precautionary action.
The latest launch has therefore required more than an ordinary product approval.
In July 2026, the Gambling Commission varied Allwyn’s National Lottery licence to permit a controlled pilot of £10 scratchcards beginning in September.
The regulator assessed whether the new product could be licensed and whether appropriate safeguards were in place to protect participants.
Its decision considered the potential contribution to National Lottery Good Causes alongside the risks associated with higher-priced games.
The Commission concluded that the pilot could proceed with suitable controls, monitoring and evaluation.
It has also stated that Allwyn must continue assessing possible gambling harm throughout the trial.
The decision is not evidence that the higher-priced product presents no risk. It is permission to test the game under the regulatory arrangements approved for the pilot.
A higher price puts retail safeguards to the test
The £10 scratchcard also introduces practical responsibilities for retailers.
National Lottery products can only be purchased by people aged 18 or over. Allwyn has additionally reminded participating stores that customers must not be sold more than ten scratchcards during a single visit.
When all ten are £10 cards, that represents £100 in one visit.
These controls differ from the account-based systems used by online gambling operators. Digital players can access deposit limits, time-outs and self-exclusion measures, explained in guidance on how to gamble responsibly, while a customer purchasing a physical scratchcard is subject to safeguards applied at the retail counter.
That makes staff training and consistent enforcement particularly important.
Allwyn’s Operation Guardian mystery-shopping programme provides evidence of how retailers have performed against existing requirements.
During 2025, the programme conducted 16,298 store visits across age-verification, excessive-play and staff-knowledge assessments.
Retailers correctly challenged customers for identification in 93.5% of first age-verification visits, the highest result reported by Allwyn.
Performance was lower for scratchcard purchase restrictions. In visits examining excessive play, 80.7% of retailers correctly enforced the existing limit of ten scratchcards per transaction.
The results suggest that age checks are more consistently applied than purchase restrictions, although both measures require continued attention.
Allwyn has been carrying out face-to-face visits and distributing additional guidance to retailers involved in the new pilot. Mystery-shopping checks will continue.
For stores stocking the £10 game, the challenge is to accommodate a higher-value product without allowing sales targets or promotional activity to undermine responsible-selling procedures.
One operator, thousands of retail counters
The National Lottery’s retail structure also shapes how the pilot operates.
Allwyn holds the National Lottery licence and determines the scratchcard’s design, game conditions, retailer commission and participant-protection framework. Individual shops sell the product as authorised retail partners rather than operating separate lottery businesses.
This differs from commercial online gambling groups, where one company may operate several consumer-facing brands. Directories such as Sisters Network UK document these related casino businesses, but the National Lottery model involves one licensed operator distributing its products through thousands of independent retail outlets.
For participating shops, that means the £10 game is sold under centrally established conditions.
Retailers cannot alter the jackpot, introduce different wagering terms or independently change the commission attached to the product.
Their commercial decisions instead concern stock management, display space and how the scratchcard fits within the wider shop offer.
They must also apply the age-verification and purchase restrictions communicated by Allwyn.
The pilot’s results will therefore depend both on the performance of a nationally developed product and on how effectively participating stores manage it.
What would make the pilot a success?
The commercial results will become clearer as Allwyn collects information from participating retailers.
Sales per store and commission earned will be important, but those figures alone will not provide a complete assessment.
The operator will also need to understand whether the £10 game attracts additional customer spending or replaces purchases of cheaper scratchcards.
Stock turnover, sales during the Christmas campaign and any additional income from eligible prize payments could help establish its contribution to retailers.
Player-protection outcomes are equally important.
The Gambling Commission has made monitoring part of the pilot approval, including assessing the potential for excessive play and whether the controls operate effectively.
A rise in sales accompanied by weaker purchase-limit compliance would present a different outcome from one delivering sustainable retailer income while maintaining appropriate safeguards.
The contribution to National Lottery Good Causes will also form part of the wider assessment.
There is currently no confirmed decision to extend the pilot to every National Lottery retailer or make £10 scratchcards a permanent part of the retail range.
For shop owners, the immediate attraction is clear: a premium product with a 60p commission per sale, a substantial advertised jackpot and marketing support during the Christmas period.
Whether it represents a worthwhile long-term addition depends on evidence still being collected.
The return of the £10 scratchcard could deliver additional income for participating stores, but a higher selling price is not the same as higher profitability.
Its broader future will depend on whether the pilot generates new business, provides meaningful returns for retailers and meets the player-protection standards required of National Lottery products.

items.body:
Indian single malt whisky brand Indri Trini is launching at selected Tesco stores and online this week. Made by Piccadily Distilleries and distributed in the UK by Mangrove Global, part of the SPIRIBAM Group, the 50cl bottle will be available in 157 Tesco stores for £34 RRP.
Nick Gillett, managing director of Mangrove Global, said: “Small format bottles have moved out of convenience and into the multiples this year and so far it’s been a volume game. Shoppers want a way to buy something genuinely good without committing to a full bottle every time, so a 50cl answers that at a price that suits how people are actually shopping. There’s real opportunity here for premium spirits where the liquid justifies the shelf space. Indri does.”
Indri Trini is a non chill-filtered single malt made at Piccadily Distillery in the village of Indri, Haryana. It’s distilled from six-row barley grown in Rajasthan and aged in a combination of ex-bourbon, French wine and PX sherry casks, giving it a fruity, sweet and nutty character. The 50cl whisky is the same as the 70cl whisky.
Claire Pennington, Channel Director, Grocery, Convenience & National Routes to Market at Mangrove Global, added: “Tesco has supported Indri from the start and this listing is the next step in that relationship. Getting a bespoke format made and landed takes months, so it only happens when both sides are committed. It’s a good example of what a retailer and a distributor can build together.”

items.title: HMV to close Oxford Street store after three years
items.summary: HMV says it is looking for a new site in London's West End, but its current site is "unviable".
items.body:
HMV to close Oxford Street store after three years
- Published
HMV has said it will shut its flagship Oxford Street store three years after it reopened the site, blaming a proposed doubling of the rent for the closure.
The entertainment chain said it would leave the shop in March 2027, in a move affecting more than 50 staff.
It said it was looking for a new site in London's West End district for its flagship shop and said it planned to maintain a "significant presence" in the capital.
Phil Halliday, managing director of HMV, said it was "frustrating" that the Oxford Street shop was "commercially unviable".
He said: "This is a special store, it's where we began 100 years ago and bringing it back to life in 2023 was a big moment in our recent history.
"We are looking ahead, and our focus is now on what we do to make exciting steps for HMV in 2027."
The group said its landlords had proposed doubling the rent on the site at 363 Oxford Street, and it was also facing a bill for "substantial" renovation works at the store, which together would make the shop "commercially unsustainable".
HMV said it would look to transfer affected workers to its two other London stores and head office while it looked for a new site.
The chain reopened its historic Oxford Street store in November 2023 after a four-year absence following a deal secured with landlords. It first opened the Oxford Street site in 1921.
HMV has 113 stores across the UK, including six sites under the Fopp brand, as well as another eight in Europe. The group said it remained committed to high street stores.

items.body:
Eaten Alive the award-winning fermentation specialist, founded by two Michelin trained chefs, has landed a 521-store listing with Tesco. The fermented food experts are supplying the supermarket with three of its hand-made, gut boosting delicacies that will be available nationwide from 12th October at Tesco stores and online.
Launched 10 years ago in Battersea by chefs Pat Bingley and Glyn Gordon, Eaten Alive is renowned for its high quality ‘live’ fermented creations that are not only delicious but also support gut health. The business supplies some of the UK’s top restaurants and chefs including Gordon Ramsay Restaurants, LEON, Gail’s, Wagamama’s and Tortilla.
The Tesco listing is a milestone for the Eaten Alive business that will see the brands biggest ever retail presence, taking its fermented goodies to gut-conscious foodies all over the UK. It has almost doubled its production space and now has more than 50 employees to cater for the increased volumes the team will now be making.
The Tesco Eaten Alive range includes two new products – a delicious new ‘Rainbow Kraut’ that’s bursting with gut-friendly bacteria and eight different vegetables; the ultimate ingredient for 2026 – ‘Smacked Cucumbers’, and the original chef’s favourite ‘Classic Kimchi’ that Eaten Alive first launched in 2016:
- Classic Kimchi (£3.85, g) – Funky, fiery & bold, with crisp Chinese leaf and crunchy shredded veg with heaps of ginger, chilli & garlic. It has a unique blend of spicy and rich umami flavours, combined with a crisp texture that adds a delightful crunch to any dish. Perfect as a topping, or as a dynamic side dish, it brings vibrant colour and robust flavour to any plate. Kimchi is rich in probiotics that promote digestive health, packed with vitamins A and C, as well as being low calorie.
- Fermented Rainbow Kraut (£3.85, g) – Crunchy mix of eight fermented vegetables – tangy and herby, with a touch of spice. Delicious as a condiment or side, straight on sandwiches and wraps, stir through veggies, mix into salad or spoon it onto a ploughman’s. Add it at the end rather than cooking it, to keep the crunch and the live cultures.
- Soy and Chilli Smacked Cucumbers (£3.85, g) – the ultimate foodie ingredient for Autumn 2026, crunchy fresh and a little bit spicy. Perfect for snacking, stacked on salads, on top of a rice bowl or alongside noodles.
Pat Bingley, Eaten Alive Managing Director, comments, “Eaten Alive is all about sharing the delicious, unique flavours and health benefits of fermentation. Landing a place on the shelves of Tesco is a milestone moment for our business and a huge step forward in our mission ‘To Put Fermented Foods on The Plates of the Nation’. Adding fermented ingredients to dishes brings layers of complexity and umami that really make the finished dishes zing, plus a health boost for the gut.”
The Eaten Alive range aims to be not just the tastiest, but the most-healthy products available – they are all additive free, completely raw, vegan and teeming with good bacteria. Only the finest ingredients are used and made to the secret recipes created by the founders Pat and Glyn, at their kitchen in Battersea.
Helena Dennis, Tesco Lead Accelerator Programme Manager, commented, ”Eaten Alive is putting fermented foods on the plates of the nation delivering its award winning fresh, crunchy, live food.”
Eaten Alive founders Pat and Glynn have over 20 years combined experience in some of the UK’s top restaurants (The Ledbury, L’Enclume, Fera). They bonded over a shared passion for fermentation, flavour and the link between live cultures and health, and Eaten Alive was born.
The pair first began supplying the restaurant trade with their Classic Spicy Kimchi in 2016, a runaway success that was quickly followed by fermented hot sauces and krauts. They supply a host of renowned venues from Tonkotsu to Soho House and the Gordon Ramsay Restaurant group, as well as a having a retail offer that is sold in Planet Organic, Whole Foods, Borough Market, various independent delis and now Tesco stores and online.

British oral care brand Waken is entering the Christmas gifting market for the first time, with two new products launching at Sainsbury’s this September. The launch marks Waken’s first move outside the traditional oral care aisle, with its Whitening Toothpaste Cracker and Sonic Smile Washbag set to land in around 180 Sainsbury’s stores for Christmas 2026.
Since January 2025, Rylan Clark has been an investor and Creative Director at Waken, helping the brand bring a playful approach to oral care. Rylan will also feature in the campaign supporting the new Christmas range.
The Waken Whitening Toothpaste Cracker puts a full-size Waken Whitening Toothpaste inside a Christmas cracker, creating a practical stocking filler designed to be used well beyond Christmas Day. The Waken Sonic Smile Washbag contains a graphite grey sonic toothbrush, full-size whitening toothpaste and a travel size toothpaste and mouthwash. This is Waken’s first complete gift set and brings its everyday oral care routine into a giftable format.
Both products are assembled in the UK and will be available at Sainsbury’s from September 2026. The launch comes as Waken continues to grow ahead of the wider oral care category. The brand has now sold more than 5.6 million products, is stocked in more than 1,350 UK stores, and retail sales are up 45% year-on-year.
Rylan Clark, creative director and investor at Waken, says: “Waken has always been about making oral care less boring, so I love the idea of taking it into Christmas gifting. These are gifts people will actually use – and hopefully have a bit of fun opening too.”

items.body:
PG Tips, one of the UK’s most famous tea brands[1], today announced a significant investment in its future and the future of the UK’s black tea category. Centred on a significantly improved blend, refreshed packaging and a substantial integrated marketing programme, the ambitious brand refresh is designed to drive reappraisal, strengthen shopper engagement, and support long-term value growth. New packs will begin rolling out across major UK retailers from autumn 2026.
With black tea continuing to account for eight in 10 cups consumed in the UK[2], the relaunch follows a year in development, including extensive consumer research with over 1,000 consumers*, identifying taste and overall quality as the main drivers of purchase and value perception in the category.
The new blend retains the brand’s signature rich and smooth taste profile, with a fuller flavour that outperformed the current PG Tips Original blend in consumer testing. It increased both purchase intent and overall preference by 13 percentage points. The tea bag weight has also increased from 2.9g to 3.125g, delivering more flavour in every cup. With RRPs** across all pack sizes remaining unchanged, the improved blend offers consumers a better cuppa and better value.
Alongside the new PG Tips Original blend, PG Tips Gold, Decaf and English Breakfast will benefit from refreshed packaging. Drawing on the brand’s heritage, the new artwork is designed to strengthen on-shelf standout.
Jonny Briscoe, managing director UK&I for Lipton Teas & Infusions, says: “This is the most significant investment we’ve made into the PG Tips blend in recent years, and underlines our commitment to the long-term value growth of the black tea category. By focusing on what matters most to tea drinkers, taste, we have created a blend that is preferred by consumers. Supported by a major marketing campaign and a full packaging refresh, we are confident this launch will drive shopper reappraisal, increase trial and help our retail partners unlock value growth in the category.”
Q4 2026 has a £1.5m integrated marketing launch campaign to support the rollout and drive visibility and trial. Activity will span trade and consumer PR, social media, bespoke shopper marketing, out-of-home advertising from November, sampling and retail partnerships. The refresh builds on the return of PG Tips’ iconic Monkey and the brand’s Live Life One Tea at a Time campaign to maintain shopper engagement throughout the launch.
As part of its commitment to sustainability, all cartons are recyclable, and the tea bags remain plant-based and compostable.
Retailers are encouraged to stock the refreshed PG Tips range from launch and maximise its category growth potential through prominent in-store visibility and activation.

items.title: New data: beauty drives high street footfall with hidden contribution to jobs, high streets and wellbeing

A landmark report commissioned by the British Beauty Council has revealed that beauty and personal care is more than a cosmetic luxury; it is a fundamental driver of British high street vitality, social connection, and personal wellbeing. Compiled by Oxford Economics and supported by L’Oréal Groupe, the findings highlight how the sector acts as essential […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! items.body:
A landmark report commissioned by the British Beauty Council has revealed that beauty and personal care is more than a cosmetic luxury; it is a fundamental driver of British high street vitality, social connection, and personal wellbeing. Compiled by Oxford Economics and supported by L’Oréal Groupe, the findings highlight how the sector acts as essential social infrastructure across the UK.
Titled The Impact of Beauty: Revealing Its Social, Cultural, and Economic Value, the report unveils how deep-rooted the sector is across every postcode of the UK. Building on findings that the sector contributed £28.3 billion to UK GDP and supported 595,000 jobs in 2025, this new research highlights the human story behind the numbers and the extended value of the industry.
A necessity for daily life, not an indulgence
The study reveals that British consumers treat personal care as a day-to-day essential rather than a discretionary luxury.
- Daily Routines: UK adults spend an average of 13 minutes a day on their grooming and care routines. Skincare leads daily product habits, with over half of all adults using skincare products daily or most days.
- Prioritised Spend: Consumers rank personal care spending above gym memberships, streaming subscriptions, and dining out. Only 7% of adults view personal care products and services purely as a “treat.”
- Everyday Investment: Surveyed consumers spend an average of £27 per month on products and services, rising to £35 per month among frequent users.
Anchoring the UK high street economy
Across the UK’s 191,200 beauty and personal care establishments, local salons, barbershops, and retailers act as indispensable anchors for physical retail zones.
- Driving Footfall: 55% of consumers’ most recent hair or beauty appointments took place on a high street or town centre. Crucially, for 86% of these visitors, the appointment was the primary reason for their trip.
- Boosting Local Businesses: 50% of high street appointment visits led directly to additional spending at nearby shops, cafés, and restaurants.
- Small Town Hubs: Personal care makes up more than 35% of all leisure businesses on smaller local high streets matching the combined total share of pubs, bars, and cafés.
- Beyond London: The sector’s footprint is distributed nationwide. 39% of beauty amenities are located outside large cities, providing vital local services and jobs in smaller towns, villages, and rural areas.
Trusted spaces for community and connection
Beyond high street commerce, local beauty salons and barbershops serve as essential social infrastructure, offering safe, face-to-face environments that foster community ties and fight isolation.
- Meaningful Connections: 44% of frequent users report having had a meaningful conversation with a personal care service provider in the past six months, with 42% discussing personal matters or life events.
- Tackling Loneliness: For 1 in 5 frequent users – and a striking 42% of young men aged 18–24 – visiting their barber, nail technician or beauty therapist represents one of the few times in a week that they interact with other people.
Powering confidence, resilience, and self-expression
The emotional and psychological benefits of personal care routines directly influence how people navigate everyday life, work, and social occasions.
- Self-Esteem & Wellbeing: 75% of frequent users report a positive impact on how they feel about themselves after using personal care products and services.
- Daily Resilience: 48% say their routine helps them feel more resilient when facing daily challenges, and 52% note that their personal care routine improves their mood.
- Showing Up for Work & Life: 64% enjoy social occasions more when they feel good about their appearance. In professional settings, 56% say taking care of their appearance helps them make a positive first impression at work, and 51% report that it builds their confidence in the workplace.
- Youth Identity: For younger adults (aged 18–24), beauty is a vital medium for self-discovery: 55% say their routines reinforce their sense of self, while 53% use personal care as a creative outlet for experimentation.
Millie Kendall, CEO of the British Beauty Council, said on the launch of the report. “For too long, beauty has been thought of as frivolous and superficial. Since the launch of the British Beauty Council, we have annually assessed how much it contributes to the economy, but this new research shows that its value goes much further.
“Beauty is about how people feel, how they connect and how they participate in everyday life. From the confidence to walk into a room, to the conversation that takes place in a salon chair, to the high-street visit that supports another local business, beauty is enabling things that matter.
“At a time when we are thinking seriously about wellbeing, loneliness, high-street regeneration and economic participation, we need to recognise the role that beauty businesses and professionals already play in communities across Britain.”
“The report determines that beauty and personal care should be understood not simply as a consumer sector, but as part of the social and local infrastructure of everyday life in Britain, and as such must be safeguarded now and in the future.”
The Rt Hon Jonathan Reynolds MP, Secretary of State for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade said: “I love a chat with my local barber, and this report is a good reminder that these businesses are about much more than the services they provide. For many people, they’re places to catch up, have a chat and feel good about themselves. They help keep our high streets busy and support local jobs in every corner of the country, and I want to make sure the industry has the backing it needs to keep growing.”
Thierry Cheval, managing director and chairman, L’Oréal Groupe UK & Ireland said: “As the world’s number one beauty player, and one that has proudly operated in the UK for over 90 years, we have long understood the true scale of this industry’s contribution – and this research proves it. Beauty is universal, yet intensely personal. It has an impact in every postcode across the UK, from our homes to our high streets.
“This industry is a pillar of economic growth, innovation, and even public health, with a significant contribution to UK GDP and growth. I am pleased to see that reflected so clearly in this new report: a sector with a presence in every corner of the country, a role in people’s confidence and wellbeing, and a place in the daily rhythm of national life.”

items.body:
Leading UK fashion footwear retailer schuh has appointed Nick Scott as its new chief financial officer, effective 2nd November 2026.
Scott most recently served as chief financial officer at sportswear and streetwear retailer Footasylum, where he played a key role in the business’s transformation under private equity ownership. Under his financial leadership, the retailer achieved consecutive record revenue and profit, completed a significant refinancing to fund its growth, and accelerated store expansion and its digital-first investment programme, including a landmark international franchise partnership.
Prior to Footasylum, Scott was chief operating financial officer at Baird Group, owner of Suit Direct and UK licensee for Ben Sherman and Ted Baker formalwear. There he led a transformation that moved the business from department-store concessions to its own stores and e-commerce, secured the Ted Baker global formalwear licence and completed a growth refinancing, work that earned him back-to-back finance leadership awards in 2021 and 2022.
“I’m delighted to be joining schuh and the wider Genesco family. schuh is a brand with real heritage in UK footwear and a deep connection to youth culture. For more than four decades, it has stayed relevant by staying close to its customers and the brands that matter to them,” said Scott. “This is a fascinating moment for our industry, with trends evolving rapidly and customers shopping across more channels. schuh’s carefully curated brand partnerships, strong store estate and growing digital presence put it in a great position to meet those changing needs. I’m looking forward to working with Tomas and the hugely talented teams across the business to drive value creation, sharpen our commercial focus and support the delivery of the strategy as we build schuh’s next chapter.”
Scott will succeed David Gillan-Reid, who was CFO of schuh for 28 years and will report to schuh president, Tomas Petersson.
Petersson, schuh president, said: “I’d like to thank David for his incredible contribution as CFO of schuh over the last 28 years. He leaves behind a business with strong foundations for its next chapter. Nick is an accomplished finance leader with outstanding experience, combining strategic financial expertise, strong commercial acumen, and proven leadership skills. Just as importantly, he shares our belief in the importance of culture, collaboration and strong teams in driving performance. His track record of supporting businesses through change and delivering improved performance will be invaluable as we continue to strengthen our position as the UK’s go-to fashion footwear destination and deliver an even better experience for our customers.”

London Stock Exchange faces ‘material depopulation’
The London Stock Exchange is facing “material depopulation” following a boom in the M&A landscape dominated by overseas buyers, a top investment bank has warned.
Some 42 bids for London-listed firms are currently ongoing with a total market capitalisation of £74bn, according to a new note from Peel Hunt. The figure is more than double the £35bn from the entirety of 2025 across 40 bids.
Overseas bidders make up 64 per cent of the 2026 figures, broadly flat with the previous year.
But the buoyant deals market has come amid a “dearth of IPOs”. Since the start of 2023 there have been 166 bids for firms with a price tag over £100m with the collective value topping £180bn. This is compared to just 11 IPOs above £100 for a total value of £6bn.
“To say that the UK has a problem retaining its companies and listing new ones would be a massive understatement,” said Charles Hall, head of research at Peel Hunt.
He added the number and value of bids for UK firms were running at “exceptionally high levels, raising concerns that the UK equity market is seeing a material depopulation”.
Airtel Money completed its IPO on the London market last week with a valuation of £5.3bn, marking the biggest listing in five years. It marked the first time since 2021 that the London Stock Exchange landed an IPO north of £1bn.
The City has struggled to compete with the lure of US markets and lost some of its top talent to exchanges across the Atlantic. Money transfer firm Wise downgraded its London listing in favour of New York last year in a major hit to the City bourse.
Since 2023, seven UK giants have shifted their listings, blowing a £120bn hole in the London market. In the same period, seven UK-based firms have also opted to IPO overseas.
“The pace of delistings vs listings in the UK is widening,” one banker told City AM, adding the European markets were “massively lagging the US”.
Calls for government intervention
London AI infrastructure firm Nscale filed for a US listing targeting a $35bn valuation earlier this year, pouring cold water on hopes from stock exchange officials and ministers of attracting high-growth tech talent.
Hall suggested a series of intervention measures to boost equity markets, including shaking up the capital gains regime for domestic and overseas investors and fast-tracking index inclusion.
“The good news is that turbocharging UK equity markets is not difficult and can be done at pace,” he said.
City minister Lucy Rigby told City AM that capital markets reform was “not a job done” and the government was “continually looking for ways that we can ensure we’re being as competitive as possible”.
Hall pointed to ditching stamp duty on shares as a key lever to “remove friction and enhance UK competitiveness,” adding it makes “no sense for a UK investor to have a higher transaction cost for buying shares in a UK company than a US business”.
In the 2025 Budget, then-Chancellor Rachel Reeves launched a stamp duty holiday, removing the 0.5 per cent levy on UK stocks for newly-listed companies in their first three years of trading.
But the move has failed to open the floodgates for listings. Thought Machine chief Paul Taylor told City AM the levy is “anachronistic” and the recent reforms were not “big enough to really change anybody’s mind either for or against”.

items.body:
HMV shuts flagship Oxford Street store just three years after comeback
HMV is set to close its flagship Oxford Street store just three years after its comeback to the location where it was founded more than a century ago.
The music and entertainment retailer said the site will shut its doors in March next year, blaming a doubled rent bill and the cost of “substantial” renovations.
The departure of the historic outlet from Europe’s busiest shopping destination comes as retailers urge the government to help high street businesses weather soaring rents and taxes.
HMV opened its inaugural store on Oxford Street in 1921 but was forced to close the site in 2019 after the chain tumbled into administration.
The business was rescued by Canadian retail tycoon Doug Putman’s Sunrise Records when he bought 100 HMV shops, saving 1,500 jobs. 27 stores collapsed, costing 455 jobs.
HMV, which now operates at 123 locations across the UK, returned to Oxford Street in 2023 after securing a fresh deal with landlords. Putman had hailed the chain’s return as a “great moment” in its recovery.
But Phil Halliday, HMV’s managing director, announced on Monday that the company will be retreating from Oxford Street once again.
‘Frustrating’ setback for HMV
He said: “This is a special store, it’s where we began 100 years ago and bringing it back to life in 2023 was a big moment in our recent history.
“It’s frustrating that it has been made commercially unviable. However, we are looking ahead, and our focus is now on what we do to make exciting steps for HMV in 2027.”
The retailer said its recovery is gaining momentum despite this setback, pointing to the 15 per cent like-for-like sales growth it has achieved so far this year.
HMV is on track to notch £240m in revenue across its in-store and online estate this year, which would mark a 13 per cent improvement on last year’s £212m.
Halliday added: “We hope to redeploy affected team members through other London stores and head office roles and are exploring ways to minimise the impact on jobs while we seek a new flagship site.
“We’re actively looking for a new location in the West End and are determined to give London a store that music fans can be proud of.”

items.title: The next era of retail tech — with AI at the core
items.summary: Retail is changing fast. Discover how AI and mobility are redefining the store of tomorrow.
items.body:
Retail is entering its most transformative chapter since the dawn of e-commerce. Stores are evolving into hybrid hubs for fulfillment, service and brand experience—all while customer expectations rise, labor capacity shrinks and omnichannel pressure grows. The frontline is being asked to move faster with fewer people and the systems supporting them have to evolve just as quickly.
Mobility now sits at the center of modern retail execution. Associates rely on mobile tools to locate inventory, engage customers, process returns, execute pick lists and close transactions. Yet many brands are still held back by legacy scanner guns, outdated rugged hardware and fragmented solutions that require too much training and too much IT effort to keep operational. In environments where seconds matter, slow devices turn into slow lines, unhappy customers and operational drag.
Recent Stratix research reveals something important: Apple® is preferred in retail for cost, ruggedness and enterprise readiness! Today, Apple not only meets the demands of modern retail workflows but also increasingly outperforms traditional rugged devices in durability, security, ease of use and total cost of ownership. And with Apple Intelligence, the platform is built for AI-driven retail from the inside out.
But technology alone doesn’t deliver transformation. At scale, the operational execution is just as important. This is where Stratix comes in—turning devices into outcomes through deployment precision, lifecycle management, shared-device frameworks and round-the-clock support. Together, Apple devices and Stratix services are shaping what a modern, AI-powered retail workforce looks like.
Retail has reached a turning point
The frontline of retail now moves at the speed of expectation. Customers expect personalized service, instant answers and zero friction. They don’t want to wait while an associate fumbles with unfamiliar software or struggles to check inventory. Meanwhile, stores have effectively become micro-fulfillment centers—simultaneously handling BOPIS orders, curbside pickup, returns, restocking and traditional in-aisle interactions. The hardware in workers’ hands has to keep pace with that complexity.
Compounding this is the talent dynamic. With labor shortages and rising turnover, retailers must onboard workers quickly and enable them to contribute immediately. Devices that feel familiar and intuitive dramatically reduce training time and frustration. Associates gain confidence and speed more quickly and customers feel it instantly.
What about the considerations of identity management, compliance and security? With shared shifts, multiple authentication points and payment systems in play, retailers can’t afford vulnerabilities or clumsy sign-in processes that slow the day down. And running AI effectively adds another level of complexity—governance, data privacy, device capability and workflow integration all have to align.
This reality demands technology that is powerful but easy. Secure but flexible. Advanced but approachable. Apple technology fits that definition well—and many retailers are turning to Apple products because of it.
Why Apple devices are becoming a retail standard
Apple devices are also considered the most cost-effective solution for retail organizations when we examined full lifecycle costs vs. Android alternatives. Apple devices last longer, hold value better, require fewer repairs and generate fewer support tickets because associates already know how to use them. One device can also replace multiple single-purpose tools, simplifying infrastructure and cutting operational overhead.
Durability is another area where Apple products are ideal for retail environments. iPhone® and iPad® withstand high-touch retail environments with ease. Ceramic Shield protection, IP68 water and dust resistance and enterprise-grade construction make them fully capable of withstanding stockrooms, warehouse-level handling and fast-paced checkout stations—especially when paired with the rugged accessories Stratix deploys at scale.
Perhaps most importantly, Apple devices are built for enterprise. Apple Business Manager enables zero-touch deployment, security policies are consistent and predictable and identity integration works across major authentication frameworks. Retailers deploying thousands of devices across hundreds of stores get stability, simplicity and control.
And with Apple IntelligenceTM, the devices don’t just run retail—they accelerate it. Associates can retrieve inventory details through natural language, generate pick paths, access training support instantly, summarize procedures, or launch workflows without navigating menus. AI becomes an invisible assistant that speeds decision-making and boosts confidence on the floor.
The multiplying effect of Apple devices + Stratix
The technology advantage compounds when paired with the operational infrastructure Stratix provides. Rolling out thousands of devices sounds simple until every location needs configuration, security policies, charging management, accessories, spares, repairs and analytics. Stratix handles the entire lifecycle—pre-kitting devices, shipping them ready for use, automating app and profile setup and managing ongoing repairs, replacement pools and reporting.
Shared-device environments are often where deployments fail internally, but it’s where Stratix excels. Sign-in and sign-out workflows are clean, identity resets are automated and devices are always charged, available and audit-ready for the next associate. And instead of burdening internal teams, Stratix’s 24×7 support desk resolves issues quickly with experts who understand the urgency of front-of-house downtime.
This is how innovation scales—not through hardware alone, but through operational orchestration.
The outcome? Faster stores. Better experiences. Empowered people.
When associates move confidently, the store moves confidently. Customers get faster answers. Lines shrink. Orders flow. Returns don’t stall. Training becomes lighter, support becomes quieter and productivity increases without adding headcount.
Modern retail isn’t powered by devices—it’s powered by the people holding them. Apple products give those people intelligence, speed and ease. Stratix ensures the technology is always ready, always supported, always scalable.
The future of retail will belong to brands whose mobility strategy is as dynamic as their customer. With Apple and Stratix working together, that future is already here.

items.title: Could the next Vauxhall Astra really look like this? The STX Concept is an electric estate bucking the SUV trend
items.summary: Vauxhall has taken the covers off its STX concept - a car it promises showcases the British brand's 'vision of future estates' and could pave the way for the new electric Astra.
items.body:
Could the next Vauxhall Astra really look like this? The STX Concept is an electric estate bucking the SUV trend
Vauxhall has taken the covers off its Sports Tourer eXperimental (STX) concept, which could set the path for the next-generation Astra estate.
Revealed on the eve of the Paris Motor Show, the STX Concept goes against the electric SUV trend.
Instead, it's attempting to rekindle demand for more traditional – lower – cars with massive boots.
It's also the first car to feature the brand's new Griffin emblem, which has been refreshed to appear more striking when illuminated as more brands introduce back-lit emblems to stand out.
While details remain thin – this is a concept car, after all – we do know that it uses an all-wheel-drive electric architecture and will be able to achieve a top speed of 124mph.
Vauxhall says the STX EV symbolises 'the next stage of Vauxhall's design philosophy' – and is bolder, more efficient, more emotional, and purer than other STs.
Revealed at the Paris Motor Show, the Vauxhall STX Concept 'reimagines the electric estate car' and goes against the electric SUV trend
While reimagining the electric estate car, the STX features the latest evolution of the Vauxhall Vizor – the brand's front fascia.
On the STX, the Vizor is taller, more prominent, and bolder, and there's a new, angular, vertical lighting signature which moves from the outer edges of the Vizor towards the centre.
The new illuminated Griffin emblem sits in the middle here and complements the sharp, sporting front design.
The rest of the STX is shaped into a flush, aerodynamic, clean estate with a sporty and futuristic rear end and a steeply sloping profile, with C-pillars, glass light strips, and a roofline that all extend backwards.
The rear lights have the same vertical element as the front.
The STX is shaped into a flush, aerodynamic, clean estate with a sporty and futuristic rear end
It's got a steeply sloping profile, with C-pillars, glass light strips, and a roofline that all extend backwards
While people might appreciate the silhouette of the STX, most drivers will surely dislike the cameras that replace the door mirrors – a modern twist most motorists can do without.
Focused on aerodynamics, the STX Concept not only has short overhangs, sculpted bodywork, and three-section alloy wheels, but it also features an active aerodynamic system which continuously adapts to driving conditions.
A cool feature of this setup is that, at the right speed, blue-coloured diffusers extend from beneath the rear, while vertical elements behind the wheels move outwards to support the streamlined profile.
Designed to reinvent the electric estate car, the STX features the latest evolution of the Vauxhall Vizor – the brand's front fascia
The new illuminated Griffin emblem sits in the middle of the Vizor and complements the sharp, sporting front design
Members of the public will be able to ogle the STX Concept in Paris from Monday as the covers come off to the public
In the future, when the interior is revealed, it will apparently develop Vauxhall's 'Painting with Light' approach – already introduced with the 2023 Vauxhall Experimental and the 2025 Vauxhall Corsa GSE Vision Gran Turismo.
Specially developed lightweight seats and immersive lighting elements will light up the inside.
That's all we know for now, but members of the public will be able to ogle the STX Concept in Paris from Monday.
And for the rest of us, Vauxhall has said that the STX is 'more than a show car', as it 'previews the future development of the estate body style and introduces design elements that will appear on future Vauxhall models'.

2026 RTIH Innovation Awards UK Retailer of the Year finalists include Waitrose, Toolstation, Morrisons
We’re pleased to announce the shortlist for the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Most Innovative UK Retailer category. We received a record number of entries this year and many fantastic examples of technology excellence driving transformative change across the global retail sector.
Check out a rundown of our 2026 shortlists and finalists here.
Congratulations to all those who made it through the initial submission process! It’s now over to our star studded judging panel who will decide the winners to be announced at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London.
The event will be held on Wednesday, 4th November and consist of a drinks reception, three course meal, awards ceremony presided over by award winning stand-up comedian, presenter, actor and broadcaster, Aurie Styla, and after party until 1am.
Click here to book your place at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony on Wednesday, 4th November.
Our 2026 Most Innovative UK Retailer finalists as follows:
DFS and 3D Cloud
DFS Group, which owns both DFS and Sofology, had an ambitious goal. After seeing early success with AB testing of 3D product page features and experiences, it decided to take on a huge scale challenge and create 3D experiences for nearly every product in its catalogue.
Euro Car Parts and Commerce
Euro Car Parts has transformed complex automotive product data into an AI ready discovery engine with Commerce’s Feedonomics platform.
Goddiva
Over the last 12 months, British occasionwear retailer Goddiva has transformed AI from an experimental technology into a connected retail capability spanning customers, internal teams and wholesale partners.
Morrisons
Morrisons is trialling AI powered Caper Smart Trolleys for an autonomous checkout process. It has also deployed Digital Bluetooth Probing across itsOven Fresh departments to automate food safety checks. And it has rolled out a Pick to Light system using digital shelf edge labels to guide online pickers. Finally, its Everseen roll-out has supported its front end efficiency and made improvements into our loss recovery.
Toolstation
Toolstation has reimagined Click and Collect at its Toolstation GO Battersea store through a new 24/7 smart locker service developed with eLocker.
Waitrose and SOLUM
Waitrose and SOLUM are delivering a nationwide digital shelf transformation using Newton Pro electronic shelf labels. Following pilots, the programme has expanded to more than 200 stores and over three million labels.
Editor and Founder of Retail Technology Innovation Hub

items.body:
2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Emerging Retail Technology finalists include Hanshow, ZigZag, and shopreme
We’re pleased to announce the shortlist for the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Emerging Retail Technology Innovation of the Year category. We received a record number of entries this year and many fantastic examples of technology excellence driving transformative change across the global retail sector.
Check out a rundown of our 2026 shortlists and finalists here.
Congratulations to all those who made it through the initial submission process! It’s now over to our star studded judging panel who will decide the winners to be announced at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London.
The event will be held on Wednesday, 4th November and consist of a drinks reception, three course meal, awards ceremony presided over by award winning stand-up comedian, presenter, actor and broadcaster, Aurie Styla, and after party until 1am.
Click here to book your place at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony on Wednesday, 4th November.
Our 2026 Emerging Retail Technology Innovation of the Year finalists as follows:
AIMETECH
Chefs For Foodies (CFF) is a curated dropship marketplace for UK speciality food and premium kitchen brands. It works with more than 100 artisan brands, including DeliVita, Tracklements, Hilltop Honey and Luigi Bormioli, and lists over 1,000 products.
Stock stays with the producer until it sells. AIMETECH is building an agentic commerce platform for CFF on top of this model
Augmodo
Augmodo builds physical AI infrastructure powered by wearable computer vision for frontline teams. Store associates wear a passive Smartbadge during normal shifts.
As they move, outward facing cameras capture shelf conditions, using egocentric vision models to build a dynamic 3D spatial map of inventory, identifying out-of-stocks, gaps, and misplaced items in real time.
EDEKA and eyefactive
EDEKA Jensen in Uetersen near Hamburg runs the first self-order kiosk at a fresh food counter within EDEKA. Since December 2025 the EasyOrder Terminal has let customers place their meat and sausage order on a touchscreen, carry on shopping while the counter team prepares it, and collect it at the self-service counter. Payment happens at the regular checkout.
Fixit
Talos is an AI sales and support agent for online shops that works from the shop's own live data: catalogue, stock, prices, shipping rules and orders. One agent answers on web chat, Instagram, Messenger and WhatsApp, recommends in-stock products using the merchant's own attributes, answers "where is my order", hands over to a human when needed, and writes the shop's product copy from the same catalogue.
It runs on Fixit's own GPU infrastructure in the EU, with no third-party model API. Live in production with 18 retailers across WooCommerce, Magento 2, Shopify and custom storefronts.
Focal Systems
Computer vision in stores has mostly been judged on detection: how many empty shelves a system finds. Focal Systems has taken it further. Fixed cameras read every shelf in the store every hour, and in 2026 that view extended to the stock stacked above the shelf and, in trials, the back room.
The system now matches each gap to stock the store already has, sends staff a prioritised task, and uses the same camera to confirm the gap was filled. Focal runs 500,000 cameras in more than 1,000 stores, captures over 40 million shelf scans a day, and has confirmed more than 23 million gaps filled.
Goddiva
Goddiva is a British occasionwear brand using emerging AI technology to transform how customers discover, choose and purchase fashion online.
Its proprietary AI ecosystem combines conversational commerce, semantic search, intelligent personalisation, AI powered product tagging, Fit Intelligence, Virtual Try-On and automated customer support within one connected retail experience. Customer interactions also generate intelligence that improves search, merchandising and product development.
GrowStocks
GrowStocks reads a UK FMCG brand's own weekly retailer data and finds the store level stockouts that stay invisible inside a "healthy" national figure. No new systems, no analyst required just automated detection that ranks every issue by pounds lost per day and tells you exactly who needs to fix it.
Hanshow
Hanshow, shopreme and Lucky Cart are building a connected Smart Cart ecosystem that brings digital retail capabilities directly into the physical shopping journey.
Combining Hanshow’s Smart Cart hardware platform, shopreme’s in-store operating system and Lucky cart’s retail media expertise, the solution creates a scalable foundation for modern grocery retail.
InnoXR Labs
InnoXR Labs’ Atmos OS is an intelligence layer for physical retail that turns in-store customer interactions into decisions retailers can act on.
Using glasses free holographic and interactive surfaces (HoloInteract, AR Mirror, Smart Kiosk, Retrofit Kit) plus on-device Edge AI, Atmos OS shows what attracts attention, what gets ignored, and what shoppers respond to, then helps adapt on-display content.
Mys Tyler
Fashion tech startup, Mys Tyler, partnered with City Chic to improve shopper fit confidence and reduce online returns. Using Mys Tyler’s FitCheck technology, the partnership combined diverse creators, visual fit reviews and structured fit data. This content was embedded on City Chic’s product pages across Australia, New Zealand and the US.
shopreme
At retailers like famila Nordost, shopreme's snap cart Smart Cart software transforms shopping carts into a digital self-checkout touchpoint: shoppers "snap on" the Hanshow Smart Cart tablet, scan products, receive personalised assistance, recommendations, and coupons, and check out directly on the cart.
ZigZag
ZigZag launched its WhatsApp Returns initiative to respond to a fundamental shift in consumer expectations: post-purchase experiences must now be as fast, intuitive, and mobile first as the purchase itself.
