items.title: Boots has a new owner: Three ways it could affect you
items.summary: The stalwart of Britain's High Street has been sold to a Canadian billionaire family. What will that mean for you?
items.body:
Boots has a new owner: Three ways it could affect you
- Published
If you have been looking to buy a health or beauty product, the chances are you will have shopped at a Boots somewhere in the UK.
The pharmacy and retailer is a stalwart of Britain's high streets, where it has served generations of customers for decades.
But now it is set to enter its 178th year under new ownership after an Â£7bn deal was agreed this week - here's three ways it could affect your shopping experience.
Revamped shops
Upgrading its portfolio of 1,800 stores is high on the list of Boots' new owners, Wittington Investments. This is the holding company of the Westons - a wealthy and retail-steeped Canadian family who used to own Selfridges and currently own several large retailers across the Atlantic.
The UK branch of the family also controls the owner of Primark, Associated British Foods (ABF).
What Boots stores might look like in the future has not been disclosed.
Business has been good for Boots in recent years, and new-look beauty areas in some of its bigger shops have given shoppers more of a department store experience, according to Sofie Willmott, an associate director and analyst at GlobalData Retail.
Since the opening of its first beauty-only store in 2023 in the Battersea Power Station development, it says it has redesigned over 180 beauty halls, while also opening its first fragrance concept store and an Opticians dedicated to luxury eyewear.
"They should invest in the rest of the chain because they've got such a big store portfolio that I think some of the smaller stores have really lacked investment over time, and I think that is something that they need to kind of catch up with," Willmott says.
A more "consistent" look would also be an improvement, Willmott adds. "At the moment there is a bit of a disconnect."
Jackie Naghten, a retail industry veteran who has worked for the likes of Top Shop, Marks & Spencer and Debenhams, thinks Boots' stores need to be made "more functional" by not having their health hubs "squeezed in the corner".
But Yasmin Trimble, 22, who buys beauty products from Boots, likes how easy the stores are to navigate.
"You can get everything you need...it is not confusing. It has got a cleaner aesthetic to it as well."
Advantage card an 'asset to double down on'
Boots was an early adopter of the loyalty cards commonly offered today by companies offering points and discounts to customers who sign up.
Its Advantage card, launched in 1997, is unlikely to go away and remains popular.
Naghten doesn't think they would get rid of it. "It's the best-value store card in terms of bang for your buck."
The card offers shoppers three points for every pound they spend. Each point is worth 1p.
Katie Burrows, 23, is a fan of building up the points to get money off.
She mainly shops at Boots for skincare, first aid and medicine, but thinks prices for its sanitary products are "ridiculously expensive" - something her friend Yasmin agrees with.
Lewis Harrison believes the loyalty card is also good value, but finds it "frustrating how the rewards points only cover a full transaction".
"I wish you could use your points for a partial transaction like you can in Holland and Barrett," the 25-year-old says. "It would be good to use the points towards more expensive transactions."
Natalie Berg, retail expert and founder of consultancy NBK Retail, suggests the Advantage card gives Boots "a unique understanding of their customers" and is an asset the new owners "will want to double down on".
"As AI and social media change how people discover and buy products, that direct relationship with customers will only become more important."
Expanding healthcare services
The new owners have already signalled they plan to expand Boots' healthcare service, a booming industry at the moment.
The retailer started out as an apothecary, so health is in its roots. Today, it offers a wide range of health and wellbeing services as well as prescriptions and vaccinations through its in-store pharmacies.
It also announced earlier this summer it was expanding services for weight loss drugs, which have surged in popularity.
Naghten points out that the Weston family's purchase of Boots comes at a time when pharmacies are increasingly going to prescribe more medications and health services, in a bid to ease pressure on GP surgeries and hospitals.
"They didn't buy this thing for no reason. They have got the blueprint," she says.
While health will remain a core part of its business, Boots has other strengths, Naghten adds, in its No7 make-up and skincare products.
"When you have all these people coming in for health and wellbeing services, they will also be picking up a lipstick," she says.
Willmott suggests Boots has an "edge" over its rivals on the health side, given its reputation as an expert.
But the company is facing tough competition, which Boots acknowledged affected revenues in its latest financial results.
Shoppers, particularly younger ones, are increasingly seeking products online through influencer ads rather than heading to brick-and-mortar shops.
There are also other big players, such as Superdrug. And M&S this week announced a new partnership with Sephora, saying it would replace a hundred of its own beauty departments with the brand next year.
For 18-year-old Schekina Bourne, Boots is not a "go-to shop" for her. "Even though I can go to Boots even in my area....Superdrug is like closest to me. So, I'll prefer the convenience," she says.
Additional reporting by Ben Sturt and Anuk Weerawardana

items.title: Lost generation: the AI threat to Britain’s next great directors
items.summary: Commercials once launched careers from Ridley Scott to Guy Ritchie, now automated production is cutting costs – and the chance to learn by doing When Ridley Scott was awarded the UK’s highest accolade for a glittering career directing films from Alien and Blade Runner to Gladiator and The Martian , he reminded those attending the Bafta event eight years ago that making commercials had been his “film school” . The advertising industry has long been a breeding ground for British film and TV talent who have gone on to make the jump to Hollywood productions , including Guy Ritchie, who started out making music videos and commercials, and Paddington in Peru director Dougal Wilson, whose credits include a number of John Lewis’s famous Christmas ads. Continue reading...
items.body:
When Ridley Scott was awarded the UK’s highest accolade for a glittering career directing films from Alien and Blade Runner to Gladiator and The Martian, he reminded those attending the Bafta event eight years ago that making commercials had been his “film school”.
The advertising industry has long been a breeding ground for British film and TV talent who have gone on to make the jump to Hollywood productions, including Guy Ritchie, who started out making music videos and commercials, and Paddington in Peru director Dougal Wilson, whose credits include a number of John Lewis’s famous Christmas ads.
But the panicked race to introduce AI technology across the advertising industry, to cut client costs and avoid being pushed aside by big tech, has raised fears of a lost generation who may be denied the opportunity to develop into great British film and TV directors.
“100%, yes, I have fears,” says Luke Scott, who runs the group that includes Ridley Scott Associates, the media production company that was co-founded by his father in the 1960s.
“I’m grown up enough to recognise that change is inevitable. But what I’ve seen generally in terms of generative AI output is a very mixed bag. You can turn to it and do something and say ‘Look what I made and isn’t it edifying’. But that is very misleading and sort of introducing us to an ersatz creativity.
“The grave danger is the monoculturalisation of everything. The creative business is something you learn by doing. It is in the doing that is most valuable. Flying a drone isn’t like flying, there isn’t that visceral feeling to it, you are not actually flying. What do you do with that lost generation? Maybe in 20 or 30 years the whole notion of the ad industry as we work now will be an [anachronistic] joke.”
Last month, the global advertising group WPP officially opened its flagship production facility in a converted warehouse in east London. It was the first in an international rollout spearheading its £600m WPP Production business, as it aims to bring “world-class creativity and advanced AI capabilities under one roof”.
Cindy Rose, a former Microsoft executive appointed WPP’s CEO to turn around its fortunes, said that AI is ushering in a “golden age of marketing”.
“WPP and the industry as a whole is at a critical inflection point,” she said, against a backdrop of a Ford Capri being shot cruising the streets of an AI-generated Paris. “We have to better leverage the AI advantage we have. We no longer need to spend our clients’ budgets on expensive shoots abroad. We can do it in the studio [and] completely change the economics of our content supply chain. We can deliver content at the speed of culture.”
One industry source said that some ads can be made up to 60% cheaper, which has some clients embracing AI-led ads to “show finance directors they are making savings”, even though the output often looks “cookie cutter” and suffers a creative “erosion from the diminished role of a director”.
On the topic of the automotive sector the source questioned whether, in an increasingly AI-first ad industry, Top Gun would have become the quintessential 1980s blockbuster that it did. The film’s producers, Don Simpson and Jerry Bruckheimer, chose their director, Ridley Scott’s late brother Tony, after seeing a TV ad in which he depicted a Saab car racing a fighter jet in what could pass for a trailer for the cinematic style adopted throughout the film.
However, Richard Glasson, the chief executive of WPP Production, said that new technologies have always been embraced by the industry and the use of AI is no different.
“It is the future of where content is going, an AI production powerhouse for the future,” he said. “The underlying tech we use to create work is changing. It is being introduced in TV and film but not widely adopted in advertising to this point.”
He added that AI is being embraced by clients who need to be able to keep up with creating content across dozens more digital media platforms than ad agencies have ever had to keep pace with.
“All clients need a vastly greater amount of content,” he said. “There has been an explosion in the number of channels that they are talking to their consumers. To win against the algorithms you have to be producing new content, not just repurposing one ad campaign for six months, those days are gone. It is about speed to market, making the previous impossible possible. We can place a brand anywhere in the world in a single afternoon.”
Yet he does not believe that the days of the classic blockbuster ad campaign, and the need for the talent to create award-winning work, are numbered.
“We still make Super Bowl ads that take nine months, football World Cup campaigns and ads with celebrities in exotic locales,” he said. “They still exist and will continue to exist. The elephant in the room is whether AI is coming for jobs, in production we are seeing the opposite. I see AI as an enabler of abundance, and the people working in production as infinitely adaptable and curious about tech and what it will allow us to do.”

items.body:
After it emerged that China reached an “understanding” with the EU on trade, the Chinese ministry of commerce, led by Wang Wentao, has said the country is: “willing... to continue facilitating the approval of export licenses for rare earths and permanent magnets destined for the EU.”
While they acknowledged “differences” between them, the two sides were committed to maintaining trade and to hold a further meeting in March.
China said both sides would adhere to “procedures concerning company price undertakings” of hybrid cars, Beijing’s commerce ministry said, citing a joint statement, suggesting a deal to find minimum prices for hybrid cars exported to the EU.
The talks follow months of rising tensions between the 27-nation EU and the Asian powerhouse that threatened to escalate into a trade war.
EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič had said it was “crucial” that the talks deliver “tangible outcomes”, after he met with Wang on Thursday.
Maroš Šefčovič said earlier in the day that the EU’s trade deficit with running at around £1bn a day (€1.18bn) every day, was “unsustainable”.
China reaches "understanding" with EU on trade - reports
Lisa O’Carroll
Breaking:China has reached an “understanding” with the EU, to avert deterioration in trade tensions after two days of talks in Beijing, according to a Chinese statement.
EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič is due to hold a press conference around 3pm CET, but China says the two sides of agreed a 16 point agreement allowing for a relaxation of restrictions on rare earth exports from China to the EU in return for concessions on electric vehicle exports.
Diesel falls below £2 per litre as oil prices ease
Diesel prices have gone under £2 a litre, providing some momentary relief from climbing fuel prices.
However, the RAC notes that prices are still significantly higher than they were before the US launched its war on Iran, leaving households paying much more every time they fill up their tanks.
RAC head of policy Simon Williams said:
While it’s positive to see the average cost of a litre of diesel dipping back below £2 a litre, we’re a long way from being out of the woods when it comes to high fuel prices.
Diesel remains around 57p a litre higher than before the US/Iran conflict, and petrol 42p higher – meaning households are paying £31 and £23 more respectively every time they fill up a family-sized car.
And as things stand, this year is still set to be the second most expensive year on record for drivers.
Williams went on to say that prime minister Andy Burnham’s government had the power to take some of the sting out of higher fuel costs, either by extending and increasing the fuel duty cut or reducing VAT, as the government have already done with domestic electricity.
He added:
Without action, 3p a litre in duty will be added on 1 January, and another 2p on 1 March, which will only make prices at the pump even more expensive.
At a time when Treasury VAT takings from fuel remain exceptionally high, drivers will be looking to this month’s budget for some much-needed relief.
Former Deutsche Bank trader overtuns rate rigging conviction
The UK’s Court of Appeal has overturned the conviction of Christian Bittar, the Deutsche Bank trader who was jailed for conspiring to rig benchmark interest rates pleaded guilty to conspiracy to defraud.
He was the final trader whose case was being appealed in the UK. Five former Barclays traders had their convictions overturned on Wednesday this week. The cases of seven Libor and Euribor defendants have been overturned in total.
The decision on Bittar’s case comes despite the former trader having pleaded guilty to the charges eight years ago.
Bittar was sentenced to five years and four months in jail, after pleading guilty in 2018 to rigging Euribor, the Euro interbank offered rate that determined the rates on trillions of dollars of financial contracts and loans across the world.
The ruling on Friday further unravels one of the UK Serious Fraud Office’s most high-profile prosecutions.
Jason Williams, head of division at the SFO said in a statement:
We argued for a different outcome but respect the court’s decision in relation to Christian Bittar.
The SFO remains committed to tackling the most complex fraud, bribery and corruption.
The European Union is granting temporary trade preferences to Armenia following trade restrictions recently imposed by Russia,our senior correspondent Lisa O’Carroll reports.
In a move which shows how flexible the EU can be, it said the temporary trade preferences “will help alleviate the difficult situation faced by Armenian producers and exporters and support the resilience of Armenia’s economy by facilitating access to the EU market.”
The measures, which will enter into force tomorrow for a period of two years, temporarily allow 80% of Armenian exports to the EU, including almost all exports of fresh fruit, vegetables and flowers affected by the Russian measures, as well as over 91% of exports of beverages and spirits.
Armenia is not an accession state, but has been singled out for support as part of the EU a broader solidarity support package
Data storage firm Snowflake denies Asos breach caused by platform flaw
Data storage firm Snowflake has said hack at Asos was not caused by a vulnerability or flaw with its platform.
It comes after Asos’ investigation this week found an “unauthorised party gained access to an Asos employee account by impersonating a trusted contact to obtain log-in credentials”. Asos said the credentials were then used to access information on third-party platforms used by the company.
But on Friday, Snowflake – a US cloud-based AI data storage business – distanced itself from the incident despite being referenced in the message from the hackers.
(The message had read: “Dear ASOS DPO and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance. Engage with us, or we will leak it,” followed by a Telegram link.)
A Snowflake spokeswoman said:
We are aware of Asos’s notification to their customers regarding this incident. We can confirm this issue did not in any way result from a vulnerability, weakness, flaw, or misconfiguration with the Snowflake service, platform, or internal environments, and was not caused by Snowflake.
No remediation is required for Snowflake customers. We continue to encourage adherence to our security best practices.
Asos has stressed that no payment card information or account passwords were accessed. They added the website and app were safe to use:
There is no action you need to take on your account. However, please remain cautious of unexpected messages or calls claiming to be from Asos. We will never ask you to share passwords, security codes or payment details through an unsolicited message or call.
European stock markets are trading higher, with the FTSE 100 up 0.8%, France’s CAC 40 up 0.77% and Germany’s DAX up 1.07%.
US futures are pointing to a strong start for Wall Street, with Dow futures up 0.17%, S&P futures up 0.4%, Nasdaq up 0.81%.
In London, the FTSE 100 is up despite a 5.4% drop in Airtel Africa shares, which started conditional trading today, as well as a 4.2% drop in Vodafone shares and a 2.3% drop in BT, amid jitters over the prospect that SpaceX could start offering retail telecoms services to US consumers.
Airtel Money shares start trading on London Stock Exchange
Shares in Airtel Money have begun conditional trading on the London Stock Exchange, marking the biggest float in five years.
It is also the fifth biggest company by market value to float on the exchange, excluding those on the international main market.
Shares were priced at £1.96, valuing the company at £5.3bn. (Unconditional trading is expected to start on 14 October.)
Its parent company Airtel Africa – the telecoms provider ultimately controlled by the billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal –had originally targeted a listing in the first six months of 2026 but delayed it to the second half of the year, blaming unfavourable market conditions as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Several other companies have pushed back planned IPOs amid market volatility.
Airtel Africa was already listed on the FTSE 100, but bosses wanted Airtel Money to be listed separately.
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said it has the potential to encourage more companies to list on the UK stock market:
Chief executives sitting on the fence about whether to choose London as a listing destination might be watching Airtel Money’s success with great interest and noting the decent show of support from retail investors.
Airtel Africa’s success will have certainly played a part in Airtel Money also selecting to list in the UK, but so too will the market’s reputation of having a broad range of investors willing to consider companies from any sector and not only being interested in AI-related technology.
The UK stock market might have suffered from low tech representation, yet its more diversified interests have shone in recent times when investors have started to question if there is a new tech bubble, and whether it’s about to burst.
Brent crude prices are now down 1.3%, easing further s from where we started – having been down around 1% earlier this morning.
Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, says Trump’s comments regarding a pause in strikes, have “allayed fears” of a fresh flare-up in the war in the Middle East, following reports that the US was going to resume military action.
Fresh strikes would disrupt the flows that have been painstakingly re-established over recent weeks to pre-war levels, and represents a clear material upside risk to crude prices and term structure.
Brent scaled almost $106 before the comments from Trump took it down a couple of bucks to $104 this morning.
OpenAI has revealed that it is making about $20bn less in projected revenue than it had recently indicated to investors, raising questions about the break-neck growth rate in demand for AI.
The ChatGPT-maker company has told investors that its revenues for this year would reach $50bn (£37bn), a projection based on sales up to the end of September.
However, this is significantly less than the $70bn that it had signalled in information provided to investors last month, which was widely reported.
Forecasts of annualised revenues by the leading artificial intelligence players, including by OpenAI’s rival Anthropic, the maker of Claude, are closely watched by markets as an indicator of overall demand for a technology that is attracting huge investment.
OpenAI is in early-stage talks to raise $30bn in a funding round that values the business at about $1.4tn.
News of the $20bn gap buffeted US tech stocks on Thursday, with the tech-led Nasdaq closing down by 1.4%. Chip giant Nvidia fell 2.9%, Oracle was down 5.5% and Micron declined 4.8%.
Full story:Donald Trump has promised not to attack Iran before November’s US midterm elections, outlining a pause on the protracted war he has struggled to end after almost eight months.
In a Truth Social post on Thursday, the US president said Washington was “having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran”, which he claimed was “in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily”.
The strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas passed through before the war, was all but closed after the US and Israel struck Iran in late February.
On Thursday, however, Trump suggested that oil was moving through the strait in record volumes: “22 Million Barrels, last night alone”, he claimed, “with not one barrel coming from, or going to, Iran”. The figure could not be independently verified.
“We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd,” Trump wrote. “IRAN WILL NOT HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON!”
It’s worth remembering that this morning’s pullback in oil prices comes after Brent crude posted its biggest daily jump in two weeks, rising more than 4% to $104.28 per barrel.
That was driven by mounting fears of further escalation of the US war on Iran, which this past week was punctuated by Houthi attacks on two attacks in Saudi Arabia, and new attacks on ships in the strait of Hormuz.
US magazine The Atlantic also reported overnight that the White House had asked the Pentagon to develop strike options that could be used before the midterms.
As Deutsche Bank analysts note, “that that ran counter to assumptions that there wouldn’t be an escalation before the midterms.”
UK and US telecom stocks have tumbled after Elon Musk’s SpaceX took a major step towards launching a Starlink mobile service for American consumers.
The company announced it had bought a nationwide low-band spectrum license portfolio that it said would help it launch a full mobile business in the US.
This would be done by providing what it claimed was the world’s “most advanced broadband network from space”:
This prime low-band spectrum addresses one of the key remaining technical gaps that will pave the way for Starlink Mobile to become a major mobile carrier in the US.
The potential competition has spooked investors in some of the US’ biggest mobile carriers. Verizon Communications tumbled 7%, AT&T dropped 7.5% and T-Mobile US fell 6.7%.
Those jitters also weighed on UK telecom stocks, pushing BT (which owns EE) down 0.5% and Vodafone down 2.6%
SpaceX currently runs high speed internet connections in more than 160 countries, via its constellations of satellites.
Trump’s pledge to pause attacks on Iran, and China’s resumption of fuel exports, are offsetting concerns about potential disruptions to oil supplies in the US Gulf coast as a result of Hurricane Isaias.
The hurricane, which intensified from a tropical storm into the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season on Wednesday night, has prompted state of emergency declarations in Florida, Alabama and Georgia.
US producers in the Gulf of Mexico have temporarily halted operations, representing around 1.3 million barrels per day of oil production and 1.1 billion cubic feet per day of natural gas.
Reuters reported that personnel had already been evacuated from 121 production platforms, , citing the Marine Minerals Administration. That represents around 33% of the 371 manned platforms in the Gulf, and workers had been removed from five of 11 non-dynamically positioned rigs, it said.
Introduction: Oil prices ease as Trump pledges to pause Iran attacks, and China restarts fuel exports
Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy.
We’re seeing a dip in oil prices this morning, with Brent crude down about1% at $103 per barrel, following another momentary pause in US attacks on Iran.
Prices eased overnight on news that US president Donald Trump had pledged not to attack Iran ahead of the US midterm elections, which take place on 3 November.
It comes as public support for his war in the Middle East is waning and ultimately weighing on Republican election campaigns.
We are having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran. I want to make it clear to everybody that, while Iran is in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily, and while the Blockade will remain in full force and effect, with Oil flowing in Record Numbers of Barrels through the Hormuz Strait (22 Million Barrels, last night alone, with not one barrel coming from, or going to, Iran!), we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd. IRAN WILL NOT HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON!
An Reuters/Ipsos survey from late September show thats only a third of Americans approve of strikes on Iran, while approval for Trump among Republicans had fallen from 82% to 73% in a week.
Polling averages now show Democrats leading Republicans by roughly nine points on the generic congressional ballot, according to forecaster Nate Silver, the widest margin of this election cycle.
Oil prices have also eased on news that China is set to resume fuel exports, after a pause in deliveries during the country’s Golden Week holiday. The resumption of exports are expected to boost tight global supplies of diesel, gas, and jet fuel.

items.title: Shein outsells British rival Asos as UK revenue hits £2.58bn
items.summary: Online retailer’s 26% jump sharpens focus on exemption letting cheap parcels into the country duty-free Shein, the online fast-fashion retailer founded in China, increased sales in the UK by just over a quarter last year, overtaking its British rival Asos. The company, whose global parent group listed on the Hong Kong stock exchange valued at just over $26bn (£19.6bn) last month, increased sales at its UK division by 26% to £2.58bn, according to accounts filed at Companies House. Continue reading...
items.body:
Shein, the online fast-fashion retailer founded in China, increased sales in the UK by just over a quarter last year, overtaking its British rival Asos.
The company, whose global parent group listed on the Hong Kong stock exchange valued at just over $26bn (£19.6bn) last month, increased sales at its UK division by 26% to £2.58bn, according to accounts filed at Companies House.
Pre-tax profits rose 18% to £45.2m even as the number of people employed by the group in the UK, mostly in sales and marketing, rose to 113 from 91 a year before. The company paid £11.2m in current tax – understood to be mainly corporation tax – up from £9.6m a year before.
Shein said sales had been helped by a marketing partnership with the Wireless and Creamfields music festivals, a pop-up shop on London’s Oxford Street and Christmas gift events in Edinburgh, Manchester and Liverpool as well as London.
The strong trading figures are likely to increase pressure on the government to bring forward action to change the “de minimis” rule that has underpinned the rise of the fast-growing online specialists Shein and Temu.
Fears about China’s retailers and manufacturers dumping goods in the UK have grown since the US last year revoked its own de minimis exception for Chinese-made goods, crimping Shein’s expansion there.
The retailer’s model is based on shipping orders of cheap clothes from Chinese factories to homes so that each order is low enough in value to avoid import duties.
Under the US exemption, which was scrapped last year, parcels with a value of less than $800 (£600) shipped to individuals had been spared from import tax.
The EU is also phasing out its exemption on customs duties for low-value parcels. It began in July by replacing the €150 de minimis relief with a flat €3 customs duty.
The former UK chancellor Rachel Reeves said she would get rid of the UK’s rule, which allows overseas sellers to send goods valued at £135 or less direct to British shoppers without paying any customs duty, by 2028. However, major retail bosses have said the government should move sooner.
Investors’ concerns about global government regulatory changes meant Shein’s value was far lower when it listed on the stock market than had been expected several years ago.
It reached a valuation of $100bn in an April 2022 fundraising round, making it the third most valuable startup in the world, and then considered a £50bn ($66bn) float on the London Stock Exchange in 2024 before eventually launching in Hong Kong.
Shein, founded by the entrepreneur Chris Xu, runs most of its operations from China but sells all its goods outside the country. It moved its headquarters to Singapore at the start of 2022 and has recently begun manufacturing in other countries including Turkey and Brazil.
After forced labour concerns were raised, Shein said it had tightened its supplier policies, enforced through regular audits, with any child or forced labour violations becoming grounds for immediate termination of contract.
Last week, Shein reported a 67% fall in group quarterly profits to £173m in its first results since the float, blaming higher oil prices and freight rates linked to the war in Iran.

items.title: Birkenhead store shut down after raid
items.summary: A Merseyside convenience store has been issued with a three-month closure order after almost 10,000 illegal cigarettes and unlicensed alcohol were discovered. Tranmere Convenience Store on Borough Road, Birkenhead, had its doors shut under the Anti-Social Behaviour, Crime and Policing Act 2014. The closure order… This story continues at Birkenhead store shut down after raid Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
Tranmere Convenience Store on Borough Road, Birkenhead, had its doors shut under the Anti-Social Behaviour, Crime and Policing Act 2014.
The closure order was secured by Wirral trading standards and the council’s legal services team, working closely with Merseyside Police.
A search warrant for an address linked to the store resulted in the seizure of 9,440 illegal cigarettes and 2.95kg of hand-rolling tobacco.
When officers served the closure notice, they found four bottles of alcohol behind the counter despite the premises not holding an alcohol licence.
An illegal packet of cigarettes was also discovered, along with pre-packed food products that did not have the required UK labelling.
Officers also found the business was not displaying the required A3 tobacco age restriction notice or business name notice.
The illicit products seized had an estimated street value of £3,717 and a potential retail value of £10,679.
Wirral Magistrates’ Court concluded that nuisance and criminality had occurred at the premises in connection with the supply of illegal tobacco products.
The court imposed the maximum permitted three-month closure order, explaining it was necessary to prevent the identified nuisance and criminality from continuing or recurring at the premises.
Trading standards is now talking with the landlord regarding the removal of the tenant.
The action represents the 26th closure order secured in the Wirral since the council first used these legislative powers in December 2025.

items.body:
Poor sight and hearing can contribute to homelessness and make it harder for people to leave it behind, according to new research from homelessness charity Crisis and Specsavers.
Nearly half (47%) of people surveyed reported that their sight or hearing difficulties had worsened while experiencing homelessness, while one in five (21%) developed problems for the first time. People forced to sleep rough were most affected and shared feelings of increased risk to their safety, less independence and overall lower quality of life.
The study, based on research with 292 people currently or recently experiencing homelessness in the UK and Republic of Ireland, also found that nearly one in five (18%) experiencing homelessness with sight or hearing difficulties said their condition made it harder to access homelessness services, while 17% said it made it more difficult to secure housing or find employment.
The findings highlight the far-reaching impact sight and hearing difficulties can have on people experiencing homelessness, with half (50%) of respondents who were sleeping rough saying they felt at greater risk of accidents and a third (33%) felt more vulnerable to violence or exploitation.
One person interviewed for the report described how rough sleeping affected their hearing: ‘I was sleeping in a park and ended up getting an ear infection… It took a long time to heal… I’m still affected by it now.’
Another explained the challenges of managing poor eyesight while homeless: ‘I was wearing the same contact lenses [daily disposables] for multiple days, maybe up to a week… there was no other option… [My glasses] would have been broken or stolen.
Access to eye and ear services remain limited for people experiencing homelessness, with many people struggling to access the support they need.
More than a third (36%) said cost was the biggest barrier to receiving eye and hearing care with other difficulties being competing priorities, transport challenges and a lack of accessible services.
Four in five (80%) said free or low-cost glasses and hearing devices would have helped most, while 65% said support delivered through accommodation or homelessness services would have made access easier.
In response, Specsavers is providing free eye and hearing care to anyone experiencing homelessness through its Charity VIP scheme across all stores in the UK and Ireland. Since the programme began, it has supported more than 7,000 people by breaking down barriers to receiving essential services and delivering care where it’s needed.
Dimple, aged 39, experienced homelessness three times, first at the age of 17 when she was forced to leave her family home.
Dimple said: ‘I knew my eyesight wasn’t great but when you’re trying to find somewhere to live and put food on the table, going to an optician can feel like a luxury. I’ve met many people who needed glasses but couldn’t access them. Everyone should be able to access these services in a safe place and see the world clearly.’
Jo Osborne, social impact lead at Specsavers, said: “We’ve learned through our Homelessness Programme that there is no single experience of homelessness, so there cannot be a single route to care.
“Some people are comfortable accessing support on the high street when it is free and delivered with dignity, while others need services to reach them through trusted community and homelessness settings.
“Since 2023, we’ve helped more than 7,000 people affected by homelessness access free eye and hearing care through our Charity VIP scheme and specialist outreach partnerships.
“But no one organisation can solve this challenge alone. We need government, healthcare providers and the wider optical and audiology sectors to work together so that everyone can access essential eye and hearing care, regardless of their housing circumstances.”
Matt Downie, chief executive at Crisis, said: “Through our frontline services we know just how difficult it can be to access healthcare, like eye and ear care, when experiencing homelessness. There are many barriers people face, from worries about the cost of tests and travel to appointments, to fears about stigma or being turned away due to not having a fixed address.
“Not being able to see or hear clearly can have a detrimental impact on someone’s confidence and dignity, making everyday tasks even more challenging. This makes our partnership with Specsavers so crucial, offering quality care to people experiencing homelessness to help them improve their health and regain their independence.
“Together with Specsavers, we’re determined to keep breaking down barriers to healthcare so that everyone, regardless of their circumstances, can take their first steps to a life out of homelessness.”

items.body:
New Look, one of the UK’s leading fashion brands, is set to unveil its newly refurbished store at Festival Retail Park, Stoke-on-Trent, on 9 October, with a weekend of exclusive rewards and in-store experiences for local shoppers.
The refreshed store has been designed to create a more inspiring and convenient shopping experience, giving customers the opportunity to browse New Look’s latest collections across womenswear, footwear and accessories, alongside its 915 teen range.
Spanning over 10,800 sq ft, the store forms part of New Look’s continued investment in its store estate and wider omnichannel strategy, as the retailer continues to bring its physical and digital shopping experiences closer together. The refurbished store will feature a returns kiosk, part of a wider rollout across New Look’s store estate designed to make online returns or exchanges quicker and more convenient for customers.
The refurbishment builds on New Look’s continued investment across its store estate, including recent openings and upgrades at Bluewater, Lakeside and Milton Keynes, as well as the opening of its largest-ever concept store at Metrocentre this summer.
The investment also builds on the continued growth of Club New Look, the retailer’s loyalty programme, which has surpassed one million members, alongside its £30 million investment in digital capabilities. Together, these investments are helping New Look create a more personalised, convenient and connected experience for customers across its stores and online channels.
Mark Matthews, chief retail and digital officer at New Look, said: “We’re excited to welcome customers back to our newly refurbished Festival Retail Park store and mark the reopening with a fantastic weekend of activity.”
“This refurbishment reflects our continued focus on selectively investing in and upgrading our store estate. The changes we’re making bring our digital and physical channels together, whilst also showcasing our fantastic collections in a way to inspire our customers.”
“We’re looking forward to opening the doors and welcoming everyone to experience the refreshed store for themselves.”
To celebrate the reopening, customers visiting across the weekend can enjoy complimentary experiences and rewards, including goody bags for the first 100 customers who make a purchase, surprise prizes hidden across the store and complimentary coffee.

Matalan, the leading UK fashion and homeware retailer, is set to open its first store in Clacton this November, bringing its latest fashion and home collections to customers in the area.
Located at Brooke Retail Park, the new 30,000sq ft store will offer Matalan’s full range of womenswear, menswear, childrenswear and homeware, including its new Autumn/Winter collection. The collection brings a more effortless and modern approach to style, with greater focus on fabric, fit, quality and the design details that elevate the finished product – while continuing to offer the value Matalan customers expect.
The Clacton opening, delivered through collaboration between Tendring District Council, Britton Construction Ltd and Matalan, is one of several new Matalan stores set to open before the end of the year as the retailer continues to invest in its store estate. The new store will feature a bright, modern design, with improved navigation and visual merchandising making it easier for customers to discover and shop the ranges.
Annette Ormandy, sore manager at Matalan Clacton, said: “We’re really looking forward to opening our doors in Clacton for the first time this autumn. A huge amount of work is going into getting the store ready, and we can’t wait for local customers to see it.

Matalan has recruited over 30 colleagues from the local area to join the new Clacton store.
Once open, the store will trade from to 9am to 9pm Monday to Friday, 9am to 7pm on Saturday and 10am to 4pm on Sundays.

items.body:
Golden Phoenix, the established Cantonese restaurant in London’s Chinatown, has partnered with gluten-free vegan bakery Borough 22, located in Selfridges Food Hall, to create a limited-edition collection of three Chinese-inspired doughnuts, made exclusively for the restaurant. Available from 9th to 23rd October 2026, the collection brings together Golden Phoenix’s Chinese culinary heritage with Borough 22’s expertise in gluten-free doughnuts.
The collection comprises three flavours:
- Five Spice Caramel Ring
- Fresh Mango Pudding Doughnut
- Osmanthus Flower Cream Doughnut
The partnership marks Golden Phoenix’s first collaboration of this kind. Golden Phoenix has more than 30 years of experience in Chinese cuisine and is known for its Cantonese menu and dedicated gluten-free offering. Its current gluten-free menu includes dim sum and a range of main dishes, with measures in place to reduce the risk of cross-contamination, including dedicated cooking areas, utensils and separate storage for gluten-free ingredients. The restaurant is located at 37–38 Gerrard Street in Chinatown.
Borough 22 is a London-based dedicated gluten-free bakery founded by Ryan Panchoo. The business operates a concession in the Selfridges Food Hall on Oxford Street and produces gluten-free and vegan doughnuts and other treats. Borough 22 says its dedicated bakery does not have wheat brought into the building.
The collaboration was developed by Golden Phoenix’s Marina Lai-Lentz and Ryan Panchoo, with the aim of bringing together the two brands’ approaches to gluten-free food and creating something specifically for their respective audiences.
For Marina, the collaboration also reflects Golden Phoenix’s own family history. The restaurant was founded by her father, Winston Lai, who went on to build a portfolio of eight restaurants in the area. Following her son’s diagnosis with coeliac disease, she introduced a gluten-free menu at Golden Phoenix, which has since become a distinctive part of the restaurant’s offering.
Marina Lai-Lentz at Golden Phoenix said: “Gluten-free food has become such an important part of what we do at Golden Phoenix, so this collaboration feels really special to us. We wanted to bring together the flavours of Chinese cuisine with Borough 22’s expertise in gluten-free baking and create something genuinely new. We’ve had so much fun developing the flavours, and we can’t wait for people to try them.”
The limited-edition doughnuts will be available exclusively at Golden Phoenix, 37–38 Gerrard Street, London W1D 5QB, from 9 Oct to 23 Oct, subject to availability. Each box contains one of each flavour and is priced at £15.80

Myprotein, the UK and Europe’s No. 1 Sports Nutrition Brand[1] and part of the global THG Nutrition portfolio, has teamed up with Krispy Kreme® for a new collaboration bringing Krispy Kreme’s iconic flavours to Myprotein’s industry-leading protein range.
The first product from the partnership is an Original Glazed™ doughnut flavoured Whey Protein Milkshake inspired by the iconic taste of Krispy Kreme. Building on the success of Myprotein’s Impact Whey Protein, the UK and Europe’s No. 1 best-selling whey protein[2], the new milkshake delivers 20g of protein per serving, with 116 calories and a low fat content.
Launching exclusively on Myprotein.com across the UK and EU from 8 October, the product will then move into UK retail early October, including 730 Boots stores and five Boots wellness destinations. It will also expand to the US later in the year, through health and wellness retailer GNC.
The launch marks the start of a broader collaboration between Myprotein and Krispy Kreme, with additional flavours and products planned as the partnership develops. These will include Protein Blend, a new dairy protein powder mix available in flavours inspired by Krispy Kreme’s Original Glazed™ doughnut, Chocolate Iced doughnut and Strawberry Iced doughnut. Each serving will contain 25g of protein and 140 calories, with no added sugar.
Neil Mistry, CEO of THG Nutrition, commented: “Our community loves flavours that feel like a genuine treat, and few are more recognisable than Krispy Kreme’s Original Glazed™. People will always want treats. Our job is to make them better: the taste they love, with 20g protein per serving, in a Whey Protein they already trust.
It also shows how much the protein category has changed. Protein is no longer a niche product for a small group of gym-goers. It’s part of mainstream food and drink, and people expect to find it wherever they shop. That’s why we’re launching online and in stores across the UK from day one with a global roll out to follow.
This is the first of several flavours and products we have planned together, combining Myprotein’s sports nutrition expertise with Krispy Kreme’s flavour credentials.”
“We’re always excited to find new and unexpected ways for fans to experience the iconic taste of Krispy Kreme,” said Alison Holder, Chief Product & Brand Officer at Krispy Kreme.
“Partnering with Myprotein brings together two brands people love in a completely new way, starting with a Whey Protein Milkshake inspired by our Original Glazed™ doughnut. We can’t wait for fans around the world to give it a try and see where this collaboration goes next.”

Announced at Tesco Media’s 2026 Upfront, the developments form part of Tesco’s ambition to be the most strategic partner for brand building. By combining […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Today Tesco Media unveils a series of new capabilities designed to help brands turn deeper customer understanding into more helpful media experiences, more connected shopping journeys and clearer proof of growth.
Announced at Tesco Media’s 2026 Upfront, the developments form part of Tesco’s ambition to be the most strategic partner for brand building. By combining the scale and depth of Tesco customer insight with the group’s unique reach across stores, online and offsite media, Tesco Media can help brands build long-term customer relationships as well as drive sales.
Echoing Tesco’s message to customers, the evolving offering is brought together around one simple question: ‘Need anything from Tesco Media?’ and is grounded in Tesco Media’s Moving Mindsets research, which shows that relevance for customers is about being helped in the right moment, whether through inspiration, value, reassurance or ease.
Linking brand building and performance
At the centre of Tesco Media’s announcements is Ad Manager, a new client-facing platform designed to make planning, booking, measuring and optimising media simpler, more connected and more useful for brands. The self-service platform gives advertisers greater control and transparency over how they work with Tesco Media, while helping them turn customer insight into action with less complexity.
Today, Tesco Media Ad Manager delivers Sponsored Products and will expand shortly into Display and Video as Tesco Media builds towards a more unified experience across its media ecosystem. Over time, AI-powered workflows and recommendations will help advertisers reduce manual tasks, uncover new opportunities and make faster optimisation decisions, while greater interoperability will allow agencies and brands to connect the platform with the tools they already use. The aim is to make control feel enabling rather than burdensome, giving brands simpler ways to create media that is timely, relevant and genuinely helpful to customers. The infrastructure behind Ad Manager is powered by Kevel, a specialist provider of API-first ad technology for retailers and commerce media networks and designed to help Tesco Media deliver a seamless advertising experience across its digital channels.
Tesco Media is also launching a new influencer proposition, designed to help brands connect creator-led inspiration more directly with purchase. With data stating around 40% of shoppers under 45 actively follow influencers for suggestions on good brands and products, the proposition allows approved creator content to appear beyond social platforms in relevant Tesco Media touchpoints. This includes Tesco.com, the Tesco app and digital screens in store, enabling brands to get more value from their existing creator investments, and bringing trusted, engaging content closer to the moments when shoppers are browsing, considering and buying.
Tesco Media will also begin testing shoppable video within search and shoppable display within Favourites, allowing customers to add advertised products directly to their basket. The feature has been developed in response to research showing shoppers highly value this ease of access, as long as it doesn’t disrupt the overall experience.
Following initial trials with brands, Tesco Media will also test new creator-led formats across Special Offers and Favourites, aiming to cut the journey from inspiration and discovery to purchase, while keeping the experience useful and relevant for customers.
Tash Whitmey, managing sirector, Tesco Media, said: “Every Little Helps isn’t just Tesco’s retail promise; it’s how we think about media too. We start with the customer and ask how every interaction can be more useful, timely and relevant. These innovations connect what we know about customers with the moments and channels where brands can make a difference, from Tesco Media Ad Manager to creator content to smarter in-store experiences. Leveraging the unique customer insight and reach of Tesco, ultimately everything comes back to the same goal: making media more useful for customers and more effective for brands.”
Bringing greater intelligence to the store
Tesco Media is also taking a more dynamic approach to its in-store network with the launch of Intelligent Store Orchestration. Powered by Barrows Connected Store technology, the capability enables a single campaign to adapt according to real-world context, including store location, time of day, product availability, promotions, weather and local events.
Underpinned by Tesco Media’s Moving Mindsets research, the capability builds on the principle that shoppers’ needs change throughout the day and across different missions, helping brands move from static messaging towards more moment-led marketing.
The technology has been successfully trialled by a number of brands, including Costa. Its campaign ran across Tesco Express stores in January, resulting in a 47% uplift amongst customers that were new to the product, with brand repeat rate across all customers reaching 29%.
Stacy Gratz, revenue and growth director, Tesco Media, said: “The physical store remains one of the most powerful environments in retail media because context changes constantly. What is useful to a customer at 8am can be completely different at lunchtime or on the way home from work. Bringing greater intelligence into how campaigns respond to those moments allows brands to be much more relevant without making activation more complicated.”
Proving and improving impact
Tesco Media also announced further investment in measurement as it looks to help advertisers understand not only whether campaigns worked, but why.
Over the next six months, it plans to expand incrementality measurement across Display, Video, Sponsored Products, Scan as you Shop and Meta, enabling deeper insights across 93% of Tesco Media spend.
It has also developed a new multichannel geo-lift testing solution to help advertisers understand how media channels work together, including their combined impact on reach, frequency, conversion and incremental uplift.
Further work will focus on making full-funnel brand measurement faster and more scalable, alongside improving the Tesco Media insights available for advertisers’ own marketing mix modelling.
Turning customer understanding into action
Tesco Media’s proposition continues to be underpinned by the scale and depth of Tesco customer insight, with 24 million Clubcard holders and more than 85% of Tesco sales accompanied by Clubcard.
It is increasingly using these insights as a planning framework, helping brands move beyond simply identifying an audience towards understanding the needs, motivations and context shaping their purchase decisions.
To further streamline the process for brands, it is developing AI-powered conversational audience recommendations designed to make those insights faster and easier to activate. Instead of advertisers navigating audience taxonomies themselves, recommendations begin with the objective a brand wants to achieve, reducing audience-building time from five to ten minutes per segment to under a minute for multiple segments.
Nick Ashley, propositions and go to market director, Tesco Media, said: “All these developments are targeted at streamlining the journey for shoppers and brands alike. Customers do not distinguish between “brand” and “performance” journeys: they encounter a series of touchpoints that collectively influence the decision to purchase.
“The opportunity for brands is to use that understanding to make media more helpful – whether that means inspiration, value, reassurance or simply making a decision easier. Our job is to turn the depth of insight Tesco has into something brands can use much more easily in their planning to drive relevance and foster long-term customer loyalty.”

With just 50 days until Black Friday, new analysis has revealed that the traditional post-Christmas dip in retail returns is shrinking, while the volume of returns during the Black Friday and January peaks continue to grow year-on-year. Traditionally, returns volumes drop sharply between Christmas and New Year, giving retailers and warehouses a brief window to […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
With just 50 days until Black Friday, new analysis has revealed that the traditional post-Christmas dip in retail returns is shrinking, while the volume of returns during the Black Friday and January peaks continue to grow year-on-year.
Traditionally, returns volumes drop sharply between Christmas and New Year, giving retailers and warehouses a brief window to recover before activity spikes again following the early January sales. In 2024, the returns during that week were the lowest throughout the year.
However, data from ReBound Returns shows that in 2025, returns during Christmas week remained in the top third of all weekly returns figures for the year, rather than the usual sharp dip.
The scale of the seasonal peak is also intensifying. The biggest returns peak of the year tends to fall the week after Black Friday and Cyber Monday. In December 2025, this peak was around 23% higher than the equivalent point in December 2024. This growth trend continued into this year, with January 2026’s spike around 24% higher than January 2025. Following that pattern, this year’s peak season returns could be around a quarter higher than last year.
The data also showed that returns activity began to climb during Black Friday week itself in both 2024 and 2025, suggesting that a growing number of shoppers are returning items bought in the sale almost as soon as they arrive. Returns then continue to build, with the second week of December consistently the busiest week of the year for returns.
The findings suggest that retailers and logistics partners should not expect the usual breathing space between the December and January returns peaks this year. Instead, returns management experts at ReBound Returns are predicting that elevated returns volumes could run continuously from Black Friday week into the new year.
Liselotte Reijrink, sales director at ReBound Returns, said: “Retailers have got used to a short lull in returns over Christmas itself, before volumes traditionally picked up again in January. Our data suggests that gap is closing; in 2025, returns during Christmas week stayed high rather than dipping as they did the year before. Combined with a growing post-Back Friday peak, it suggests sustained pressure on reverse logistics lasting throughout the entire peak season.
“Retailers, logistics firms, and warehousing teams now need to plan not just for a Black Friday and New-Year surge, but for a relentless peak period of returns. Processing sent-back items quickly so products can return to stock and customers are refunded ready to spend again, will be essential. Preparing to manage the sheer volume expected will help to avoid a backlog that lasts well into 2027.”

items.body:
Retailers suffer ‘sharp decline’ in footfall
Retail footfall took a dive in September as shoppers stayed away from shopping centres, prompting calls for the Chancellor to slash taxes for high street firms.
In September, the UK’s total retail footfall fell by 2.9 per cent, far worse than the 1.7 per cent decline recorded in the month prior, according to the British Retail Consortium (BRC).
The trade body said the rising tax burden facing retailers means they cannot invest to boost footfall, adding that businesses are “fighting with one hand tied behind their backs”.
The headline decline in footfall was driven down by a 3.5 per cent drop in footfall at shopping centres, which had fallen by only 0.5 per cent in August.
The slowdown in footfall at retail parks worsened from one per cent in August to 1.7 per cent last month, as high street footfall marginally improved from a decline of 3.1 to three per cent.
The BRC said retailers were expecting a seasonal slowdown in shopping trips as the summer’s warm weather faded, but had not predicted the drop-off in traffic to be this pronounced.
Retailers had already suffered mixed fortunes from this year’s multiple heatwaves, as the record temperatures sent online sales soaring at the expense of in-person shop visits.
Andy Sumpter, head of analytics at Sensormatic, which produced the BRC”s data, said retailers “cannot attribute this month’s performance to the weather”.
“Instead, consumers appear increasingly focused on broader economic concerns, including the continued impact of inflation, household spending pressures, fuel costs and uncertainty ahead of the Autumn Budget.”
Inflation ticked up to 3.1 per cent in August and economists have warned that the knock-on effects of the Iran war have eaten away at the government’s fiscal headroom, restricting the number of interventions it can make at the Budget without cutting spending.
‘Help retailers keep prices down’
Helen Dickinson, the BRC’s chief executive, said that retailers will “do all they can to attract shoppers with great value and choice” following last month’s “sharp decline” in footfall.
“But until [the] government acts to reduce the cost of doing business, retailers are fighting with one hand tied behind their backs,” she added.
“By pulling back from another increase in business rates, the Chancellor can use his first Budget to unlock vital investment in our shops and high streets, help retailers keep prices down and provide jobs across the country.”
On Thursday, the boss of Tesco called on the government to exempt retailers from the highest business rates multiplier, following up similar calls by the chief of John Lewis.
Ken Murphy, chief executive of the UK’s biggest grocer, said: “We have long argued that the rate system is fundamentally unfair, that retailers pay – on average – four times their fair share of rates.”

items.title: Adidas accuses Australian label White Fox of ‘trading off its reputation’ with use of four-stripe branding
items.summary: Global sportswear brand is suing online retailer in the federal court for selling clothes featuring ‘deceptively similar’ design Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Global sportswear brand Adidas claims Australian label White Fox is trying to trade off its reputation by infringing its distinctive three-stripe trademark. Adidas is suing the online fast-fashion retailer in the Federal Court for selling clothes with a four-stripe design, which it argues is deceptively similar to its classic design. Continue reading...
items.body:
Global sportswear brand Adidas claims Australian label White Fox is trying to trade off its reputation by infringing its distinctive three-stripe trademark.
Adidas is suing the online fast-fashion retailer in the Federal Court for selling clothes with a four-stripe design, which it argues is deceptively similar to its classic design.
White Fox rejected repeated requests to stop selling and promoting clothing bearing the four parallel stripes, its rival claims.
During the first mention of the dispute on Friday, Adidas’s barrister Patrick Flynn SC argued the Sydney-based company had been using the stripes as a trademark for months.
He pointed to a picture of a White Fox-endorsed influencer wearing the company’s four-stripe shorts with genuine Adidas shoes as a promotion that would confuse consumers.
“There’s an intention to trade off our reputation,” Flynn said.
Adidas has held the trademark for a three-stripe design in Australia for more than 50 years and successfully sued another retailer for infringement over shoes bearing four stripes in 2013.
It meant the action filed against White Fox in September was “not uncharted territory”, Flynn noted.
“This is a pretty simple matter,” he said.
White Fox’s barrister Ed Heerey KC said the Australian company would argue the four stripes emblazoned on the label’s clothing were simply decorative rather than a trademark.
He highlighted similar items bearing the four stripes from other brands such as fast-fashion labels Princess Polly, Glassons, and Shein.
“Obviously Adidas has a reputation,” Heerey said.
“Their own slogan is that it’s the brand with three stripes. Emphasis on the three.”
The boutique will interrogate whether the use of four stripes was deceptively similar to Adidas’s trademark and whether any consumers would actually be misled.
He noted the 2013 judgment in favour of Adidas found it was common for branding to be placed on the side of shoes, but there was no such common practice for clothing.
Adidas is seeking orders that will prevent White Fox making clothing with four stripes and force it to hand over profits it made on the products.
Justice Ian Jackman – brother of one of Australia’s most famous exports Hugh Jackman – set the dispute down for a hearing in early 2027.
It marks the first high-profile litigation of this kind against White Fox Boutique, which has become a major player in the retail industry since it was launched in Sydney in 2013.
Co-founders Georgia and Daniel Contos, who own the company with Daniel’s mother Melina Maceri, focused on social media and influencer marketing to build their brand.
The online retailer later expanded to the US and UK and generated $542m in revenue in the year to June 2025.
Meanwhile Adidas, which generated a record $39.9bn in 2025, has vigilantly defended its three-stripe trademark across the globe with varying success.
The sportswear giant recently lost its trademark infringement cases against luxury brand Thom Browne in the US, UK, and Germany.
The upcoming battle in the federal court could prove to be a battleground for Adidas in a world of fast fashion and prolific imitation.

items.body:
UK grocery giant Tesco raids Kingfisher to bring in Chris Blatchford as its new CTO
Tesco has announced the appointment of Chris Blatchford as Chief Technology Officer (CTO) and a member of the executive committee from March 2027. He will replace Guus Dekkers, who is retiring in December following eight years with the UK grocery retailer.
Blatchford joins Tesco from Kingfisher, where he currently serves as Group CTO across its B&Q, Screwfix, Castorama, and Brico Dépôt businesses.
“There are so many opportunities for technology to improve the experience for customers and colleagues across the Tesco ecosystem,” he says. “Tesco has built an outstanding technology organisation under Guus's leadership, and I'm looking forward to working with the team to build on that momentum and continue delivering technology that makes a real difference for customers, colleagues and the business."
"Leading the technology team at Tesco has been a huge privilege,” Dekkers comments. “I know the team will continue to go from strength to strength under Chris's leadership, and I wish him every success in the role.”
Tesco’s Technology Director Jane Mustoe will become acting CTO from the beginning of next month. Group Chief Executive Ken Murphy says: “Guus’s leadership has been central to strengthening our technology capabilities and delivering our strategic ambitions. I'm also grateful for the contribution he has made as a member of our executive committee and his commitment to developing technology talent."
“Chris has led technology, data and digital transformation at scale and brings a combination of strategic vision, deep technical expertise and a strong track record of building high performing teams,” he adds. “I am confident he will help us continue to strengthen the role technology plays in serving customers and colleagues and supporting our long-term growth."

items.body:
2026 RTIH Innovation Awards finalists assemble! Presenting this week's biggest retail technology stories
It's Friday, the weekend is almost upon us, so let’s kick back and reflect on another eventful week for the retail tech space. Here's your briefing on the most important stories from the past few days, including Lidl GB, Deliveroo, Walmart, OpenAI, Morrisons, StrongPoint ALS, VoCoVo, The Very Group, Jysk, Enactor, Zalando, Asda, and Rokt.
1. Lidl deploys new self-checkouts that show UK shoppers on screens across retailer's store network
Lidl is rolling out new self-checkouts across its UK stores which play video footage back to customers while they are scanning their shopping. These will be deployed in all new stores and retrofitted into existing locations.
They will feature built in overhead cameras, vertically mounted large format screens, and LED lights to alert staff if people need help while scanning their shopping. To leave, customers must scan a receipt printed by the machine at a gate at the exit.
Roll-out is also taking place across hundreds of Lidl and Kaufland stores in Germany.
A Lidl spokesperson told RTIH: “The new self-checkouts are designed to be more customer friendly, enhancing the shopping experience while boosting efficiency.”
2. Morrisons partners with StrongPoint ALS and VoCoVo on Click & Collect pilot at Skipton store
Morrisons has launched a pilot of StrongPoint ALS’s temperature controlled Click & Collect lockers at the retailer’s Skipton store in North Yorkshire.
The aim here is to provide a convenient and flexible way to collect ambient, chilled and frozen groceries.
In a LinkedIn post, Christopher Evison, Senior Productivity Manager at Morrisons, said: “This is a great step forward for Click & Collect at Morrisons. It brings faster pickups - orders are pre-packed in paper bags and loaded into the lockers in advance. Simply enter your unique six-digit code when you arrive and go. And more flexibility - the lockers are helping us extend operating hours by two hours a day, giving customers even more options for when they collect. Freshness is guaranteed - the multi-temperature lockers can accommodate ambient, chilled and frozen products, whether customers are picking up a few essentials or their full weekly shop.”
He added: “There is also support when you need it - integrated VoCoVo headsets provide a direct two-way connection to store colleagues, making it easy to get assistance or complete any required ID checks. Huge thank you to all that have supported from both StrongPoint and Vocovo. It’s another great step forward in investing in our online proposition while keeping customer convenience at the heart of what we do. A huge well done to everyone involved in getting the launch over the line - a fantastic team effort. We’re really looking forward to seeing customers using the lockers and continuing to drive our online propostion forward.”
3. Walmart joins OpenAI's ChatGPT fashion push as Virtual Try On and Favourites launch
A dress spotted on social media, an outfit for an autumn wedding or a new style to try: OpenAI is adding tools to ChatGPT that let shoppers move from an idea to an image of themselves wearing it, with Walmart among the retailers involved from launch.
The new Virtual Try On and Favourites features allow users to visualise clothing and accessories using their own photographs, then save products to return to later. Shoppers can describe what they want, upload an image of an item or use a screenshot as the starting point for a search.
Walmart is bringing its fashion range into the experience. Daniel Danker, EVP AI Acceleration, Product, and Design, said on LinkedIn that the US retail giant was working with OpenAI “from day one” to make its fashion available through Virtual Try On, Shop this Look and Favourites.
Sharing an example himself, he added: “Found something I like. Think I should I buy it?”
4. Deliveroo teams with Coco on launch of food and grocery on demand delivery robots in some parts of UK
Deliveroo is gearing up to roll-out delivery robots, supplied by US company Coco, in the UK. These will be used for takeaways and groceries, with Deliveroo claiming that the robots will not replace human riders but rather complement them during off peak hours.
Canary Wharf, Milton Keynes, Leeds, Stockton-on-Tees, and Nottingham are the initial areas to get the service, with plans afoot for a broader UK roll-out.
Deliveroo runs a three-sided marketplace across roughly restaurants, grocers and retailers, all promising delivery in as little as 30 minutes. It is also a DoorDash subsidiary now, after being taken over by the US giant in a deal valuing the business at £2.9 billion. So this move shouldn’t come as a huge surprise.
5. The Very Group teams with AI powered e-commerce personalisation platform Made With Intent
The Very Group, which operates digital retailers Very and Littlewoods, has partnered with Made With Intent. By using over 800 behavioural signals, Made With Intent’s agentic decision engine predicts customer’s intent in real-time, helping to decide what they see and when.
Very says it will now be able to spotlight discount offers unique to customers based on individual shopping trends, as well as provide prompts at crucial moments throughout the shopping experience. Made With Intent’s engine is built on a proprietary model and optimisation AI agent that work together to allocate experiences across hundreds of intent combinations, learning what works for which visitors and contexts then applying it to future sessions.
Sarah Hanna, Digital Director at The Very Group, comments: “Made With Intent’s agentic platform unlocks fast paced, scalable real-time personalisation that can be executed to help enhance the customer experience, ultimately influencing our commercial KPIs. In fact, in the first month of the partnership, we’ve already seen promising results including revenue per customer increasing by a fifth in one of our agentic strategies, and an uplift in overall conversion.”
“Made With Intent gives our e-commerce team a brand new lever that they can effortlessly activate to make a difference on what our customers see and when, whether that’s one-off discounts or personalised payment options. It’s all about giving customers the right experience at the right time.”
6. John Lewis, Asda, Morrisons, H&M, Dunelm, and Waitrose among 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards finalists
We're hugely pleased to present the finalists and shortlists for the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards, sponsored by 3D Cloud, Business France, and Retail Technology Show 2027. We received a record number of entries this year and many fantastic examples of technology excellence driving transformative change across the global retail sector
Congratulations to all those who made it through the initial submission process! It’s now over to our star studded judging panel who will decide the winners to be announced at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London.
The event will be held on Wednesday, 4th November and consist of a drinks reception, three course meal, awards ceremony presided over by award winning stand-up comedian, presenter, actor and broadcaster, Aurie Styla, and after party until 1am.
Click here to book your place at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony on Wednesday, 4th November.
7. Ceva Logistics taps Sereact AI robotic systems for Zalando returns handling in Germany and Poland
Sereact, Zalando and CEVA Logistics have announced the launch of AI powered automated returns processing across key fulfillment facilities in Germany (Greven) and Poland (Świebodzin). Powered by Cortex, Sereact’s physical AI platform, the dual-arm robotic systems have entered live operations to autonomously process returned fashion items, marking the initial phase of a broader initiative to scale returns automation across Europe.
Cortex groups previously unseen objects - identifying, grasping and sorting items dynamically without requiring article specific training or pre-determined article sets. The technology is designed to work alongside humans. By taking on highly repetitive handling, it aims to reduce physical strain on employees, allowing them to move into higher value roles where human expertise and judgement are required.
“At the heart of our collaboration with Sereact and CEVA is a fundamental belief: true innovation happens when technology and human potential advance together. By solving the most complex challenges in modern fulfilment today, we are actively shaping the future of e-commerce logistics for fashion and lifestyle,” says Masood Choudhry, SVP Logistics at Zalando, which in July joined Sereact’s Series B round as an investor.
8. Currys ramps up social activity as it goes live on TikTok Shop
Currys has launched on TikTok Shop with a curated range of products, from health and beauty and coffee to seasonal and audio.
Building on the retailer’s TikTok activity, with its page having bagged over ten million ‘likes’, it will partner with content creators to showcase products to new audiences, and will host TikTok Live shopping events, bringing real-time product demos and instant purchasing to customers' feeds.
This will start as a trial in partnership with THG Commerce who will provide strategy, trading, shop management, weekly live streams and affiliate management services. As an official TikTok Shop partner, THG Commerce says it has generated over £44 million in GMV for its partners by providing a complete solution that covers everything from initial storefront setup and compliance to content creation, global fulfilment and customer services, managed under one roof.
9. Asda and Rokt team up to bring AI powered relevant offers to customers at checkout
Asda has partnered with Rokt to deliver relevant offers to the UK grocery retailer’s customers at checkout across its online grocery business and George, its clothing and home brand. Using Rokt Pay+ on the payment page and Rokt Thanks on the order confirmation page, Asda says it has created a new retail media revenue stream at the point of purchase, while customer conversion remains unchanged.
Rokt uses AI to determine the most relevant next action for each customer in real-time on both the payments and confirmation pages.
“Checkout is a critical part of the customer journey, so we were deliberate about how we approached it,” says Chris Chalmers, Vice President Customer Data and Loyalty at Asda “The results show we can make that experience more relevant for customers while creating meaningful new value for the business.”
10. Jysk rolls out Enactor powered unified commerce platform in Norway with Holland and Belgium next
Danish home furnishing retailer Jysk has gone live in Norway with its Enactor powered unified commerce platform. It has spent the last couple of months transitioning all 110 of its stores in the country to the new platform.
This integrates all store systems into one unified solution, with the aim of making everyday processes simpler and more efficient for both colleagues and customers.
“We now have several points of sale throughout the store, which means we can help customers and process payments wherever they are. My team has done an amazing job, and they really love the new way of working. It has been great to see how quickly it has become a natural part of our daily routines,” says Connie Evensen, Store Manager at Jysk Furuset in Oslo.
Sweden and Finland joined the new platform a couple of weeks ago, and the Netherlands and Belgium are up next.
