items.title: Parfetts expands The Local fascia in Carlisle with four new stores
items.summary: Employee-owned wholesaler Parfetts has brought its off-licence fascia, The Local, to Carlisle for the first time after securing a four-store deal with experienced independent retailer, Mark Duckworth. The move sees four long-standing sites across the city, located at Old Raffles Parade, Denton Holme, Harraby and… This story continues at Parfetts expands The Local fascia in Carlisle with four new stores Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
The move sees four long-standing sites across the city, located at Old Raffles Parade, Denton Holme, Harraby and Furze Street, move to Parfetts.
All four stores had previously traded under the Bargain Booze fascia for more than 20 years.
Significant investment across Duckworth’s four stores has seen each shop overhauled with new branding, fresh interior layouts, upgraded refrigeration and modern checkout systems to speed up service.
All 35 members of staff have been retained across the estate, ensuring familiar faces remain behind the counter for regular shoppers. Converting to The Local has enabled the stores to extend their alcohol range and introduce Parfetts Go Local Own-Brand.
The stores also continue to host community services, including National Lottery, parcel pickup and drop-off, and PayZone terminals, and promote locally sourced produce.
Duckworth, said: “When you’ve been with the same wholesaler for over two decades, making a change is a big step, but joining Parfetts has turned out to be the right decision for us. The Local gives us the flexibility we need to grow and maintain our margins.
“We are firmly rooted in the communities we serve and on first-name terms with many loyal customers who have been shopping with us for 20 years. Parfetts really understands the importance of a community connection, and it’s equally important to them as it is to us, which made the decision to become part of The Local the perfect move for us.”
Parfetts launched The Local fascia to sit alongside its fast-growing Go Local symbol group. The Local is an off-licence fascia focused on helping retailers maximise margins and drive sustainable growth.
Jackie Scott, area manager for the stores, said: “We wanted the freedom to set the range and prices in each store around what our customers actually buy, rather than having to follow a set format. Since moving to Parfetts, we’ve extended our alcohol range and improved margins by up to 3%.
“The promotions give us plenty of opportunities to offer good value, and the Go Local Own Brand range has gone down particularly well with customers. We’ve also had great support from the depot and retail teams.
“Free, reliable deliveries mean we can keep the stores well-stocked and change ranges more often, something we couldn’t do with our previous wholesaler. Moving to The Local has worked really well for us, and the business has continued to grow.”
The model offers the same simplicity that has helped Go Local become one of the fastest-growing symbol groups in the UK.
“All retailers in The Local fascia benefit from a 2% rebate, free delivery and regular promotional offers across a wide range of beers, wines and spirits.
Guy Swindell, joint managing director of Parfetts, said: “Mark and his committed team bring the experience and drive that underpins the growth of The Local.
“Having an experienced operator trust us with four sites that have served Carlisle communities for over 20 years shows the real strength of what we offer.
“Our focus is to give independent retailers competitive pricing, direct promotional support and total flexibility without locking them into rigid contracts. We’re delighted to welcome Mark to The Local and look forward to building on this initial success together.”

items.body:
Electricals and technology retailer Currys ramps up social activity as it goes live on TikTok Shop
Currys has launched on TikTok Shop with a curated range of products, from health and beauty and coffee to seasonal and audio.
Building on the retailer’s TikTok activity, with its page having bagged over ten million ‘likes’, it will partner with content creators to showcase products to new audiences, and will host TikTok Live shopping events, bringing real-time product demos and instant purchasing to customers' feeds.
This will start as a trial in partnership with THG Commerce who will provide strategy, trading, shop management, weekly live streams and affiliate management services. As an official TikTok Shop partner, THG Commerce says it has generated over £44 million in GMV for its partners by providing a complete solution that covers everything from initial storefront setup and compliance to content creation, global fulfilment and customer services, managed under one roof.
"Social media has become a genuine shopping destination for consumers, and we want to meet them where they are already scrolling. Launching on TikTok Shop feels like a natural next step, given our strong presence on social. As the UK's leading omnichannel tech retailer, we now offer customers more ways than ever to discover and buy the tech they love, whether that's in one of our almost 300 stores, on our website, or now, directly through TikTok Shop,” says Ed Connolly, Chief Commercial Officer at Currys
“For years, online shopping has been very transactional. You search, you click, you buy. What we have learned from operating on TikTok is that commerce is now an extension of entertainment and community. People are discovering products through creators they trust and content they connect with. For a household name like Currys, this isn’t just about opening a new sales channel, it's about joining a new kind of conversation with their consumers and bringing new customers into the Currys ecosystem. We are thrilled to be partnering with Currys,” says Darren Rajanah, Chief Revenue Officer at THG Ingenuity.
2026 RTIH Innovation Awards
Social commerce will be a key focus area at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards.
The awards, which celebrate global retail technology innovation in a fast moving omnichannel world, have now closed for entries. Our winners will be revealed at the 2026 RTIH Innovation Awards Ceremony, taking place at The HAC in Central London on Wednesday, 4th November.
Check out our 2025 winners here.
Our 2025 hall of fame entrants were revealed during a sold out event which took place at The HAC on 16th October and consisted of a drinks reception, three course meal, and awards ceremony presided over by award winning comedian, actress and writer Tiff Stevenson.
In his welcome speech, Scott Thompson, Founder and Editor, RTIH, said: “This is the awards’ fifth year as a physical event. We started off with just 30 people at the South Place Hotel not far from here, then moved to London Bridge Hotel, then The Barbican, and last year RIBA’s HQ in the West End.”
“But I’m conscious of the fact that, to quote the legend that is Taylor Swift, You’re only as hot as your last hit, baby. So, this year we’ve moved to our biggest venue yet, and also pulled in our largest number of entries to date and broken attendance records.”
He added: “This year’s submissions have without doubt been our best yet. To quote one of the judges: The examples of innovative developments across both traditional and digital retail spaces were truly remarkable.”
Congratulations to our winners, and a big thank you to our sponsors, judging panel, the legend that is Tiff Stevenson, and all those who attended our 2025 gathering.

items.title: 5pm Monday revealed as Britain’s parcel rush hour
items.summary: New data reveals that Britain’s parcel activity peaks at 5pm on Mondays, when shoppers are most likely to visit local retailers and parcel shops to collect, send or return items. As Brits get on top of their parcel admin at the start of the week… This story continues at 5pm Monday revealed as Britain’s parcel rush hour Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
As Brits get on top of their parcel admin at the start of the week the data from Collect+, part of the PayPoint Group, found Monday late afternoons to be the nation’s parcel rush hour, with activity reaching its highest level for the week at 5pm, closely followed by 4pm on the same day.
With one in five (19.5%) parcel transactions taking place on Monday, the top seven busiest hourly slots across the whole week all fall on Mondays between midday and 7pm.
This time of the week is said to be so popular it is a substantial 27% busier than Tuesday afternoons, which are the next busiest period for parcel visits to convenience retailers.
Across the week, late afternoons are the busiest time for parcel services, suggesting consumers fit collections, returns and drop-offs around their commute or the school run.
The dataset found 4pm is the peak hour collectively for parcels, followed by 5pm and then 3pm. Naturally, Sundays are the quietest time, with local retailers seeing nearly half the amount of customers (47%) looking to collect, send or return parcels, in comparison to Monday.
Although Sundays are quieter than weekdays, weekend demand remains strong, with more than one fifth of parcels (21.4%) processed on Saturdays and Sundays.
Together with late-evening and early-morning use, this means more than a third of all parcel transactions (35%) take place outside traditional working hours, as consumers fit sorting parcels around their busy schedules.
Sam Holden, director of parcels and e-commerce at PayPoint, said: “Our data shows that shoppers are starting the week by getting their parcel admin sorted, with more people using our retailers to collect, send and return parcels on Mondays than on any other day.
“Our network is designed to give consumers the choice and flexibility to manage parcels when and where it suits them, whether that’s commuting, doing the school run or out and about at the weekend.
“As we head into peak shopping season, that convenience is even more important as consumers want to collect and drop off multiple parcels in one place and would rather avoid risking lots of deliveries being left on their doorstep.”

items.summary: Hollywood Bowl called on its dynamic pricing system to endure falling ten-pin demand during the summer’s record heatwaves, prompting a share price boost. Britain’s biggest ten-pin bowling operator said the summer’s “exceptionally prolonged, dry weather” had “heavily impacted” its trading, as UK like-for-like revenue fell 5.6 per cent in the second half of this year. [...]
items.body:
Hollywood Bowl calls on dynamic pricing as heatwaves hit sales
Hollywood Bowl called on its dynamic pricing system to endure falling ten-pin demand during the summer’s record heatwaves, prompting a share price boost.
Britain’s biggest ten-pin bowling operator said the summer’s “exceptionally prolonged, dry weather” had “heavily impacted” its trading, as UK like-for-like revenue fell 5.6 per cent in the second half of this year.
“Demand remained resilient during the extended period of record hot weather in the UK, supported by our disciplined cost and pricing model, and our operational initiatives to drive footfall,” chief executive Stephen Burns said.
The London-listed group saw like-for-like revenue slip by one per cent across the group in the year to September, as poor summer sales were softened by 2.3 per cent growth in the first half of the year.
“Our affordable, inclusive proposition has continued to ensure we are well-positioned in an environment where consumers are closely watching what they spend,” Burns told shareholders.
Hollywood Bowl beats ‘unhelpful weather’
Hollywood Bowl operates a dynamic pricing system which allows it to hike or drop prices by as much as a pound, based on the footfall at its venues.
Burns has previously told City AM that this allows the group to deliver better value for customers who are willing to visit at less convenient times.
He said: “Those who are time-rich but money-poor can come at a time that better suits us and pay a significant discount, and then the money-rich time-poor will pay a slight premium to come at a time that suits them.”
Investors were heartened by Hollywood Bowl’s ability to weather record temperatures, as shares in the group jumped six per cent in early trading to 260p.
Ross Broadfoot, an analyst at RBC Capital Markets, praised the company’s “impressive update given the unhelpful weather endured by the group.
“We continue to believe the stock has been unfairly penalised by weather, if a more “normal” weather pattern were added to the measures taken by the group on cost and dynamic pricing, we would have most likely been looking at a decent beat for this year.”
Hollywood Bowl opened four new UK sites in the year to September, taking its total to 95 sites. The group operates a further 13 locations in Canada, under its Splitsville brand.

items.body:
FT Live Future of Retail Summit review: B&Q, Sweaty Betty, The Works bosses debate volatility, crime and AI
“We know we’re going to get inflation so we’ve got to be atop of costs,” said Graham Bell, CEO at B&Q at the FT Live 2026 Future of Retail event in the City of London yesterday, when debating trade and tariff volatility, a renewed cost-of-living crisis, shrinkage and AI with fellow CEOs from Sweaty Betty and The Works.
AI is a way to keep on top of costs, as well as being an IT and data cleansing expense, and another element in the omnichannel landscape in its emerging agentic AI guise. This was addressed in a separate panel at the event.
“AI can remove the gruntwork from design and speed up creativity,” said Melissa Mullen, CEO at Sweaty Betty, amid a discussion about how the technology will impact operations and future commerce, alongside other crucial drivers impacting the industry presently, such as distressed supply chains, theft and so on.
“AI is everywhere,” added Mullen, while discussing its impact on pricing, data, inventory, and email tag lines. However, as B&Q’s Bell countered: “AI has been around for a long time (in its non-agentic guise). It’s used for forecasting and on multiple end uses. If you’re doing Far Eastern sourcing and shipping, for example, it can aid faster, cheaper shipping and routing.”
Bell was also keen to stress that the volatility in supply chains and the cost-of-living pressures evident in retailing now, are not new either. “Since the Covid pandemic volatility is the new norm. Six years ago you might have had seasonal plans but we’re much more dynamic and agile in our supply chains now,” he said.
This was just as well during the summer 2026 heatwave in the UK, where B&Q’s DIY stores would’ve experienced huge demand for BBQ and garden goods for instance, but less so on other lines. Bell also candidly admitted that if you’re seeking to maintain margin as a retailer: “Your first port of call is suppliers. There is always value to be found, especially as we know we’re going to get inflation. Therefore, if timber is up, where else can I find value?”
Generative engine optimisation new tool in the omnichannel space
GEO in the coming era of agentic AI was also touched on during FT Live 2026 Future of Retail. Bell shared that B&Q “has entered into a big contract with Google”, with the aim of refining its data and discoverability by AI agents to enhance its searchability, as the former SEO era will imminently be eclipsed.
But this doesn’t mean physical stores, where advice and experiences can be given, will disappear, or other digital channels. The omnichannel approach still prevails. Instead, the agentic AI era will join retailers’ offerings just as their online and social commerce offerings have in the past. It is just that the practice of structuring and tailoring online content so that AI large language models (LLMs), such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity, can find and recommend your brand in their generated responses will bed evident, thereby giving retailers greater sales potential.
“We did 1,400 events in-store last year,” said Sweaty Betty’s Mullen, as she extolled physical retail’s branding and virtues, such as allowing people to try clothes on and providing a cheaper returns option for the online channel, alongside Click and Collect - not just delivery fulfilment options - in an increasingly omnichannel world.
“Consumers that shop across our multi channels are five times more valuable,” added Mullen. “It’s about getting them to engage, download the app and so forth. When intelligence becomes the commodity (in an AI era) the human element and customer experience becomes even more important.”
Physical retail has a future but must curb crime
One downside to physical retail is old fashioned shoplifting and staff intimidation, although as B&Q’s Bell pointed out M&S suffered due to a cyber attack last year. “You need to train staff against phishing and online threats,” he said. “But we’ve also seen people try to physically impersonate our engineers to gain access to stores and systems, so all round protection is needed.”
Bell also cited the Project Pegasus Taskforce between the UK police and the British Retail Consortium (BRC) as evidence that a fightback against rising crime levels is underway. This targets the organised crime gangs that are often behind the rising physical shoplifting figures seen in the UK in recent years.
Fellow panellist, Gavin Peck, CEO at The Works, bemoaned the “unfair tax on physical stores” in UK business rates. Sites on traditional high streets typically suffer much higher rates in comparison to out-of-town warehouses serving e-commerce players. Whether this issue will be addressed in the imminent UK budget was much debated at the FT Live event, alongside any potential help on national insurance pension contributions, the minimum wage, training programmes, and so forth.
Getting the proposition right for you is what matters
The entry of Primark into a home delivery and online market that it previously cooled on was much debated as part of wider discussions about omnichannel among panellists. For The Works’ Peck, it is something he is monitoring with interest having recently overseen his company’s exit from that market. “Our typical £1.50 margins make it difficult online,” he said.
Indeed, The Works has closed its website to transactions and its loyalty programme as it pivots back to its physical in-store 500+ storestrengths. “It was less than 10% of sales, loss making and we had two years of Christmas technical problems, so we closed it. It was the biggest thing we could do to respond to the present volatility, cost-of-living pressures and so on. We’ve still seen sales go up 7% year-on-year and our control has been enhanced.”
“We’ve invested the money in pricing instead,” said Peck, although he did admit The Works may return to the digital world later when it is more on top of its data and thus in a stronger position.

items.title: Will anyone turn Badenoch’s looming battle into a tapestry?
items.summary: The Tory party has been enjoying itself in Birmingham, not least thanks to the delightful wheeze of mocking up the Bayeux Tapestry to tell the story of British politics under Labour’s first two years in power. The exhibition may well prove to be among the most popular offerings at the party conference; behind Jeremy Clarkson [...]
items.body:
Will anyone turn Badenoch’s looming battle into a tapestry?
The Tory party has been enjoying itself in Birmingham, not least thanks to the delightful wheeze of mocking up the Bayeux Tapestry to tell the story of British politics under Labour’s first two years in power. The exhibition may well prove to be among the most popular offerings at the party conference; behind Jeremy Clarkson and ahead of Kemi Badenoch.
The former quipped on Monday that “a lot of people seem to have come dressed as seats” as he surveyed the hall from the main stage, but there’s no denying that luring the nation’s most famous farmer to address what’s left of the Conservative party was something of a coup. But what’s on offer beyond the celebrity guests and novelty embroidery? Well, quite a lot, actually.
Of course it’s hard for the opposition to generate a buzz when they’re still raw from a terrible election defeat and the new man at Number Ten has a spring in his step, but putting empty seats to one side the party is undergoing an intellectual renewal. Ahead of the Conservative gathering, Badenoch published a 30,000 word essay called The Right Way, modelled on the party’s Right Approach document that articulated Margaret Thatcher’s philosophy in the late 1970s.
‘A battle for the soul of this nation’
The document of 50 years ago stated that “the Conservative approach entails living within our means, paying our way in the world, mastering inflation, reviving the wealth-creating part of the economy and encouraging all those on whom it depends.” Our problems today are very different, but the solutions are remarkably similar. With Labour moving to the left as it rolls out state control into ever more areas of national life, Badenoch’s essay offers a vital alternative. It sets out the moral and economic case for a smaller state and argues in favour of “private ownership and competition within a free market overseen by light-touch regulation.”
It laments that, under successive governments, including recent Tory ones, “responsibility has been drained away from individuals, families, businesses and communities by a state that grows not because the public wants it but because fewer and fewer things are expected to happen without it.” In her speech today she will take this argument to the country, promising “a battle of ideas” that will constitute “a battle for the soul of this nation.”
It is a monumentally important fight and who knows, perhaps many years from now, scenes from this battle will be immortalised in another tapestry.

items.title: Australian supermarkets need more competition, but would government stores actually work? | Allan Fels
items.summary: A government supermarket would have to compete not just on price but on quality, convenience and range. It is no small undertaking Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast The Green Institute, the research arm of the Greens party, has proposed establishing a nationwide chain of government supermarkets. The proposal arises from a genuine problem, but whether it offers a feasible solution is doubtful. The retail groceries market is less than fully competitive. Coles and Woolworths account for about two-thirds of national supermarket grocery sales, while Aldi accounts for about 9%, and other supermarkets even less. Continue reading...
items.body:
The Green Institute, the research arm of the Greens party, has proposed establishing a nationwide chain of government supermarkets. The proposal arises from a genuine problem, but whether it offers a feasible solution is doubtful.
The retail groceries market is less than fully competitive. Coles and Woolworths account for about two-thirds of national supermarket grocery sales, while Aldi accounts for about 9%, and other supermarkets even less.
In this concentrated environment, consumers struggle with high grocery prices, and farmers and other suppliers complain that a lack of bargaining power leaves them short-changed. There are also formidable barriers to establishing a new supermarket chain on anything approaching a national scale.
Max Chandler-Mather, the executive director of the Green Institute and a former MP, said it was “common sense” that affordable prices on essentials require public ownership, comparing the publicly owned supermarkets to Medicare and public schools.
The Green Institute claims establishing 624 supermarkets and 13 distribution centres through new construction and acquisition of existing stores would cost $25.1bn over five years, after which revenue would make them cost-neutral. The new chain would have about 20% of market share; still below that of Woolworths and Coles, but significantly more than other competitors.
The large initial investment will presumably be added to Australia’s national debt and hopefully paid off over time.
The strongest case for publicly owned supermarkets is not that governments are naturally better retailers, but that food is an essential good and some communities may be poorly served by ordinary commercial incentives.
But inadequate competition does not mean the government should become a supermarket proprietor.
A government supermarket would have to compete not merely on price, but on quality, convenience, range and reliability. Most Australians are accustomed to large stores carrying tens of thousands of products, fresh food year-round, home delivery and sophisticated online services. Replicating that is no small undertaking.
Above all, scale is critical. Coles and Woolworths possess enormous purchasing and distribution networks developed over decades. Even Aldi, one of the world’s largest supermarket businesses, took years to establish a substantial Australian presence.
Could a new government enterprise do better?
Government ownership could also disguise the true economics. A public supermarket might charge lower prices because taxpayers provided its capital, subsidised its premises or covered operating losses. Consumers might save $5 at the checkout while paying more indirectly through taxation.
There may be a stronger case for public intervention in remote communities where normal commercial supermarket provision is inadequate. But even there, a national government supermarket chain seems disproportionate. Targeted freight assistance and support for existing local stores or particular communities would probably be cheaper and more flexible.
Public ownership would create another problem: government would acquire more direct responsibility for supermarket prices. It is inconceivable that political decision-making would be left out of the equation.
The Greens would do better to strongly advocate for one of their established policies – introducing a divestiture power into competition law, enabling courts to break up large businesses that seriously breach the law. Even if such a power could not readily be used against supermarkets, its existence could provide a powerful deterrent against anti-competitive conduct by large businesses generally.
Unfortunately, there is no simple answer to Australia’s supermarket competition problem.
Useful things can be done at the margin. Governments can make suitable sites more readily available to newcomers, merger law can prevent competition worsening, price transparency can be improved and independent supermarkets can be given every reasonable opportunity to expand.
But the only development that could realistically affect Australian supermarket competition would be entry of another large international group with the capital, technology, buying power and management expertise to compete seriously with Coles, Woolworths and Aldi.
Australia has already seen how difficult that is. The German supermarket giant Kaufland made extensive preparations to enter Australia, acquiring sites and committing substantial resources before abandoning the project in 2020 without opening a single store.
That experience is sobering. If one of Europe’s biggest and most experienced retail groups decided that Australian entry was unattractive, there is reason to doubt that a government retailer would find the task easier.
Australia may have to live with a supermarket industry that is less competitive than ideal for the foreseeable future. Governments should continue looking for practical ways of lowering barriers to competition to protect consumers and suppliers.
Establishing a taxpayer-funded national supermarket chain is unlikely to solve the underlying problem. Instead, it risks replacing concerns about supermarket profits with something just as troublesome: a large, never-ending bill for taxpayers.

items.title: Ikea to pilot online buyback service for secondhand furniture
items.summary: Service to be tested in Spain and Portugal this year, with a UK rollout if successful, as pre-loved markets boom Ikea is to test an online version of its buy-back service where the retailer offers vouchers for unwanted secondhand furniture. The service will be tested in Spain and Portugal before the end of December and will be launched in the UK if it proves successful. Ikea already offers buy-back in stores, including in the UK. The online version will extend it to a much wider audience, with Ikea predicting pre-owned goods are likely to grab 16% of the UK homewares market by next year Continue reading...
items.body:
Ikea is to test an online version of its buy-back service where the retailer offers vouchers for unwanted secondhand furniture.
The service will be tested in Spain and Portugal before the end of December and will be launched in the UK if it proves successful. Ikea already offers buy-back in stores, including in the UK. The online version will extend it to a much wider audience, with Ikea predicting pre-owned goods are likely to grab 16% of the UK homewares market by next year
The new plan emerged as the world’s largest furniture retailer takes on Vinted and eBay with its own secondhand online marketplace which launches in the UK this week.
The platform, which is already online in other countries including Spain and Portugal with bestsellers including the Kallax shelving system and Malm chest of drawers, will enable shoppers signed up to the Swedish company’s membership scheme to connect directly to one another to buy and sell pre-owned Ikea items locally.
The UK service will be free initially, but a “buyer protection fee” of about 5% of an item’s price will be introduced in time. At launch, buyers and sellers will arrange collection or delivery directly with one another through the marketplace. Ikea said it is exploring ways to make delivery easier in future.
“The secondhand market is growing and growing. It is now really significant,” said Greg Lucas, sustainability manager at Ikea’s UK & Irish division. “Secondhand browsing and shopping is now mainstream.
“The way people furnish their homes has changed. Whether they are moving, redecorating or looking for a particular piece, more customers are considering pre-owned furniture alongside new and are actively searching for items that can help create a home that feels personal to them.”
The secondhand home products market is now worth more than £4.5bn in the UK and is growing at about 6.5% annually. Ikea said its products accounted for about 9% of furniture sold on secondhand marketplaces in the UK.
Ikea said it was making the sale of used versions of its products easier by providing pre-filled product descriptions and price suggestions. The company also offers sellers 15% extra on the price of the item sold if they agree to be paid in the form of an Ikea gift card.
The change is part of a revolution in retail, where shoppers of all ages are now prepared to consider secondhand items.
In 2025, 63% of UK consumers bought products through reselling platforms, up from 51% in 2024.
The trend has boosted sales at Vinted, which began as a clothing resale site but is now expanding into homewares and electronics, as well as at Facebook Marketplace, Gumtree and smaller, more upmarket sites such as Vinterior.
The US secondhand site eBay recently bought UK fashion seller Depop for $1.2bn (£900m). Preloved items now make up about a 10th of global fashion sales.
There is heavy competition for the secondhand market, with the electrical goods retailers Currys and AO, for example, both selling pre-owned items.
AO expanded its secondhand position after acquiring MusicMagpie, which sells refurbished electronics and secondhand video games, in 2024. It recently also bought camera specialist Jessops, which controls the Camera Jungle secondhand site.

items.title: Asos shares tumble after cyber hack: Will incident hit embattled fashion firm's recovery?
items.summary: Asos enjoyed booming business during the Covid lockdowns, but has had a tough time in the years since. Today, customers were sent a message threatening a data leak.
items.body:
Asos shares tumbled by nearly 15 per cent after a phone alert from the company's app told customers it had been hacked.
The fashion retailer admitted customer data may have been stolen after users of its app received a notification on Tuesday morning with a message titled 'ASOS HACKED'.
It read: 'Dear Asos DPO and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance. Engage with us, or we will leak it.'
The fashion retailer later said it was 'investigating unauthorised activity involving third-party platforms that we use to communicate with customers'.
While customer names and contact details appear to have been stolen, Asos said it did not believe payment information or passwords had been compromised.
Shares in the company fell as much as 14.5 per cent on Tuesday before ending the day down close to 7 per cent after staging a mini-recovery.
Blow: Analysts said that the cyber incident at Asos did not seem as disruptive as the hack that hit Marks & Spencer last year - but it could spook customers at a key time
The incident couldn't have come at a worse time for the clothing giant.
Asos enjoyed booming business during the Covid lockdowns, but has had a tough time in the years since due to waning demand, rising costs and greater competition from the likes of ultra-cheap Chinese behemoth Shein.
It has tried to stem the decline by ridding itself of excess stock and clamping down on returns, even taking steps to ban customers from its platform.
And before the cyber-attack, there were signs that a turnaround was well underway.
Even after the share price fall on Tuesday, the stock is up around 81 per cent over the past 12 months. However, it is down 83 per cent over the past five years.
And bosses will be worried about the impact of the hack on the firm's recovery.
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said the incident had come 'at a terrible time' as it was 'happening so soon after positive signs of a business turnaround'.
He added: 'The company risks losing customer trust if there is a sense that its systems aren't secure.'
Latest in a long line of hacked firms
A string of household names have been hit by cyber attacks in recent years including Marks & Spencer, Jaguar Land Rover and Harrods.
'While the cyber incident is still unfolding, Asos will be starkly aware of the risks of any hack to its business,' Coatsworth continued.
'It wasn't long ago that Marks & Spencer was knocked for six by a cyber-attack and that had a major negative impact on its earnings.'
But not all cyber attacks are created equal. John Stevenson, an analyst at City broker Peel Hunt, said this incident seems 'very different' to the attack on M&S by teenage hackers last spring.
He said: 'We don't know how far this has gone yet but based on the information we have at the moment it looks like a fairly basic data breach - it shouldn't impact its ability to trade.'
By contrast, the M&S hack impacted most of the retailer's systems and customers were unable to make online orders for weeks.
Although the business could still feel 'reputational' side effects if some customers feel 'less secure than they did yesterday', Stevenson said he did not think there would be a 'material impact' on the brand's recovery.
The retailer has seen its number of active customers begin to grow again and has had a major restructure, involving selling warehouses and discouraging customers from returning clothes.
Katie Cousins, equity research analyst for investment bank Shore Capital, added: 'Asos has spent the last few years successfully fixing fundamental issues, and the strategy now is all about re-engaging the customer base and sustaining positive sales volumes, which it has made good initial progress on.'
Whether that progress will continue in the wake of the cyber incident remains to be seen.
In a statement on Tuesday, Asos said: 'We took immediate action to restrict access to the notification platforms and are working with our internal and external specialist advisers, as well as all relevant authorities.
'Basic personal information including name and contact details may have been accessed. We do not believe that payment-card information or account passwords, were impacted.
'Our website and app are operating as normal, with no current disruption to any aspects of our operations. Customer trust is incredibly important to us, and if the situation changes an update will be provided as appropriate.
'The company has cyber security insurance with a large global provider, including business continuity insurance. It is too early to quantify any potential impact on trading.'

items.title: Strong cooking smells waft into our house from next door if we leave the window open. What are our rights? DEAN DUNHAM replies
items.summary: Our neighbour has a powerful extractor fan on their cooker. The outlet is close to our property the cooking smells spread into the house.
items.body:
Strong cooking smells waft into our house from next door if we leave the window open. What are our rights? DEAN DUNHAM replies
Our neighbour has a powerful extractor fan on their cooker.
The outlet is close to our property and if our back door or windows are open, the cooking smells spread into the house. It is also unpleasant to sit in the garden.
The neighbour tried to redirect the air with a pipe, but it still smells. What is the legal position?
Name and address supplied
Dean Dunham replies: Persistent cooking odours forced into your home and garden are not something you have to endure. The law recognises this as a genuine grievance.
The key legal concept here is private nuisance – where someone’s use of their property causes an unreasonable and substantial interference with your own home enjoyment.
Strong cooking smells that regularly fill your house when a door or window is open, and that make sitting in your garden unpleasant, can fall within this.
A reader wants to know if they can legally do anything about the cooking smells coming out of their neighbour's kitchen
The courts have long accepted that noxious or persistent smells can amount to an actionable nuisance.
That said, I must be balanced. Not every cooking smell qualifies. The law expects a degree of give-and-take between neighbours, and the occasional waft of dinner is part of normal life.
The question is one of degree: how strong, how frequent, how prolonged and how much it genuinely interferes with your everyday living. Given your account of regular, strong intrusion affecting both house and garden, there could be a credible case.
Encouragingly, there’s also a statutory route that costs you nothing. Under the Environmental Protection Act 1990, odours can, in certain circumstances, amount to a statutory nuisance, so your first and best step is to contact your council’s environmental health department.
Officers can investigate and serve an abatement notice requiring your neighbour to resolve it, for instance by repositioning or upgrading the extractor outlet. Ignoring such a notice is a criminal offence.
Before you take any steps, try to resolve the issue directly with your neighbour. There are encouraging signs as they have attempted a fix, which shows goodwill.
Tell them, politely, that it hasn’t worked and ask them to try repositioning the outlet or fitting a carbon filter. Keep a diary of dates and times. If informal efforts fail, environmental health is your route.
Garage door I bought a week ago won't open but the firm I bought it from won't answer the phone
I bought a garage roller door a year ago with a five-year warranty. For the past three weeks, it has been broken and I can’t get into my garage.
The firm I got it from doesn’t pick up the phone, return calls or answer WhatsApp messages.
Is there a reasonable time I should wait for a repair before asking for a refund?
P.M., Hampshire
Dean Dunham replies: You have solid rights and practical protection. First, that warranty is not your only safeguard and often not even your best one.
Aside from the guarantee, the Consumer Rights Act 2015 gives you protections that can’t be sidestepped – goods must be of satisfactory quality and durable.
A roller door failing after one year falls well short of what you’re reasonably entitled to expect, so you have a clear claim.
Where you’re relying on a repair, the law requires it to be carried out ‘within a reasonable time and without significant inconvenience’.
Three weeks with no access to your garage, and a company refusing to even answer the phone, has comfortably exceeded what’s reasonable.
Being locked out of your garage is precisely the kind of ‘significant inconvenience’ the act has in mind.
If a repair isn’t done within that reasonable time, you become entitled to move on to the next remedy – a replacement or a price reduction, and potentially to reject the goods.
Here’s what to do. Stop chasing by phone and WhatsApp, which leave you with little proof.
Write formally, by email and by post, citing the Consumer Rights Act 2015, setting out the fault, the three-week delay, and giving a firm final deadline (say 14 days) to repair or replace before you claim a refund.
Check how you paid. If you used a credit card, Section 75 may make the card provider jointly liable.
A debit card offers a similar remedy called chargeback, but you must have paid within the past 120 days. Both are valuable fallbacks.

items.title: Morrisons is not a must-do deal for Sainsbury’s
items.summary: Odds are good the CMA would approve of a supermarket merger. But does Sainsbury’s need Morrisons? Would competition regulators really smile upon a combination of Sainsbury’s and Morrisons? One must assume the two companies believed the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) would give a thumbs up if asked, otherwise they would not have initiated their now-aborted merger talks . It’s easy to list the arguments the duo could make. First, the combined market share of Sainsbury’s (15.2%, on the latest numbers from Worldpanel analysts) and Morrisons (8.4%) would still be less than that of mighty Tesco (27.8%). It would not be a case of leap-frogging the market leader, which was Sainsbury’s big idea back in 2018 when Asda was in its sights . Continue reading...
items.body:
Would competition regulators really smile upon a combination of Sainsbury’s and Morrisons? One must assume the two companies believed the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) would give a thumbs up if asked, otherwise they would not have initiated their now-aborted merger talks.
It’s easy to list the arguments the duo could make. First, the combined market share of Sainsbury’s (15.2%, on the latest numbers from Worldpanel analysts) and Morrisons (8.4%) would still be less than that of mighty Tesco (27.8%). It would not be a case of leap-frogging the market leader, which was Sainsbury’s big idea back in 2018 when Asda was in its sights.
Second, Aldi and Lidl are a stronger force in the land. Together, the German discounters represent almost a fifth of the UK market and, since they’re backed by serious international buying muscle, their role as the country’s grocery price police might not be affected one jot.
Third, since Morrisons has already sold its petrol stations, the CMA needn’t worry about the touchy issue of fuel. Fourth, at a push, Sainsbury’s and Morrisons could argue that the UK’s food security (a growing political worry) would improve if the latter’s 18 food-processing factories were housed within a stronger company that could boost local production.
So, yes, one would probably bet that the CMA would ultimately approve some version of a deal. But what version? How many store disposals would be demanded?
The CMA, as in 2018, would presumably conduct a site-by-site analysis of drive-times to judge local competition. The regulatory instinct, one suspects, would be to err on the side of intervention in light of the overall national picture. Never mind Tesco’s size, it would still not be a simple decision for a competition regulator to sanction a supermarket setup in which half the trade, or thereabouts, would be in the hands of just two companies.
Would a deal still make sense after the CMA’s remedies? It’s impossible for Sainsbury’s and Morrisons to know until they go through the process. That’s the distraction factor for Sainsbury’s. Does its chief executive, Simon Roberts, really want to spend a year bogged down in regulatory back-and-forth? In the Asda episode, the effort sucked the life out of his predecessor’s reign.
It’s not as if Sainsbury’s is struggling today. The group is winning market share, profit margins are stable, there’s enough spare cash for share buy-backs and the strategic headaches of its bank and Argos have been solved by selling both. While it would be preferable to square up to Tesco’s buyers on more equal terms, life ain’t bad.
Round at private equity-owned Morrisons, the calculation will be different. Five years after buying the chain for £7bn, owners Clayton, Dubilier & Rice’s thoughts will be turning to how to exit a tricky investment. A disposal will surely look easier than a stock market flotation and the list of potential suitors is short: Sainsbury’s is indeed the obvious candidate.
All of which says Sainsbury’s can afford to do nothing, or wait for the terms of any deal to improve. It was the party that walked away from the talks, reported the FT. That’s not a surprise. If a relative bargain is possible, the hassle of a CMA process might be worthwhile. But this is not a must-do deal for Sainsbury’s.

items.title: 'He's absolutely bang on': Entrepreneurs back Jeremy Clarkson after star asked 'who would set up business in UK now?'
items.summary: Entrepreneurs have backed Jeremy Clarkson's warning over how hard it is to start a business in Andy Burnham's Britain.
items.body:
Entrepreneurs have backed Jeremy Clarkson’s warning over how hard it is to start a business in Andy Burnham’s Britain.
On the main stage of the Tory party conference this week, the former Top Gear presenter turned farmer and publican attacked Labour’s treatment of farming and enterprise.
Suggesting he may open another pub – but not in Britain – the Clarkson's Farm star asked: ‘Why would anybody set up a business in this country right now?’
The comments, ahead of what looks set to be another bleak Budget for business this month, won the backing of employers still reeling from £75billion of tax hikes since Labour came to power.
Jeremy Clarkson made a surprise appearance at the Tory party conference where he attacked Labour's treatment of farming and business
Hotelier and entrepreneur Steve Perez, chief executive and founder of Hooch and VK maker Global Brands, said: ‘He's absolutely bang on. I mean, this government in particular has had a smash-and-grab on business. They just see it as a cash cow to get more money for their schemes.’
He pointed to the £25billion national insurance tax raid on employment and inheritance tax raid on family-owned firms and farms.
‘There’s no way I would buy another hotel or pub because it’s just not worth the hassle,’ said Perez.
‘I think Rachel Reeves got it all wrong; she didn’t really understand business. And as Jeremy Clarkson said, they didn’t really know what they’re doing.
'I really hope John Healey will have some common sense and understanding of business.’
Matthew Elliott, president of the Jobs Foundation, a charity that supports business in creating work, said: ‘Jeremy Clarkson has asked why anyone would set up a business in the UK, and anyone who has watched his show will struggle to answer.
‘Hospitality is often the first rung on the jobs ladder, so with even the likes of Clarkson under pressure, it's no surprise that nearly a million young people are stuck in their bedrooms.
‘Government schemes to help people into work are welcome, but the more meaningful step would be to cut costs and make it easier for businesses to create those jobs in the first place.’
Andreas Adamides, chief executive of Helm, which represents more than 400 founders of fast-growing firms, said: ‘Jeremy Clarkson has put his finger on a problem I hear about from founders every week.
'A £146,000 national insurance rise is not a problem unique to a celebrity's pub, and thousands of growing businesses face the same pressure.
‘Clarkson says the rise landed just as his pub reached profitability, which is exactly where it hurts growing businesses most. For a scale-up, higher employers' national insurance can mean hiring five people instead of ten.
‘Founders are being squeezed at both ends, paying more to employ people and keeping less when they sell, and now there is talk of capital gains tax rising again.
'Nearly 6,000 business owners have already left in two years, and we should be persuading them to stay.'
He added: 'Successful scale-ups create jobs and the tax revenue Britain depends on, so backing them is not special treatment. The Budget is the Prime Minister's chance to show founders that if they build something here, Britain wants them to stay.’
The comments came after analysis showed billionaires with £120billion to their names have fled high-tax Britain since Labour came to power and there could be worse to come.
Figures from the Bloomberg Billionaires Index laid bare the vast sums of money and assets behind the exodus of the super-rich over the past two years in what was described last night as ‘a disaster for the country’.
Luke Johnson, the entrepreneur and co-owner of Gail’s Bakery, said: ‘It is a disaster for the country that big taxpayers and important investors are leaving.
‘They help fund public services and create jobs, and their exits will create a growing hole in the national finances.
‘We should be attracting talent and wealth, not alienating it.’
Hugh Osmond, the former Pizza Express entrepreneur, said: ‘It’s what we all said would happen and Labour didn’t believe it. Too high tax – big taxpayers leave. Obvious.’

Today, leading accessible health and beauty retailer Superdrug, has revealed how health and beauty shopping habits vary across the country, as the retailer celebrates the 15th birthday of its Health & Beautycard.
Based on Health & Beautycard purchases over the past 12 months, Scotland topped the skincare rankings with an index of 125, while Hampshire and Sussex led for cosmetics at 126. West Yorkshire recorded the highest wellness index at 139, while Central and West London led for sexual wellbeing at 133, followed by East London at 131.
| Rank | Top regions for skincare | Top regions for cosmetics | Top regions for sexual wellbeing | Top regions for wellness | 
| 1 | Scotland (125) | Hampshire and Sussex (126) | Central London (West) (133) | West Yorkshire (139) | 
| 2 | Birmingham West (117) | Birmingham East (121) | East London (131) | Birmingham West (131) | 
| 3 | Birmingham East (116) | Manchester (121) | Kent (128) | Lancashire and Cumbria (129) | 
| 4 | North East (111) | Birmingham West (111) | Manchester (125) | Hampshire, Berkshire and Wiltshire (125) | 
| 5 | West Yorkshire (111) | Scotland (111) | Birmingham West (107) | Hampshire and Dorset (109) | 
Index: 100 represents the national average. A figure above 100 indicates that the region spends proportionally more than the national average on that category.
Toria Bloomfield, from Thetford, Norfolk, is Superdrug’s second most loyal Health & Beautycard customer. She said: “I’ve been shopping at Superdrug for as long as I can remember, from weekend trips into town with my mum as a teenager to now stocking up on my favourite skincare, beauty and fragrance products. I’ve always loved the choice and value for money, and there’s always something new to discover.
“The Health & Beautycard was a game changer for me. I love taking advantage of the member prices and offers, especially when treating myself on payday! Over the years I’ve found so many favourites, including the Naturally Radiant Hot Cloth Cleanser, Collagen Day and Night Creams and Fruity shower gels.
“The team at my local store are always so friendly and helpful too, which makes shopping there such a lovely experience. After all these years, Superdrug is still my go-to for health and beauty.”
Simon Comins, chief operating Oofficer at Superdrug, said: “For 15 years, Health & Beautycard has been about giving our customers more value every time they shop with us and rewarding them for choosing Superdrug. Reaching this milestone is an opportunity to thank our members, particularly those who have been with us for many years.
“Value has always been at the heart of Superdrug. We want our customers to know they can come to us for the health and beauty products they love at accessible prices, with their Health & Beautycard giving them even more from every shop. We’re proud of what the programme has delivered and look forward to continuing to offer our members great value and meaningful rewards.”
For more information, or to sign up for a Superdrug Health and Beautycard and get access to member exclusive benefits please visit: https://www.superdrug.com/beautycard

This is the first trial location where Just Eat doesn’t already offer grocery delivery, therefore opening the service up to potentially thousands of new customers. Autonomous delivery is designed to complement Just […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Just Eat is expanding its autonomous delivery robot trial with Starship Technologies to Cambourne in Cambridgeshire, bringing AI-powered delivery to over 12,000 residents. This is the first trial location where Just Eat doesn’t already offer grocery delivery, therefore opening the service up to potentially thousands of new customers.
Autonomous delivery is designed to complement Just Eat’s existing delivery network where courier services are available, while also allowing expansion to customers in areas where traditional logistics services are more limited. The aim is to test innovative delivery solutions that expand access to delivery and create additional opportunities for customers and partners, rather than replace the existing courier workforce.
Building on strong customer demand in Sunderland and Milton Keynes, Just Eat is scaling its deployment of Starship’s autonomous robots, which use AI to navigate independently, avoid obstacles and make real-time delivery decisions. Starship Technologies has had an agreement in place with Cambridgeshire County Council since 2022 to operate in Cambourne.
As the trial has expanded so have the partners available to customers. Morrisons has become one of the first grocery brands to embrace the technology, recognising the potential benefits, including adding delivery capacity in the run up to the festive season and during offers such as the regular ‘Half Price Wednesdays’ on Just Eat – perfect for mid-week top ups. The robots are the ideal size for an average mid-week shop of around 12 items.
The Cambourne Morrisons supermarket which is now live is the fourth Morrisons to begin autonomous robot deliveries with three Morrisons Dailys live across Sunderland and Milton Keynes. Across all of these stores customers have access to thousands of products from everyday essentials and Market Street fresh favourites to last minute dinners and must-have treats – all direct to the customer’s chosen address via autonomous robot. Driven by ‘Half Price Wednesdays’, which offers 50% off essentials, cucumbers, chicken, milk and eggs are currently the most popular products across all Morrisons deliveries.
To encourage customers in Cambourne to try robot delivery Just Eat is running £5 off when you spend £25 with free delivery on all orders until the 21st of October. Just Eat is also helping customers across the UK to save with the recent integration of the Morrisons More Card into the Just Eat app.
Charlotte Exell, group online director at Morrisons said: “We are pleased to be working with Just Eat and Starship Technologies to trial autonomous robot deliveries from our Cambourne supermarket as we continue exploring innovative ways to serve our local community. Marking our first time offering Just Eat delivery in the area, shoppers ordering from our Cambourne store via the app will have their orders delivered exclusively by robot. In addition to Cambourne, the trial is also underway across three of our Morrisons Daily stores.”
Caroline Bates, grocery & retail director for Just Eat, said: “Our autonomous delivery trials are all about innovating to improve the customer experience – whether that’s enabling us to offer delivery in new areas like Cambourne or increase delivery capacity and speeds in the run up to Christmas. We’ll be listening closely to customer feedback on this new and exciting service.”
David Ringer, director of corporate accounts in Europe at Starship Technologies: “We’re delighted to be serving households across the UK alongside partners as strong as Just Eat and Morrisons. Our smart robots bring advanced autonomous technology to something very ordinary, and they’re built for reliability, because their first job is to serve the community and make the grocery shop convenient and fast.”
This trial is part of Just Eat’s wider investment in AI-driven logistics and customer experience, using technology to expand access to rapid delivery and improve the service customers receive, for example the introduction of Voice AI earlier this year.

items.title: Lithium batteries behind the counter: simple fire safety for c-stores | Viewpoint Mustafa Celik
items.summary: Every vape device on the shelf, and every used one handed back over the counter, contains a lithium battery - small stores can store and handle them safely without expensive equipment. Most retailers think about vapes in terms of age checks, duty and compliance. There… This story continues at Lithium batteries behind the counter: simple fire safety for c-stores | Viewpoint Mustafa Celik Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
Most retailers think about vapes in terms of age checks, duty and compliance. There is a quieter issue that sits on the shelves and in the stockroom every day: lithium batteries. Every vape device contains one, and many convenience stores hold dozens, sometimes hundreds, of devices, often packed in cardboard and stored close to other stock.
Since shops that sell vapes must also take used ones back for recycling, there is a second stream of returned devices and parts whose condition nobody really knows.
Lithium batteries are reliable when they are intact and handled properly. Fire services point to the same few triggers again and again: overcharging, short circuits, water, physical damage (crushing or puncturing) and very high temperatures. A shop cannot remove those risks completely, but it can make sure that one faulty device does not turn into a stockroom fire.
Treat stock as a fire load
New stock is the lower risk, but quantity matters. Keep boxed vapes away from heaters, radiators, sunny windows and the area behind the till where chargers and other electrics are plugged in. Avoid stacking them directly against piles of cardboard, crisp boxes or paper bags, which give a small battery fire something to grow into. Stockrooms are often where the fridge compressors, routers and spare chargers live as well, so a short look at what is plugged in next to the vape stock is worthwhile.
In England and Wales, the Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005 requires the responsible person for a shop to carry out a fire risk assessment and keep it under review; Scotland and Northern Ireland have equivalent duties under their own fire safety law. If yours was written before you started selling vapes or collecting used ones, it is worth updating it to cover where batteries are kept and who checks them.
The take-back bin is the bigger risk
Vape retailers are excluded from the Distributor Takeback Scheme, so every shop that sells vapes must run its own free take-back service. At a minimum, it must accept a used vape when a customer buys an equivalent product.
The Association of Convenience Stores’ guidance for retailers recommends keeping collected vapes in a separate container, in a cool, dry place away from windows and direct sunlight, away from other electrical waste and loose batteries, and only temporarily, generally for no longer than three months. Government guidance is blunt: unsafe storage of vapes is a fire risk, and they should go in vape bins only and be collected regularly.
A few simple rules for returned devices work in any small store:
Check each device briefly when it is handed in. Swelling, a bulging or split casing, leaking liquid, scorch marks, an unusual smell or a device that feels warm are warning signs.
Put anything that looks damaged into a separate metal container with a loose-fitting lid, ideally part-filled with sand, away from anything that burns – not into the general collection tube – and tell your collection provider, as damaged batteries need special handling. Never put it in the general waste bin.
Do not try to open, repair or “test” returned devices by charging them. The London Fire Brigade advises against removing the casing of a swelling battery or tampering with the equipment.
Book collections regularly instead of letting the container fill up over months. Count the units before each collection and keep the paperwork your collection provider gives you. ACS notes that take-back records must be kept for four years.
When a device heats up or smokes
Staff should know in advance what to do, because there is no time to look it up. If a device on the counter or in the bin starts to hiss, smoke or get hot, do not touch or try to move it. Keep customers and staff well away. If it smokes or flames, get everyone out, close the door behind you and call 999. Lithium battery fires can flare up suddenly and re-ignite. Staff should not try to tackle a battery fire that has taken hold.
A two-minute briefing during the next shift handover, covering where the damaged-device container is, what the warning signs look like and who calls the fire service, costs nothing and makes a real difference.
Small changes, low cost
None of this requires specialist equipment. A metal container, a clear spot for vape stock away from heat and cardboard, an updated fire risk assessment and a short staff briefing cover most of the risk. With battery-powered products now part of almost every convenience range, these habits are worth building in now rather than after the first incident.
Mustafa Celik is managing director of SOMUVA UG, which runs German online vape retailer Vapechamp

items.title: Asos app users receive threatening messages after hack
items.summary: <p>Online ‘fast fashion’ retail powerhouse <a href="https://www.asos.com/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Asos</a> is probing a potentially serious data breach after an apparent compromise of its <a href="https://www.computerweekly.com/feature/Snowflake-pivots-to-AI-platforming" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Snowflake data platform</a> resulted in threatening messages being sent to users of its mobile app.</p> <p>Customers across the UK reported receiving notifications headed ‘ASOS HACKED’. The messages read: “Dear ASOS DPO [data protection officer] and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance. Engage with us or we will leak it.”</p> <p>An Asos spokesperson said: “Asos can confirm that, at around 10am today, an unauthorised customer notification was sent to Asos customers. &nbsp;</p> <p>“We are investigating unauthorised activity involving third-party platforms that we use to communicate with customers.
items.body:
Andrey Popov - stock.adobe.com
Asos app users receive threatening messages after hack
A previously unknown hacking group sent threatening messages to customers of fashion website Asos after allegedly breaching its Snowflake data platform.
Online ‘fast fashion’ retail powerhouse Asos is probing a potentially serious data breach after an apparent compromise of its Snowflake data platform resulted in threatening messages being sent to users of its mobile app.
Customers across the UK reported receiving notifications headed ‘ASOS HACKED’. The messages read: “Dear ASOS DPO [data protection officer] and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance. Engage with us or we will leak it.”
An Asos spokesperson said: “Asos can confirm that, at around 10am today, an unauthorised customer notification was sent to Asos customers.
“We are investigating unauthorised activity involving third-party platforms that we use to communicate with customers. We took immediate action to restrict access to the notification platforms and are working with our internal and external specialist advisers, as well as all relevant authorities.
“Basic personal information including name and contact details may have been accessed. We do not believe that payment card information or account passwords, were impacted,” they said. “Customer trust is incredibly important to us, and if the situation changes an update will be provided as appropriate.”
Snowflake also confirmed it was aware of the notification and said it had begun an investigation itself, but at the time of writing there was no evidence to suggest a compromise of its platform akin to a series of breaches that unfolded in 2024.
Both the Asos website and app are operating normally and there has been no disruption to its core business.
The firm said it holds a cyber insurance policy with a large global provider but noted it was too early to quantify any potential impact on trading.
Hackers’ claims
The message received by Asos customers also included a link to a channel on social media platform Telegram, which, for operational security reasons, Computer Weekly is not including here. Should you have received the message, it should not be opened under any circumstances.
However, according to the BBC’s Verify service, the channel appears to belong to an operation going by the name Xuanye Group.
The BBC reported that messages posted to this channel claim that payment information has not been compromised and that the data stolen was “safe on our server” and will not be released for a “designated period”. The broadcaster has not verified these claims.
Virtually nothing is known about the previously unobserved Xuanye Group, although its name and terminology used in its messages suggest that the threat actor may originate in China. The name Xuanye may be a reference to the Qing dynasty Kangxi emperor who ruled from 1661 to 1722.
Eset global cyber security adviser Jake Moore described what was likely “one of the most visible hacks in history”.
He said: “The fact the threat actors managed to send a push notification to customers suggests they have gained access to at least some of Asos’ connected systems, but it doesn’t prove their full claims about the extent of the data breach.
“The hackers say they have compromised the Snowflake cloud data platform, which would put a lot of customer data at risk. By broadcasting their breach directly to Asos app users, the threat actors are likely trying to apply pressure to Asos, showing how extensive their access is so they can leverage some sort of ransom,” added Moore.
Next steps
With no indication as yet of what data has been compromised in the Asos hack, Natalie Page, threat intelligence head at Talion, advised Asos customers to use caution online.
“Avoid clicking on links in messages from unknown senders, be wary of app notifications and avoiding sharing personal and financial information with unknown senders,” she said. “Other attackers will likely jump on the incident to send out malicious communications, so customers of Asos should be aware of this social engineering tactic.
Page added: “Updating passwords on Asos accounts is also advisable, plus on any other accounts that share the same password. Asos does not currently offer mandatory multi-factor authentication [MFA] to its customers, but maybe given this incident, it is something the company should consider for the future.
“Alternatively, users can log in using authenticated third-party providers like Google, Apple ID or Facebook. If those external accounts have MFA enabled, it effectively adds a layer of protection when accessing Asos,” she noted.
But with the full story yet to emerge, Boris Cipot, principal security engineer at Black Duck, said the hack may yet prove to be a damp squib.
“The ability to send a push notification doesn’t automatically prove access to the data platform the attackers claim to have compromised,” said Cipot. “[Asos’] investigation needs to establish which accounts, credentials and systems were accessed, and whether any data was taken.
“We’ve seen this type of scenario before. Earlier this year, for example, the D1R group claimed it had breached Synopsys and obtained sensitive customer information, but Synopsys said its investigation found no evidence that its systems or customer technical data had been accessed without authorisation.
“We’ve also seen the 0APT group claim large numbers of victims, while security researchers later concluded that many of those claims appeared to be fabricated or involved organisations that had not actually been breached,” he said.
“That’s why, for Asos and everyone involved, the strongest approach is to keep calm, contain what you can and investigate. Treat the attackers’ claims seriously, but don’t treat them as facts. Follow the evidence, not the attackers’ narrative.”
Learn more about IT at Asos
- Earlier this year, the Computer Weekly Downtime Upload podcast met to Przemek Czarnecki, chief technology officer at Asos, to discuss how the company is deploying AI and agentic AI.
- In 2022, we reported on how Asos was preparing to go deep into the Microsoft Azure cloud portfolio, as it looked to ramp up its use of data analytics to support its business growth goals.
- Amid the first Covid-19 lockdown, Asos rolled out augmented reality technology to let customers see how an outfit might look on them.
