items.body:
Asos investigating after thousands of customers get notification saying retailer has been hacked
Sarah Butler
Asos is investigating after users of its phone app received a notification claiming hackers had “fully compromised” the online fashion retailer’s data.
The value of Asos’s shares on the London stock exchange dived almost 12%, after thousands of customers received a mobile app notification titled “Asos hacked” which sent them to a message on the Telegram messaging service.
However, the website and app appeared to be continuing to operate on Tuesday morning and it is understood that Asos is still investigating whether any hack has taken place.
The message was sent out to customers said “Dear ASOS DPO [data protection officer] and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance.”
Snowflake is a cloud platform used to store, process and analyse data collected by Simon AI including transactions and demographic information, such as clothing sizes and body measurements. It also enables push notifications to clients’ phones.
Dray Agha, senior manager of security operations at Huntress, an online security firm, said:
Snowflake is a massive cloud database where retailers typically store sensitive customer information, a real worry if cyber criminals have indeed accessed it as they claim. The push notification suggests attackers have breached the systems controlling the ASOS mobile app also. This is clear public extortion.
Sending a ransom demand directly to consumer devices is an aggressive extortion tactic designed to force the business into a quick negotiation. I strongly advise shoppers to watch out for targeted phishing attempts while we wait for official confirmation of a data breach.
The potential hack comes after a string of British retailers including Marks & Spencer, the Co-op and Harrods suffered major hacking events last year. M&S and the Co-op experienced stock shortages and the former was forced to close its website for several weeks as it battled to ensure its systems were clean.
Bank of England policymaker Catherine Mann says above-target inflation 'embedded' in UK
Bank of England policymaker CatherineMann, who voted to raise interest rates in July and September, said that inflation has become embedded in the UK economy.
Inflation running above the Bank of England’s 2% target risks getting further entrenched in wage negotiations early next year, she said today.
Last week, she said the Bank had erred in March, just after the start of the Iran war, by letting investors think it was happy to take a wait-and-see approach to raising rates.
Mann, who joined the monetary policy committee (MPC) in 2021, said at a conference hosted by economic advisors TS Lombard:
We’ve had inflation well above target for the entire time that I’ve been in my position.... And so inflation has become embedded.
Unlike the European Central Bank and the US Federal Reserve, the Bank of England has kept interest rates unchanged since the outbreak of the Iran war. Traders now see an 80% chance of a rate hike at its November meeting, and a total of 100 basis points of rate rises by the end of next year. The Bank’s base rate is at 3.75%.
Mann expressed concern that inflation looks set to hit 4% around the turn of the year, when many employers negotiate annual pay increases.
Other MPC members have said they will look for early signs of big wage increases, but have highlighted a weaker job market than when inflation last soared because of Russia’s Ukraine war in 2022.
The central bank’s governor Andrew Bailey is among a handful of policymakers speaking on Thursday.
IMF urges governments to offer targeted support for poorest households hit by energy price shock
Heather Stewart
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has urged governments to respond to the latest energy price shock with targeted support for the poorest households, instead of by subsidising bills.
In a new blogpost, published ahead of the IMF’s annual meetings next week, the Washington-based lender says energy price spikes can have long-lasting effects, and hit low-income households hardest.
By analysing the impact of the last energy crisis, in 2022-24, the IMF shows that, “for every euro spent suppressing electricity, natural gas, and gasoline prices, less than 20 cents reached the poorest fifth of households”.
It also points out that by making energy cheaper for everyone, across-the-board subsidies, “weaken incentives to conserve scarce resources”.
The IMF’s analysis comes as the UK chancellor, John Healey, weighs up how much support to offer households in the UK ahead of an expected sharp rise in utility bills next January.
Channel 4 to appoint David Brindley as new programming director
Mark Sweney
Channel 4 is set to appoint David Brindley, the boss of the producer of shows including Destination X, as its new programming director and one of the most influential roles in British broadcasting.
Brindley, who will be responsible for the vast majority of the broadcaster’s £640m annual programming budget, is effectively taking over from long-serving chief content officer Ian Katz who is departing this month.
Following an extensive recruitment process Brindley, who runs ITV-backed production company Twofour, is understood to have won out over former BBC Three and Sky entertainment boss Stuart Murphy.
The appointment, which is expected to be announced imminently, marks the final shake-up of a new leadership team by new chief executive Priya Dogra.
Last month, Dogra, the former Sky executive who took over from Alex Mahon in March, unveiled the biggest round of layoffs in Channel 4’s 43-year history as the financially challenged broadcaster seeks to dramatically cut costs.
Brindley will take on the title of director of programmes, after Dogra decided to split some of Katz’s responsibilities between several executives.
While he will be responsible for the vast majority of unscripted and all scripted commissioning, Louisa Compton, director of news, digital and audience trust, will head up current affairs and digital commissioning.
Kiran Nataraja, director of content strategy, is the third member of Channel 4’s senior commissioning leadership all of whom will report to Dogra.
Brindley previously worked for Channel 4 where he notched up credits including Educating Yorkshire, one of the channel’s biggest hits, and joined Twofour as chief creative officer in 2020. He was appointed chief executive last year.
Shares in the online fashion retailer Asos are down 13.3% now, after users of its mobile app received a notification claiming hackers had “fully compromised” the company’s data. The company is investigating whether there has been a hack.
Marty Bauer, ecommerce expert at the software company Omnisend, said:
Asos’s website never went down, but the commercial damage can start the moment customers lose trust in the messages coming through its own channels. People let a brand onto their phone because they trust it. Once that channel has been used to threaten them, they may start questioning genuine messages too.
Push notifications are one of the hardest-working channels retailers have. Across brands using Omnisend, push automations had a 22.9% conversion rate last year. If customers now switch notifications off or stop engaging with them, that could have a direct impact on repeat sales.
The first practical step is to pause any automated promotional sends. A discount arriving before an explanation of that notification risks making customers feel their concerns are being ignored.
With Black Friday approaching, Asos will want existing customers to feel comfortable buying again. If shoppers disengage from push notifications and email now, that is revenue the brand may find difficult to win back.
Tatyana Shishkova, lead security researcher at the anti-virus provider Kaspersky, said:
The ability of hackers to directly contact potential victims through push notifications in the Asos app highlights how disruptive cyber incidents can be when threat actors gain access to trusted communication channels. Beyond the immediate technical impact, incidents like this can quickly undermine customer trust, particularly when alarming messages appear to come from a legitimate organisation.
While attackers have reportedly claimed to have compromised a Snowflake environment, organisations should avoid drawing conclusions based solely on statements made by cybercriminals. Establishing what systems were accessed, what data may have been exposed, and how attackers gained entry requires a thorough forensic investigation.
Regardless of the attack path, the incident reinforces the importance of strong identity and access management across cloud environments. Recent investigations by Kaspersky have shown that cybercriminals increasingly rely on misconfigurations, exposed services and legitimate tools already present within an organisation’s environment rather than sophisticated malware. In some cases, attackers have even abused trusted business systems, including corporate printers, to deliver ransom demands directly to employees and amplify the psychological impact of an attack.
She added that customers whose data may have been compromised should remain alert to follow-on phishing and social engineering attempts. Cybercriminals often exploit the confusion surrounding high-profile incidents, using convincing messages that appear to come from trusted organisations.
Here’s our full story on Asos, and a bit of a potted history below.
Snowflake, which stores data for many major companies including Asos, has reportedly been the target of a number of data breaches in recent years, including an attack on Ticketmaster which saw customer details stolen.
London-headquartered Asos, which owns brands including Topshop and Miss Selfridge, has 17 million customers around the world, in more than 150 countries. It employs 2,800 people.
The UK is its group’s largest market, accounting for nearly half (49%) of revenues in its first half results.
However, more recently Asos has struggled against competition from Boohoo, Shein and others, and is in the middle of a major turnaround programme as it tries to reverse a drop in sales and return to profit.
Late last year, the company said it was testing “Styled for You”, which uses AI trained on its database of 100,000 curated outfits to suggest items that could go together with those a shopper has already bought or has searched.
Marie Wilcox, vice president of market strategy at the automated cyber investigation platform Binalyze, said:
This notification was psychological warfare, designed to whip up panic. Attackers know that any panic piles on the pressure on Asos to think about paying up rather than taking time to develop a rational response.
This is a clear shift in how we see breaches: from learning after the fact, to thousands of users seeing the news pushed onto their phone home screens in real time.
The next few hours are crucial. Asos cannot let panicked pressure dictate its response. The priority must be investigation, and closing the gap that allowed this mass notification to go out. Activity like this will surely have huge noise around it that leaves a clear trail, so there should be plenty of evidence of what happened and how to fix it.
This is also further evidence of the pressure security teams are under. They are overloaded: 15% of security alerts have to be flat-out ignored, 37% of vulnerabilities go undiscovered, and the focus is so totally on alerts and response that teams cannot proactively hunt threats before they strike. In this environment something will inevitably break through.
Marijus Briedis, chief technology officer at NordVPN, part of the cybersecurity software company Nord Security, said:
This is an unusually brazen and threatening message. The attackers aren’t simply claiming to have breached Asos - they’re publicly telling the company to engage with them or they will leak what they say they have obtained.
What makes it even more concerning is how that threat appears to have been delivered. A message apparently written for ASOS’s data protection and IT teams has instead been pushed directly to customers through the company’s own app notification system. That suggests someone has gained unauthorised access to at least part of Asos’s systems, although we don’t yet know how extensive that access is.
The attackers claim they have ‘fully compromised’ Asos Snowflake instance. Snowflake is a cloud data platform businesses use to store and analyse large quantities of information. If that claim proves genuine, the critical question will be what information was held there and whether any of it was accessed or downloaded. At this stage, however, customers shouldn’t assume their personal or payment information has been stolen - that hasn’t been established.
What customers should be particularly alert to now is what happens next, Briedis said.
High-profile cyber incidents create ideal conditions for phishing attacks. Criminals may exploit the publicity by sending emails and texts claiming to be from Asos, perhaps asking customers to reset a password, confirm payment details, check an order or claim a refund.
Don’t click links in unexpected messages, even if they look convincing. Go directly to the Asos app or website instead. Customers should also make sure their Asos password is unique and, if they’ve used the same password elsewhere, change it on those accounts too.
Until Asos completes its investigation, we won’t know exactly what has been accessed or how the attackers got in. But this incident shows how powerful access to a trusted communications channel can be. When an attacker can potentially speak to customers through a company’s own systems, it makes the threat considerably more convincing and potentially much more damaging.

Asos customers receive phone alerts saying retailer has been hacked
Asos customers have been sent a phone alert saying the retailer has been hacked, and the online fashion retailer is investigating.
Customers received a mobile app notification on Tuesday, titled “Asos hacked”, which directed them to a Telegram account.
The message read: “Dear ASOS DPO [data protection officer] and IT, we have full compromised the Snowflake instance. Engage with us, or we will leak it,” followed by the Telegram link.
Shares in the company tumbled almost 12%, making them the biggest faller on the FTSE 250 index.
It comes after a raft of UK retailers have been targeted by cyber attackers over the past two years, including Marks & Spencer, the Co-op and Harrods – as well as carmaker Jaguar Land Rover.
Europe needs to double its use of electricity by 2040 to reduce emissions but to also provide critical shock absorbers for gas and oil price spikes, Ursula von der Leyen has said, reports Lisa O’Carroll from Brussels.
The price of gas had soared 140% since the US-Israeli assault on Iran began on 28 February, while diesel has doubled in price, the European Commission president told parliamentarians in Strasbourg.
In total the EU has paid more than €100bn extra for fuel “without a single molecule extra of energy” being imported or produced. Von der Leyen said:
Today, electricity accounts for less than a quarter of our final energy consumption. Therefore, our Electrification Action Plan sets clear targets to double that by 2040.
Measures across the bloc were different according to need with France and Romania offering vouchers for the low-income households. It would also be prolonging state-aid energy focussed programme for industries, Accelerate EU, she announced as well as participating in the release of 100m barrels of oil, announced by the G7 last Friday.
Slowest fall in UK construction output since January, but housebuilding remains weak
Construction activity across the UK remained in decline last month, but the downturn was the least pronounced since the start of the year, according to a closely-watched survey.
The purchasing managers’ index for construction from S&P Global rose to an eight-month high of 46.1 in September from 44.3 in August, but remained well below the 50 mark that separates growth from contraction. It has been in decline since January last year.
A sharp downturn in housebuilding eased slightly but it remained the weakest area, followed by civil engineering, while commercial work showed only a small decline.
Tim Moore, economics director at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said:
The downturn in UK construction output was the least marked since January. All three sub-sectors have seen a degree of stabilisation relative to the rapid declines reported in the second quarter of 2026. In September, commercial building work saw its smallest fall in activity since May 2025. House building was again the weakest performer as rising borrowing costs and unfavourable market conditions weighed on output.
Total new orders were relatively subdued in September as construction firms reported longer sales conversion cycles and clients deferred decision-making on major projects.
The new orders measure fell to a three-month low of 45.9 from 47.7, amid subdued demand, geopolitical tensions and rising input costs.
Companies’ costs rose at their slowest rate since the outbreak of the Iran war in late February, but Moore said this was unlikely to last due to higher energy and transport costs.
Business optimism was the weakest since May.
S&P Global said its all-sector PMI survey, which includes data for services, manufacturing and construction, slipped to a three-month low of 51.5 in September from 51.8.

items.body:
Robert De Niro on $1.3billion hospitality empire: ‘I’m very protective of Nobu’
Goodfellas and Taxi Driver legend Robert De Niro talks exclusively to City AM The Magazine about his hospitality empire, which quietly occupies the 83-year-old New York-born actor in-between his film-making. Over the last 40 years, De Niro has been launching Nobu restaurants around the world, a Japanese brand he is fiercely protective of. He speaks to us about maintaining the quality at all costs, how restaurant work differs from the movies, and the concept of ‘ikigai’, which means never retiring
In an intimidatingly futuristic building made almost entirely of glass, I pass through a marble-clad lobby, up a flight of stairs and into an expensive-looking hotel suite. Here a handful of serious-looking people sit around a brightly lit boardroom table. Most of them are hospitality professionals: a general manager, a chief executive, a gaggle of publicists. One of them is the most famous actor in the world.
Robert De Niro looks at the ground, channelling all of his energy into standing up to shake my hand. He lifts slowly out of his chair but I ask him to, please, sit down, don’t get up on my account. He’s shrunk a little from his heyday, his shoulders more rounded, but that’s all that reveals his 83 years. And if he’s a little less formidable, it’s only physically. His vibe is still deadly: De Niro would rather spit than say a single word more than is necessary, or, worse, a word he didn’t mean.
Robert De Niro and the Nobu story
We’re at Nobu Portman Square hotel in Marylebone, part of the group the actor co-founded in the 1990s, a fact that still carries a sheen of unbelievability even after three decades. De Niro isn’t even the only octogenarian around this table. Also joining us is Nobu co-founder Meir Teper, the 83-year-old film producer who, like De Niro, side-hustles as a lifestyle tycoon.
De Niro is here to discuss the three Nobu Hotel & Residences opening in Egypt, including a restaurant on the north coast that’s already started plating up sushi, and the phased launches over the next five years of resorts in Cairo and the coastline. Residences are also soon-to-launch in Manchester, as is Nobu’s first wellness club and countryside retreat, Nobu Woolfox, which will open next year on an estate near Rutland in the Midlands, rivalling luxury offerings in the Cotswolds. De Niro is coming for the wellness industry, too.
Nobu is an incredible success story. There are now 19 Nobu hotels and 55 restaurants serving namesake chef Nobu Matsuhisa’s Japanese-Peruvian cuisine. International openings are green-lit by De Niro himself, who is a kind of vibe checker for the brand. As Teper puts it: “We follow his vision.” The story goes that De Niro convinced chef Nobu to open a restaurant in Tribeca in New York in 1994; that flagship, still thriving, was the beginning of a global empire now estimated to be worth $1.3 billion (De Niro, Teper and Matsuhisa are understood to own 80 per cent; with the other 20 per cent held by private equity firm Blackstone).
He’ll say, ‘I don’t think we belong here’
By all accounts, De Niro has an instinct for destinations that will – and crucially, will not – work. Sometimes that instinct seems to border on the preternatural: when our sister publication spoke to him in 2025, he admitted he’d never been to Manchester and knew nothing about the city, despite having commissioned a Nobu Residences there. So how on earth does a man regarded as one of the best actors of his generation know what makes a good location for a Japanese restaurant? “I just say, ‘Where do I wanna go?’” De Niro tells me. He really does speak in that smash-em-up, gravelly, menacing tone. “Would I like to walk into that restaurant in that particular place?” He scrunches his face to make an impression of a first-time visitor. “That first sight, where it is, what part of the world… it’s important.”
His strategy clearly works: only five Nobu restaurants have closed in 30 years, which is especially impressive when you consider the hardships faced by the hospitality industry (in London alone half of restaurants shut within two years of their first service). Madonna once said you could tell if a city was going to be fun by whether it had a Nobu in it. In keeping with De Niro’s reputation for speaking his mind, he’ll happily draw a red line through potential new locations. “He’ll say: ‘I don’t think we belong here,’” says Teper. “I don’t want to name names, but it’s not like when somebody approaches us we just say ‘Okay let’s do it.’”
De Niro inspired by eating on location
When I ask De Niro what’s unique about the brand, he says it’s simple: the quality of the food and the location. There is no pandering to trends, no evolving ‘concept’. It’s just good sushi. It was British film director Roland Joffé who first introduced De Niro to the cooking of Nobu Matsuhisa in the late 1980s and it was love at first bite. At that point, chef Nobu had only one restaurant in Los Angeles. “Roland said, ‘Come to this restaurant, you’ll like it,’” remembers De Niro. “I was maybe an hour into eating and meeting Nobu and I said ‘If you ever want to open a restaurant in New York just let me know.’
“For me it was a no-brainer. It would work in New York. And here [in London], too. The Japanese restaurants I’d been to were all the same. Very good, but conservative, staid, nothing exciting. They didn’t pretend to be. But Nobu had another thing, the Latin from his time in Peru, that made it special. So that was it: I said: ‘This will work’. I’d opened a grill with Drew Nieporent, a local restaurateur in Tribeca, a year or two before I met Nobu and I put him and Drew together. It took a while to get it going, Nobu was apprehensive. I can’t remember all the details but finally it happened.”
The question is, why?
The partnership makes sense. While Nobu, 76, was brought up slicing fish and thinking about flavour, De Niro spent years travelling the world filming, developing an eagle eye for what makes a restaurant people want to hang out in.
The bigger question, though, is… why? Why does one of the most lauded actors in the world spend his time promoting expensive condos in Egypt when he’s already worth an estimated $500m? Especially when he might not even live to see them completed? And how does an 83-year-old factor business into his life when he has a three-year-old daughter, who in a recent interview, through tears, he described as the “pure joy” in his life? “She has a very sweet kind of way of looking at you,” De Niro told AARP. “And just taking you in… They just look at you and take it in. I want to be around for as long as I can, to enjoy it, to enjoy her.” He lives with his girlfriend, 46-year-old martial arts instructor and dancer Tiffany Chen, and his youngest daughter in a 100 acre Hudson Valley property that boasts its own ski slope. He has seven children altogether with four women; the oldest, Drena, is 55.
Maintain the quality. Period. It’s that simple.
I suggest it’s unusual for someone of his age to be working at all, let alone as the co-founder of an international hospitality empire. De Niro nods deeply and puts up no defence. Does he find something here he can’t in Hollywood? Like, is the public-facing world of film sets and red carpets passé compared to the rigour of the luxury restaurant world? Just for a second, I experience old-school De Niro: He tenses his facial muscles to pull that characteristically strained expression, as if he’s just sucked on a lemon. “No, that’s different,” he says, in combat mode. “It’s just a different thing. I enjoy it and feel very protective of it because I’m part of the creative… We all want to make sure we maintain the quality and everything. That’s it. That’s the key. You’ve got to be careful with that stuff.”
What happens if the quality isn’t maintained? “We were talking about this the other day – someone was saying, ‘Why have you got to spend that?’. But somebody will visit and notice that’s something a little… off. And then maybe they notice something else and then something else, and all of a sudden it’s not the same restaurant. Then people start to say, ‘Nah I don’t wanna go there.’ The only thing you can do is maintain the quality. Period. It’s that simple.”
Nobu offers a sense of control
His acting roles have, of course, changed with age: he’s unlikely to play a character as iconic as Travis Bickle today. Perhaps the Nobu empire offers De Niro a sense of control, speculates PR guru Mark Borkowski, who has worked with Michael Jackson, Prince and Macaulay Culkin. “The parts inevitably narrow: patriarch, mob elder, grandfather. Nobu reverses the power relationship,” he says. “Here, De Niro says ‘Yes’. He chooses where to appear, when to appear and what bears his name. The business makes acting optional, and perhaps at his age optional is the only kind of work worth doing. In a curious way, it is still the same job he has always done: turn up somewhere beautifully lit, hit the mark, say very little and allow everyone else to project meaning onto him. The difference is that now he owns a piece of the room.”
Nobu has undoubtedly had a good run, but it isn’t what it once was. In the noughties, the Park Lane restaurant – the second in the world to open after Tribeca – was a celeb magnet, the number one destination for actors on the junket circuit. It’s part of the same building that housed the Met Bar, once the city’s coolest watering hole; 20 years ago, that 50 metre stretch of real estate was the most coveted in London. But the creatives have moved on: now the majority of the visitors to Nobu’s London restaurants appear to be international.
Robert De Niro: movies not to miss
Today the brand is courted not by the coolest cities in the world, but the ones that wish to replicate the aura of the coolest cities in the world. It is a brand synonymous with ‘placemaking’, helping to establish burgeoning destinations like the Egyptian coast that are keen to welcome moneyed Western visitors. “People are constantly asking us to be in their place to give them a certain cachet or credibility,” De Niro says in a press conference following our interview.
You could, at a stretch, liken the trajectory of Nobu to De Niro’s film career. He was an unstoppable heavyweight during the 1980s and 1990s, when his collaborations with Martin Scorsese on Goodfellas, Taxi Driver, Raging Bull and Casino made him the most in-demand actor in Hollywood. But his post-2000s career has been more hit-and-miss: his latest straight-to-Netflix thriller The Whisper Man was slated by critics (the Guardian accused him of “sleepwalking” through the movie). His 2025 mob film The Alto Knights also landed badly. His first TV lead, in Netflix thriller Zero Day, in which he played a former US president, received mixed reviews. The last clear hit was 2023’s Killers of the Flower Moon, in which De Niro played an ageing cattle rancher orchestrating a series of murders of Osage tribe members; it is no coincidence the project reunited him with Scorsese for the first time since The Irishman in 2019.
Early 70s breakout
Born in Manhattan in 1943 and raised in Greenwich Village, De Niro’s parents Virginia Admiral and Robert De Niro Senior were prominent abstract expressionist painters and poets (they separated when De Niro was two and his dad came out as gay). Initially a shy child, he starred in a school production of The Wizard of Oz aged 10, which helped develop his confidence. He dropped out of high school aged 16 to study acting and took his first paid role that same year in a production of Chekhov’s The Bear. Delivering food and doing extra work to bring in money while auditioning and landing bit part roles, he secured his breakout in Mean Streets in 1973, the first of ten films he made with Scorsese, who grew up in the same New York neighbourhood as De Niro. His role as ‘Johnny Boy’ Civello was a meteoric success, both critically and at the box office, establishing De Niro’s reputation for depicting violent men.
The year Robert De Niro met Nobu
His method acting style would go on to be filtered through a raft of intense, highly physical roles before he softened a little in the late-1990s, shifting towards more comedic parts, such as retired CIA counterintelligence officer Jacky Byrnes in Meet the Parents.
Two significant turning points happened in 1988: De Niro met chef Nobu, and that same year the actor first pushed away from action and into light comedy with the release of Midnight Run (Nobu took six years to come around to opening a restaurant called ‘Nobu’, which eventually launched in 1994).
Two weeks after my interview, I book into the restaurant at Nobu Portman Square. It feels slightly less exciting entering the imposing glass building this time, but only a bit: it really is a stunning place. I order chef Nobu’s signature omakase menu, on which many of the dishes haven’t changed since the 1990s, including the superlative black cod miso that he popularised during the restaurant’s heyday. House music plays as I eat my way through salmon tartare with caviar and a tiny Japanese wakamomo peach. The glamorous, moody interior is softened by floor-to-ceiling views of the trees outside. If there’s anything to criticise, it is the service, which is not at the level you’d expect.
Can I remind you he is 83?
The brand’s impending push into the wellness space feels on-the-nose, given the age of the men behind it. What does wellness look like to a man like De Niro, especially given conversations surrounding longevity? He’s explaining that he’s keen to visit the site in Rutland but hasn’t been yet, when an agitated PR runs in from the other room to close down this topic of conversation. My questions have been heavily vetted and I’ve been instructed to speak only about the Egyptian hotel launches. Time for my final question, she says, despite there still being a quarter of my interview left. The question doesn’t appear to bother De Niro, though. After I finish recording, instead of bolting, he walks past the publicists to shake my hand and tell me to “take care”.
Unlike stars half his age, who tend to disappear into waiting Mercs to the airport, De Niro goes from our interview to a conference to talk about the Nobu projects in Egypt. Then he had a cocktail reception. Then, in the evening, he has dinner with 30 or 40 journalists and industry figures. In the foyer before the conference, property writers more used to penning dry business-to-business stories could barely contain their excitement at a chance to spot such a huge star. When it comes to promoting a brand, this level of commitment is practically unheard of. Can I remind you that he is 83?
Staying active into old age embodies a Japanese concept called ‘ikigai’, which chef Nobu himself practices. At 77, some years he still travels for 10 months out of the twelve. Perhaps De Niro’s dedication to Nobu – meeting journalists, architects and business people, scoping out new developments – is his way of keeping the lights on.

items.title: Asos customers receive ‘hack’ notification threatening to leak data
items.summary: Push message claims fashion company’s data has been ‘fully compromised’, but website and app remain online Business live – latest updates Asos is investigating after users of its mobile app received a notification claiming hackers had “fully compromised” the online fashion retailer’s data. The value of Asos’s shares on the London Stock Exchange dived more than 14% after thousands of customers received a notification titled “Asos hacked” with a link that sent them to the Telegram messaging service. Continue reading...
items.body:
Asos is investigating after users of its mobile app received a notification claiming hackers had “fully compromised” the online fashion retailer’s data.
The value of Asos’s shares on the London Stock Exchange dived more than 14% after thousands of customers received a notification titled “Asos hacked” with a link that sent them to the Telegram messaging service.
The website and app appeared to be continuing to operate on Tuesday morning and it is understood that Asos is still investigating whether any hack has taken place.
The message sent out to customers said: “Dear Asos DPO [data protection officer] and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance.”
Snowflake is a cloud platform used to store, process and analyse data including transactions and demographic information such as clothing sizes and body measurements. It also enables push notifications to clients’ phones.
Dray Agha, the senior manager of security operations at Huntress, an online security firm, said: “Snowflake is a massive cloud database where retailers typically store sensitive customer information – it is a real worry if cyber criminals have indeed accessed it as they claim. The push notification suggests attackers have breached the systems controlling the Asos mobile app also..”
The link directed Asos customers to a telegram channel operated by an apparent cyber gang called the Xuanye group. Cyber experts said they had not heard of the group before and the push notification might be an attempt to grab wider attention.
“It’s not unusual to see new groups emerge, and often they wait until they have what they see as a significant opportunity before they announce themselves so as to enter the ecosystem with ‘credibility’, ” said Aiden Sinnot, the principal threat researcher at the cybersecurity firm Sophos.
Xuanye has not been mentioned before on hacker forums or other Telegram channels. Sophos added.
Marijus Briedis, the chief technology officer at the online service provider NordVPN, said: “What customers should be particularly alert to now is what happens next. High-profile cyber incidents create ideal conditions for phishing attacks. Criminals may exploit the publicity by sending emails and texts claiming to be from Asos, perhaps asking customers to reset a password, confirm payment details, check an order or claim a refund.”
The potential hack comes after a string of British retailers including Marks & Spencer, the Co-op and Harrods suffered cyber incidents last year. M&S and the Co-op experienced stock shortages and the former was forced to close its website for several weeks as it battled to ensure its systems were clean.

items.title: Vape display ban would cost local shops more than £160m, says ACS
items.summary: The Association of Convenience Stores (ACS) has called on the government to scrap plans to introduce a tobacco-style display ban on vape and nicotine products, criticising the proposals as expensive and unnecessary. The government is currently consulting on the introduction of a range of restrictions… This story continues at Vape display ban would cost local shops more than £160m, says ACS Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
The government is currently consulting on the introduction of a range of restrictions on the vape and nicotine category, including plain packaging on both vape boxes and vape devices, as well as a complete ban on the display of vape and nicotine products in shops.
ACS has estimated that a full vape display ban would cost the convenience sector over £160m in installation costs alone. This is in stark contrast to the government’s own impact assessment on the proposals, which suggested that the cost of fitting new gantries would cost each store just £151.20.
In its submission to the consultation, ACS has acknowledged the need to move vapes behind the shop counter, but does not support covered vape displays similar to those in place for tobacco products.
ACS chief executive Ed Woodall said: “A full display ban on vapes is an expensive and unnecessary overreach. If the government is committed to plain vape packaging and devices to stop them being visually appealing, there’s no extra benefit to putting those plain packs out of sight. The right approach is a common sense one that doesn’t cost every local shop thousands of pounds and weeks of unnecessary disruption fitting additional gantries.”
The government’s proposals would not allow retailers to put vapes and tobacco products in the same gantry, as retailers would not be allowed to temporarily display tobacco when someone asks for a vape, and vice versa.
The proposed timeline for the introduction of these measures is also impractical. The government has suggested that a display would be introduced just six months after the regulations were introduced to parliament, giving retailers very little time to book in shopfitters and adapt their businesses.
Woodall continued: “The six month timeline for implementation is completely impractical. We know from the introduction of the tobacco display ban over a decade ago that shopfitters get booked very quickly, leaving thousands of retailers scrambling to find temporary solutions at short notice.
“If stores can keep their displays on and behind the till then a year will be sufficient to adapt, but a full display ban will need at least two years to allow everyone time to comply.”

items.body:
From mid-October, ECOVACS’ latest OZMO ROLLER 3.0 technology will be available in physical retail across the UK and Ireland, with models including the DEEBOT X12S OmniCyclone expanding into AO, Argos, and Marks Electrical.
The move follows the initial online availability of previous ECOVACS models for the UK and Ireland. Bringing its latest roller technology into physical stores gives shoppers the opportunity to see how roller technology works in action and how it differs from more traditional dual-disc mopping systems.
The expansion comes as roller tech already accounts for over half (56%) of ECOVACS’ unit sales in Europe, and as consumer interest in robot vacuum technology continues to grow. In fact, online searches for ‘best robot vacuum’ up 129% in the UK and 243% in Ireland over the past year.
Graham Mitchell, sales manager UK & Ireland at ECOVACS, said: “Consumers are becoming more interested in how a robot actually cleans, rather than simply whether it can vacuum and mop. That’s creating more interest in the technology underneath these products and why new techniques, such as roller mopping, can make a difference.’
Why are robot mops moving beyond spinning pads?
Traditional robot mopping typically uses two rotating pads to clean hard floors but these pick up dirt and spread it around. OZMO ROLLER 3.0 technology uses a continuously rotating roller that self-cleans in real time, with no risk of wastewater returning to the floor. When coupled with FocusJet Technology, stubborn dirt and stains are washed away with ease.
What does the shift mean for the wider robot cleaning market?
For ECOVACS, roller mopping forms part of a wider portfolio of robotics spanning both indoor and outdoor environments. The company, recently named the No.1 brand in global home robotics by Forbes China, has expanded from robotic floor cleaning into areas including window cleaning, lawn care and pool cleaning, applying its robotics technology to different household environments.
The UK and Ireland retail expansion gives consumers greater access to one of the latest developments in robotic mopping, while marking another step in the wider adoption of more specialised robotic cleaning technologies.

items.body:
Today, leading accessible health and beauty retailer, Superdrug, is proud to announce the return of its fundraising campaign for mental health charity Mind, with a target of raising £150,000 through customer donations this autumn.
Running from 7 October to 3 November 2026, the campaign will give customers the opportunity to donate to Mind through Pennies at Superdrug tills. By making giving part of an everyday shop, customers can help fund Mind’s work supporting people experiencing mental health problems.
Now in its second year, the campaign supports Mind, the charity chosen by Superdrug colleagues following a vote across the business. This year’s initiative aims to raise £150,000 to help Mind provide vital support for people experiencing mental health problems.
The campaign coincides with World Mental Health Day on 10 October and supports Mind’s ‘See Me Now’ campaign, which calls for everyone to be seen and taken seriously on the day they ask for mental health support. With one in four of us experiencing a mental health problem each year, and 1.6 million people on mental health waiting lists in England, access to timely support is critical.
Mind’s message this World Mental Health Day is that support today saves lives tomorrow. The right help can stop people reaching crisis point, but too many people face delays or struggle to access support that meets their needs.
Funds raised will help support Mind’s services, including its helplines and online peer support community, Side by Side, alongside its campaigning work and network of local Minds. Together, these help people access trusted information and support, while campaigning for better mental health services.
Superdrug trading director, Megan Potter said: “We’re proud to bring our Pennies fundraising campaign for Mind back for a second year. Mind was chosen by our colleagues, and we know how much its work means to people across our business and the communities we serve.
“Our customers helped raise around £300,000 across last year’s two events, showing the difference small donations can make when we give together. This World Mental Health Day, we’re inviting customers to help us build on that support, with the aim of raising a further £150,000 so Mind can be there for more people when they need help.”
Emma Ackerman, executive director of Income Generation at Mind, said: “We are incredibly grateful to Superdrug for their continued support, and for their pledge to raise awareness and funds for Mind during World Mental Health Day.
“Every day at Mind we fight for everyone experiencing poor mental health to feel seen and understood. A huge part of this is making sure people can get the right support when they first need it – not two years down the line. We also know the people delivering care and support want this change too.
“That’s why Superdrug’s support is so important. By raising money to support our services, campaigns and local Minds, we can reach even more people and work towards transforming the future of mental health support towards a same day access model so everyone can get the help they need, on the day they first ask for support.”
Customers can support the campaign by choosing to donate through Pennies when shopping in Superdrug stores from 7 October to 3 November. To find out more about World Mental Health Day, including where to get support, visit mind.org.uk/WMHD26.

YEEP! has reached 4,000 parcel locker locations across the UK and is preparing to roll out its new Generation 3 touchscreen lockers, as the business moves into its next stage of growth. The company, which operated just over 2,250 locations when Jamie Dickinson was appointed CEO in December last year, is now aiming to reach […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! items.body:
YEEP! has reached 4,000 parcel locker locations across the UK and is preparing to roll out its new Generation 3 touchscreen lockers, as the business moves into its next stage of growth.
The company, which operated just over 2,250 locations when Jamie Dickinson was appointed CEO in December last year, is now aiming to reach 5,000 by the end of 2026, with significant funding and plans in place to support its accelerated expansion.
The developments follow a year of transformation at YEEP!, building on the foundations established during its first phase and preparing the business for the demands of operating a significantly larger open network.
Under the leadership of Jamie Dickinson, the work has included strengthening the senior leadership team, significant investment in YEEP!’s locker hardware and customer experience and developing its own technology to manage the deployment and day-to-day operation of a growing estate.
The forthcoming Generation 3 touchscreen locker rollout is one of the most visible results of that investment. Developed with YEEP!’s hardware partner and shareholder kernTerminal AG, Generation 3 combines the company’s solar and battery-powered technology with a new touchscreen interface designed to significantly improve the experience for both delivery drivers and consumers.
All new YEEP! lockers will move to the Generation 3 specification from 2 November 2026, with a programme to upgrade the existing estate by end of Q1 2027. The new generation follows YEEP!’s progression from its original battery-powered lockers to its subsequent move to solar battery technology. YEEP! has also drawn on kernTerminal’s experience of locker testing and deployment across Europe in developing the latest product for the UK market.
Alongside the hardware, YEEP! has developed a bespoke operating system designed around the requirements of an open locker network. The system manages site surveys, installation, scheduling, maintenance and upgrades, giving YEEP! greater visibility and control as the network scales.
Jamie Dickinson, CEO of YEEP!, said: “Reaching 4,000 locations is a big milestone for YEEP!, and the launch of Generation 3 gives us another reason to be excited about where the business is heading.
We’ve learnt a great deal from operating the network and from our work with kernTerminal, and we’ve used that experience to improve how the locker works for the people who interact with it every day, whether that’s a driver delivering parcels or a consumer collecting or returning one.
At the same time, we’ve invested behind the scenes, and we now have the product, people, systems, funding and plan in place to support our growth. Our next milestone is 5,000 lockers, but we are building YEEP! with a much larger network in mind.”
The investment comes as the UK out-of-home delivery market continues to expand and competition across the sector increases. As parcel lockers become a more established part of the delivery and returns mix, YEEP! is growing its open network to serve multiple carriers, combining wider coverage with continued investment in service and reliability. Its solar and battery-powered technology also allows lockers to be installed without a mains electricity connection, giving the company greater flexibility over where it can deploy.
Alan Barrie, group board advisor at YEEP! and kernTerminal AG, said: “The first phase of YEEP! established the proposition, built the network and gave us a huge amount of knowledge about the market, the technology and what our carrier customers need.
Jamie recognised very quickly what the next stage of YEEP! would require. He has brought real pace and commercial focus to the business, strengthened the team and been very clear about where we need to invest. At the same time, he has kept a close eye on the detail, particularly around the product and the experience we deliver for carriers and their customers. We’ve reached 4,000 lockers, but there’s a lot more to come.”

items.title: ASOS app users receive push notifications apparently sent by hackers
items.summary: Dozens of people appear to have received a strange message from the clothing and beauty store's app.
items.body:
ASOS app users receive push notifications apparently sent by hackers
- Published
Asos users across the UK have been sent pop-up messages from its app that appear to have been sent by hackers trying to extort the company.
Dozens of people have told the BBC about receiving a strange message from the clothing and beauty store's app, appearing on their phone screens.
"Dear ASOS DPO and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance. Engage with us, or we will leak it," the message reads.
Asos did not immediately respond to the BBC's requests for comment.
"If confirmed, this is a deeply serious attack because the hackers appear to have done something particularly brazen: turned ASOS's own app into their ransom note," says Charlotte Wilson, head of enterprise at cyber-security firm Check Point.
"Millions of people trust notifications from apps on their phones because they are supposed to come directly from the company."
Extortion message
On social media, dozens of people have posted about receiving the message - confused as to what it means.
Although the apparent extortion message has been issued directly to customers, it is addressed to Asos' data protection officer (DPO) and IT team.
The message claims the unnamed hackers have "fully compromised the Snowflake instance".
This refers to the data storage company Snowflake, whose tools are used by dozens of firms for collecting, analysing and storing data.
It is not known if ASOS is a customer of Snowflake or what data, if any, is stored with the service.
But Snowflake has been the subject of many high profile data breaches in recent years and has been linked to incidents targeting services including Ticketmaster and Santander.
It is, however, very unusual for a data breach to be revealed quite so publicly - and for customers to be informed in this manner.
Most extortions and negotiations by cyber criminals are conducted in private, with hackers hoping their discretion will result in a quiet pay-off.
The pop up message contains a link to the hackers' Telegram channel.
The new group is calling itself Xuanye Group and only created its Telegram channel today.
They have posted only three times with the latest being about the ASOS hack.
Dan Bird, from cyber security firm Horizon3 says the pop up message the criminals sent implies that their access has gone beyond the Snowflake database.
"Sending a push notification to ASOS's app users would require access to the company's notification system, which is separate from the Snowflake data platform the attackers claim to have compromised."
"If both claims hold up, it suggests the attackers got hold of credentials that opened more than one door," he said.

The Hidden Disabilities Sunflower is a globally recognised symbol that […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
The Perfume Shop, the UKs largest specialist perfume retailer, has become the first dedicated perfume retailer in the UK to join the Hidden Disabilities Sunflower, as part of a wider programme of changes designed to make its stores more accessible for customers with non-visible disabilities.
The Hidden Disabilities Sunflower is a globally recognised symbol that allows people with non-visible disabilities, conditions or health needs to discreetly indicate that they may need additional support, understanding, patience or flexibility when shopping in store.
The rollout will see quiet shopping hours introduced across all stores, with music turned off during designated periods to create a calmer shopping environment, while accessibility information including hearing loops, step-free access and quiet shopping times will be made easier for customers to find.
Alongside the customer-facing changes, The Perfume Shop has developed a dedicated Non-Visible Disabilities Policy, introduced workplace adjustment passports for its people and launched mandatory training across the business to improve awareness and understanding of non-visible disabilities. These changes form part of The Perfume Shop’s wider commitment to embedding greater inclusion and accessibility across every part of the business.
Michelle Fellows, people, sustainability and development director at The Perfume Shop, said: “Through listening to our people, we’ve learnt that hidden disabilities affect many across our business, whether directly or through the experiences of family members, friends and wider networks. That insight has helped shape our approach, and joining the Hidden Disabilities Sunflower is an important step in making our support more intentional and visible.
“We want everyone who visits The Perfume Shop, as well as our team, to feel confident that their individual needs will be understood and supported. For our customers, that means creating a more accessible shopping experience, while for our team it means building an inclusive working environment where people feel respected, supported and able to thrive.
“This is not a one-off initiative, but part of an ongoing commitment to listening to our people, learning from their experiences and continually improving how we support people with hidden disabilities across every part of our business.”
Paul White, CEO, at Hidden Disabilities Sunflower said: “We are delighted to welcome the first perfume retailer, The Perfume Shop, as members of the Sunflower. Employees with non-visible disabilities will benefit from Sunflower training, helping make the workplace more inclusive. The shopping experience should be pleasurable, but the lights, music and smells, as well as accessing the actual stores, can be barriers for many people with non-visible disabilities. Sunflower wearers who visit will now be acknowledged with an offer of support and understanding so they feel confident to return again and again.”
The membership will launch across The Perfume Shop on 5 October 2026, supported by updated customer communications, colleague awareness activity and in-store information throughout the business.

items.title: Holiday shoppers are making brands earn every purchase, with AI helping them find what’s worth buying

Shopify today launched its 2026 Holiday Retail report, revealing the traits of today’s discerning, savvy shopper, and how businesses can win them over. Consumers are entering the season under significant economic pressure, with 53% of UK shoppers saying recent conditions have negatively affected their shopping plans. Yet spending continues, as planned Black Friday weekend spending across […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Shopify today launched its 2026 Holiday Retail report, revealing the traits of today’s discerning, savvy shopper, and how businesses can win them over.
Consumers are entering the season under significant economic pressure, with 53% of UK shoppers saying recent conditions have negatively affected their shopping plans. Yet spending continues, as planned Black Friday weekend spending across the UK is expected to drop to £165 on average from £181 in 2025.
Shoppers will still spend, but with far more scrutiny
One third (34%) of British shoppers have postponed a purchase in the past year because of increased living costs. To combat this, they are value-maxxing: spending more time researching, comparing and weighing up whether a purchase is genuinely worth it. Nearly nine in ten (86%) of UK shoppers say they feel more in control after researching. They’re also turning carts into watchlists. Over a quarter of UK shoppers (28%) said they deliberately leave products in their cart to see if the price drops. When shoppers did leave items in their carts, 32% said they return to complete the purchase when the price drops, while 29% buy after a discount code, voucher or special offer becomes available.
For today’s British consumers, value does not simply mean paying less. 54% define good value as receiving higher-than-expected quality for the price, while 38% say it means products having a longer lifespan than expected. A further 37% associate good value with earning bonus loyalty points.
UK businesses are hopeful, with 82% expecting higher sales over the holiday season this year (in line with sentiment in 2025), despite grappling with rising costs (45%), increased competition (38%) and disruption to supply chains (23%). In a season where every new sale will be hard-won, they are looking beyond the immediate transaction and prioritising long-term loyalty. Returning-customer discounts (40%), loyalty or rewards programmes (38%), and improvements to delivery, tracking and returns (36%) are among the approaches businesses say are most effective at building longer-term relationships.
“UK consumers have not stopped spending, but every purchase now has to earn its place. With 53% saying recent economic conditions have affected their shopping plans, businesses cannot assume that a discount alone will secure the sale this holiday season. They need to show UK shoppers why their product is worth choosing, make the path to purchase as clear as possible and deliver an experience that gives customers a reason to come back,” said Stephen Rogan, Head of Customer Success, EMEA at Shopify.
AI is becoming a new shopping companion
As shoppers work harder to find the right product, AI is becoming part of the research process. Nearly two-thirds (64%) in the UK are likely to use AI for at least one shopping task during the holiday period, most commonly to find deals (29%) or discover products and inspiration (23%). Shoppers still draw a line at handing over the full purchase, though. Over half (52%) are comfortable letting AI recommend the right product, and 41% would let it build their cart, but only 28% trust it to complete a purchase on their behalf.
And businesses are preparing for AI-assisted shopping: 45% are creating AI-generated content, while a similar number (45%) are prioritising AI-powered chatbots and virtual assistants. Meanwhile, 41% are making their stores easier for AI assistants to read and recommend.
AI users choose independent brands more often
In addition to becoming a powerful filter for helping shoppers decide what is worth considering, AI is also creating opportunities for smaller brands to stand out more. Nearly three quarters (76%) of UK shoppers who use AI most frequently are much more likely to choose independent or niche brands, compared with 45% of non-AI users. Heavy AI users are also much less interested in buying from mass-market brands than they were last year (59%) and are choosing more products that feel personal, intentional or considered (81%).
This creates a new opportunity for businesses that can clearly communicate what makes their product different. Forty-seven per cent of UK businesses are emphasising products that are unique or hard to find, while 38% are highlighting where and how their products are made, and the same (38%) are drawing attention to their independent or small-business status.
When thinking about what would make them reach for AI tools more, access to information makes the difference. Over a quarter (29%) of British consumers said clear prices and discounts would make them more likely to use AI tools, while 27% noted the ability to compare products against similar options and a fifth (22%) said clear delivery times and shipping costs would increase the likelihood.
“AI is changing the front door to commerce for UK shoppers. They are using it to discover new products and brands, creating a powerful opportunity for independent and specialist businesses to be found. To best benefit, UK businesses need to ensure the fundamentals are in place, from accurate product information and inventory to clear pricing and delivery details, so both shoppers and their AI assistants can understand what makes their products worth choosing,”Rogan continued.
With 44% of consumers expecting to split their shopping evenly between online and offline this season, while 32% will shop mainly online and 17% mainly in-store, connected data for a seamless shopping experience will be critical. This holiday season, the brands that win will not necessarily offer the deepest discount. They’ll be the ones to make their products easy to discover, give shoppers clear proof of quality and value, and deliver an experience worth returning to.

items.title: Global licensing industry grows 5.45% to reach $389.8 billion as Brand Licensing Europe opens

Western Europe, home to many of the brands, retailers, licensees and manufacturers gathering at BLE this week, accounted for $70.1 billion, […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Brand Licensing Europe (BLE) opened its doors today with new data from event sponsor, Licensing International, revealing that European sales of licensed merchandise and services reached $82.4 billion in 2025, an increase of 3.8%.
Western Europe, home to many of the brands, retailers, licensees and manufacturers gathering at BLE this week, accounted for $70.1 billion, up 4%, while Eastern Europe rose 3.2% to $12.3 billion.
Data from Licensing International’s Global Licensing Industry Study shows that Character & Entertainment remains the largest IP type in Europe, accounting for 53.5% of sales, followed by Corporate Brands at 25.5%. Some of the biggest increases came from Publishing, up 18.8%, Sports at +13.4% and Collegiate at +7.8%. At product level, Food & Beverage rose +15.8%, Software, Video Games & Apps +15.2% and Sporting Goods was up 12.7%.
The results varied considerably between individual markets. The UK recorded the largest overall increase of the four top reporting European countries highlighted in the study, rising 7.2% to $19.2bn, driven by sharp increases for Corporate Brands at +32.6%, Publishing at +25.1% and Food & Beverage at +27.3%.
- Germany grew +5.3% to $14.6bn, where Publishing was up 20.3% and Toys +15.8%.
- France reached $8.1bn, up 1.8%, with Music rising 23.8% and Toys +14.6%.
- Italy generated $5bn, an increase of 0.8%, where individual sectors moved considerably faster, including Sports at +23.9%, Publishing at +20% and Art at +16.7%.
Ella Haynes, event drector, Brand Licensing Europe, said: “These findings feel particularly significant against the wider retail picture across Europe. Licensing continues to prove its strength as a business strategy, delivering growth across four of the major European markets highlighted in the study despite continued pressure on consumers and retailers. Time and again, we see the power of strong brands and fandom come through in more challenging trading conditions, creating opportunities for retailers and manufacturers to connect with consumers through the characters, teams, games, artists and brands they love. There are clear differences between countries and categories, which is exactly why bringing the industry together at BLE matters – to share what’s working, understand where the opportunities lie and turn those insights into new business.”
Global sales reach $389.8 billion
Beyond Europe, global sales of licensed merchandise and services increased 5.45% to $389.8bn in 2025. North Asia recorded the largest regional rise at +14.1%, followed by LATAM at 7.6% and South Asia/PAC at +5.3%, while US/Canada remains the world’s largest licensing territory, accounting for 58.3% of sales.
Character & Entertainment was the largest property type globally, up 8% to $161.8bn, followed by Corporate Brands at $98bn. Sports climbed 8.5% to $44.4bn and Publishing rose 5.9% to $22.2bn.
Apparel led product sales at $52.9bn, followed by Toys at $46.4bn and Software, Video Games & Apps at $43.1bn. Of those three categories, Software, Video Games & Apps saw the fastest increase at +12.5%.
Maura Regan, President of trade association Licensing International, which sponsors Brand Licensing Europe, said: “What really stands out in this year’s research is the breadth of opportunity across licensing, from the continued growth of art and experiences to strong performances in sport, gaming and food and beverage. It’s also fascinating to see that, in the first year we’ve measured it, social media is already generating 16% of online sales globally. With 32% of licensed sales now taking place online, this gives us an important new benchmark for understanding how and where consumers are buying licensed products.”
Further evidence of licensing’s strength comes from new Circana data released today, which shows licensed toys continuing to significantly outperform the wider European toy market.
Across the EU5 (UK, France, Germany, Italy and Spain), total toy sales grew +8% in value year-to-date to August 2026, while licensed toys surged +20% – two and a half times faster. Licensed products now account for 35% of all toy sales across the five markets, up from 31% in 2025.
Sport has been a major driver, with FIFA recording the largest increase on the back of this summer’s Men’s World Cup and highlighting the growing opportunity for sports licensing within toys. Movie-related properties also remain strong, up 10%, led by Toy Story, with sales six times higher than in 2025, alongside Spider-Man (+47%) and Super Mario (+43%). TV and streaming-related licensing rose +15%, with newer properties including One Piece Live Action and KPop Demon Hunters driving sales, while Pokémon remains the #1 one toy property and is up a further 9%.
Melissa Symonds, UK toy director at Circana, said: “Licensed toys are taking an increasingly significant share of the European toy market, and 20% growth against 8% for toys overall shows just how powerful licensing can be. What’s particularly interesting this year is the breadth of fandom behind that performance, from the huge impact of the FIFA World Cup and established movie franchises to new streaming content finding an audience through toys. With more than one in three toy sales across the EU5 now licensed, brands and characters that consumers already know and love are proving to be an increasingly important part of what drives the market.”
Brand Licensing Europe takes place at Excel London from 6-8 October 2026. More details can be found here.

items.title: Asos customers told online retailer ‘hacked’ in phone alert
Asos shares crater after ‘hackers’ threaten data leak
items.summary: Asos shares have tumbled after customers were told the online fashion seller’s systems had been “fully compromised” by hackers. Users of the Asos app received a push notification on Tuesday morning titled “ASOS HACKED”, in an apparent attempt by the attackers to contact the company’s data protection and IT teams. Asos is understood to be [...]
items.body:
Asos shares crater after ‘hackers’ threaten data leak
Asos shares have tumbled after customers were told the online fashion seller’s systems had been “fully compromised” by hackers.
Users of the Asos app received a push notification on Tuesday morning titled “ASOS HACKED”, in an apparent attempt by the attackers to contact the company’s data protection and IT teams.
Asos is understood to be investigating whether any hack has taken place. Shares in the London-listed retailer fell by as much as 10 per cent following the apparent hack, to 439p.
“Dear ASOS DPO and IT, we have fully compromised the Snowflake instance”, the message read. “Engage with us, or we will leak it”. The notification included a link to a Telegram chat.
In a message posted on the Telegram channel, a user named “Xuanye Group” told users that customers’ payment information has not been affected. “That is all for now,” the apparent hackers said.
Snowflake is a cloud platform used to process data like clothing sizes and body measurements. This platform also allows the user to send notifications to clients’ phones.
It is not yet clear how the attackers were able to send a notification through the Asos app, whether its Snowflake systems were compromised as claimed, or how many customers may have been affected.
Apparent hack ‘brazen and threatening’
Reports of the notification emerged from users in several countries, including the UK, US, Germany and Australia. The incident could trigger reporting requirements if Asos confirms personal data has been compromised.
Under UK data protection rules, organisations generally have 72 hours to notify the Information Commissioner’s Office after becoming aware of a personal data breach where it poses a risk to people’s rights and freedoms. Those affected must also be informed without undue delay where a breach is likely to pose a high risk.
Marijus Briedis, the chief technology officer of online services provider Nord VPN, said the message sent by the apparent hackers was “unusually brazen and threatening”.
He added: “The attackers aren’t simply claiming to have breached ASOS – they’re publicly telling the company to engage with them or they will leak what they say they have obtained.
“What makes it even more concerning is how that threat appears to have been delivered. A message apparently written for ASOS’s data protection and IT teams has instead been pushed directly to customers through the company’s own app notification system.”
Asos has around 17m active customers globally and operates across more than 150 countries. The London-listed retailer has been attempting to revive its fortunes following several difficult years for online fashion, reporting revenue of around £2.5bn in 2025.
Chief executive José Antonio Ramos Calamonte had been making progress, with the group’s shares up by more than 50 per cent this year before Tuesday’s incident. Last month, Asos upgraded its pre-tax earnings target to between £150m and £180m owing to “materially improved profitability”.
British retailers have suffered a number of cyber attacks in recent years, with Marks & Spencer, Co-op and Harrods among those affected.
Asos was approached for comment.

items.title: Could an exit from Europe bolster Tesco’s UK dominance?
items.summary: Like a student nearing the end of their gap year, Tesco has careened across Europe, Asia, even the United States, and is now preparing to return home and settle down.  The supermarket chain, the UK’s largest, is weighing up whether to offload its operations in Hungary, the Czech Republic and Slovakia, with grocery rival Lidl [...]
items.body:
Could an exit from Europe bolster Tesco’s UK dominance?
Like a student nearing the end of their gap year, Tesco has careened across Europe, Asia, even the United States, and is now preparing to return home and settle down.
The supermarket chain, the UK’s largest, is weighing up whether to offload its operations in Hungary, the Czech Republic and Slovakia, with grocery rival Lidl among the interested parties.
This retreat from Europe, which Tesco could confirm when it updates shareholders on Thursday, would bring to an end the grocer’s globetrotting expansion and spell nothing but trouble for its British competitors.
Back in 2007, there was no land the supermarket chain did not think it could conquer. Sir Terry Leahy, who had then been Tesco’s chief executive for a decade, hailed the retailer’s expansion into the US as just one part of a “pretty ambitious” play for global dominance.
The supermarket hoped to generate more than half of its annual revenue from overseas markets within the following decade, nearly double the 27 per cent it achieved at the time.
“We keep looking at everywhere,” Sir Terry told The Times, naming India and even Russia as potential targets. “We are on the threshold of becoming one of the few successful international retailers. There’s plenty to do.”
Fast forward nearly 20 years, and there’s little still to do. With its “central” European operations on the chopping block, Tesco has already withdrawn from France, Japan, Malaysia, Poland, South Korea, Thailand, Turkey and America.
The supermarket quit its US experiment in 2013, selling off all remaining Fresh & Easy stores, and the accounting scandal that nearly sunk the firm accelerated its turn inwards in 2014. Tesco’s Thai and Malaysian operations were sold for £8bn in 2020.
The group’s European division accounted for £4.5bn of its £66.6bn total revenue last year and was recently described by chief executive Ken Murphy as an “integral part of the group”. But the UK’s biggest grocer looks prepared to cut its losses.
European exit ‘logical’ for Tesco
Shareholders would be unlikely to shed any tears if Tesco confirmed this move later this week, analysts said. The supermarket is riding high in the UK, with a market share more than 10 per cent clear of its closest rival, Sainsbury’s.
Nicholas Found, an analyst at Retail Economics, told City AM that a sale of Tesco’s European operations would have “strategic logic at the right price”. “A disposal would simplify the group, sharpen management focus and free up capital for the UK and Ireland, where the potential returns are likely to be greater,” he said.
“The danger is selling a good asset too cheaply. Tesco has no pressing need to exit, so Ken Murphy can afford to be highly disciplined on valuation.”
Though Sainsbury’s appears rock solid in second place by market share, Tesco’s renewed focus on the UK could cause alarm for Asda and Morrisons, who have both struggled with hefty debt piles following private equity takeovers.
Investors will nonetheless hope to see renewed proof that Tesco is adding to its towering market share. The grocer’s shares slipped three per cent in one day in July, when the company revealed sales growth had slowed to just one per cent.
Market share softens
Analysts have blamed Tesco’s recent lack of market share gains on the recoveries of Marks & Spencer Food and Co-op, which were both flailing in the wake of cyber attacks at this time last year.
Tesco’s market share dipped from 28.1 to 27.8 per cent in the three months to September, according to recent figures from Worldpanel by Numerator. Though an improvement from its low of 25.6 per cent in 2020, Tesco’s market share today is far from its 2007 heyday, when it accounted for nearly £1 in every £3 spent at the checkout tills.
Tesco boss Murphy could send investors a further signal of its commitment to the UK market if it confirms its interest in Majestic Wines. Tesco is reportedly weighing up a swoop for the wine retailer, in what would be its first takeover move since it bought wholesaler Booker for £3.7bn in 2017.
Independent retail analyst Richard Hyman said a disposal of Tesco’s European business “clearly makes sense. The gradual divestment of its overseas businesses has allowed it to fully focus on the core domestic business.
“Interestingly, more recent market share has been surprisingly brittle. My view is this is a small blip but they need to reassure [investors] on this and how and why it’s going to return to positive territory soon.”
